characters.name: Sella Vail
characters.epithet: the woman who keeps the fire and asks no questions
characters.status: alive — thirty-three, keeper of the Vail fire; at the close of Day 440, Silt 16, Y.H. 814, Sixthday, keeper of the fire through three tending days lived one at a time, Silt 14, 15 and 16: the whole hearth grammar at both ends of every day — fire before basket, coals told the thaw and turned with the back of a broken pot, intake/hold/letting-go toward no opening with neither gap figured, finger on the shelf's top so the charcoal stayed unread, lips on a two-gapped row, one glance at the cold clay jar with the hand shut half over nothing and the little-door burn closing on air, twice-mended pot thumb-first with hairline showing and both proverbs to pot and fire, dressed grain turned under wool unfigured, pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, nineteen steps at the half-pace, seven walked-around places once and not twice, fold righted without a look at his face and no second fold. The widow's mark hung where it hangs on all three days — a tending day is not an opening and seven openings in seven months are seven and not a rule, no eighth came due. She told the fire it was the thaw on all three mornings and said nothing to the basket of Tarn's withheld sentence of Silt 15, of the hair-thin thaw at the corner on Silt 16 or of the softer river air, and carried him home at each going of the light saying nothing of what the yard had done or withheld. maps.title: The Bone Orchard — outside the north gate of Sill
maps.caption: The burial ground a league north of the Cross, drawn at walking scale along the north gate road: the rough-staked ground of the thin-return children's shallow graves, the east ground where pots are broken for the dead and left where they fell, the barrow of grey Ash that goes out through the north gate on every market-day and comes back empty, and the road running on through the gate to Cold Acre on the ridge with its six houses, its barley and turnips and its well that never freezes. The north bridge, the Ilm and Sill are drawn faint at the foot for neighbourhood only. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Ember, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor's notes on the barrow, the unslated graves, the pots broken for the house and the road that is clay to the ankle in Silt. An engraved broken pot in the margin.

maps.title: Cold Acre — on the ridge two leagues north of Sill
maps.caption: The farm hamlet two leagues north of Sill, one league beyond the Bone Orchard by the north gate road, drawn at walking scale: six houses and a byre in their drift-stone wall, the barley strips and turnip ground, the bare ring of ground about the well where frost will not hold and the children leave the untaken turn standing, and the well itself with its stone lip, clay dish, well-rope, eleven links to the water and the twelfth that hangs dry in the hand. The well-shrine and the children's stone stand beside the curb; a red nought marks the place where the thirteenth would stand. The road runs south to the north gate, Sill and the Bone Orchard drawn faint below, and east to the Tallow Works two leagues off; the frozen Ilm and the Singing Sill lie at the foot. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Frost, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor's notes on the ninety-four days of ice, the bell that comes up the ridge four, four and a gap with the gap not ours to fill, the assessor's column that has never held a figure, the barrow of grey Ash that goes past on market-days, and no Last Day on a ridge. An engraved clay dish set on a stone sits in the margin.

maps.title: The Cross and the Fishstairs — Sill's market and the steps below the north bridge
maps.caption: The ground the boy is carried over on every Account-day, drawn at the scale of the market: the market square with its stalls, the reading block under the moot-post and its finger's width of shade, the eight pigs on the weighing rail and the turnips left standing with figures beside them, the Court's table at the Slate Row fringe; below the north bridge the Fishstairs counting four steps, four, and the out-of-line landing, the edge of the fish-trade in the bridge's shadow, Rusk's room, the hard sill and the Singing Sill under the water, the dotted line of the Breaking, and the south bridge on the way to Low Kiln. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 813, the reed month.

maps.title: Greybank, the Court's gate
maps.caption: The Court's granary town eighteen leagues downriver of Sill, drawn as its own surveyors would draw it: the Ilm and its quay, the factor's house where the tally for Sill is kept, the Vhaleni Counting House with Veno Brine's private drawer of dry documents, the Court's granaries and banking hall, the winter ford, the burial grounds, and the ends of the Clay Road and the beginnings of the Salt and Hearth Roads. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.

maps.title: High Kiln — the glaze terrace above Low Kiln, Sill
maps.caption: The other half of Sill, drawn at the scale a potter walks: the terrace two hundred paces above the low yard with its barley strip, House Clay and the folded red cord and locked box, the Glaze Room where lead is mixed and tasted, the master potters' houses and their breathing kilns, the broken terrace lip, the steep street climbing from the north bridge and the Cross, the Ilm with its four-foot sill and Singing Sill, and Low Kiln below drawn faint for neighbourhood only. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.

maps.title: Sill and the Lower Ilm — the country of the birth-town
maps.caption: The clay country about Sill, drawn out a few days' walking: the Ilm from Nine Pots and the Ferr to Greybank, the weir, the Old Kiln, Cold Acre, Mud End and the Reedholt marsh. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.

maps.title: Sill and the Two Kilns — the birth-town
maps.caption: A detailed plan of Sill on the Ilm, drawn to the ground a child can walk: the four-foot fall and the Singing Sill, the two bridges, the Fishstairs and the Cross, Slate Row, Low Kiln with the Clay Yard and the Vail kiln-house, High Kiln and the Glaze Room, the family houses, the smithy, the meal mill, the wells and fields, the Bone Orchard and the edge of the reedbeds. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.

maps.title: House Reed and the Birth-flower Shrine — Low Kiln, Sill
maps.caption: The reed-cutter's house east of the Clay Yard, Alda Reed's dwelling, drawn close at the scale of a basket set just inside the finger's-width-open door: the one room with its hearth and slip pot, the bench by the door with a birth-slate propped writing-down, the board-bed whose grey wool holds a warmed stone at the belly, the grey Ash ridge left where it lies, bundles of cut reeds inside and at the threshold, and the loose board lifted at one end under which six narrow pages lie face-down in a second hand with no seventh written. A few paces east stands the birth-flower shrine, the hearth-maids' niche where the district's birth-slates lie overnight: five slates on the flat stone, a candle end of beeswax, a curl of grey wool, the slate-box of answered slates at its foot, and the crossed mark cut into the stone above, drawn and not explained. Around both, drawn faint: the Vail kiln-house, the Drawing house, House Silt, the smithy, the drying racks, the slip pits and the yard well; the Slip Brook clay-heavy along the north, the Ilm below, the walk the women take from the house to the niche, and the Clay Road west to the Cross and east to Greybank, with the reedbeds going off toward Reedholt. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Bone, with compass, a hundred-pace scale, a convention of signs and surveyor's notes on the hand that goes to the slate before the child, the mark for which a priest gave a date and did not look up, the six pages no Court physician has seen, and the date laid over a sign that no living person can take off. An engraved bundle of cut reeds sits in the margin.

maps.title: House Silt and the Birth Room — Low Kiln, Sill
maps.caption: The house three doors down the Clay Yard from the Vail house, drawn at the scale at which a basket set just inside the door sees it: the front birth room with its bench by the door, hearth and slip pot, board-bed of grey wool with the hollow where the pale river stone lay, the round pewter tin above the bed with its pale fold and thumb-bright rub, the shelf's chipped cup, the birth-slate and the six narrow pages turned face-down toward a floorboard, and the grey Ash ridge left where it lies along the skirting into the back room. There a neighbour scrubs at a board with lye water and a low song comes up through the floor. Around it, drawn faint: the Vail kiln-house, the smithy, the Drawing house, the drying racks, the slip pits, House Reed and the birth-flower shrine, the Slip Brook where Dessa Silt was taken, and the nineteen counted steps. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 813, the month of Tallow.

maps.title: Keld Keep and the First Seam
maps.caption: The Warden's fortress city against the Rim and the deep survey cut into the stone beneath it, drawn cold and mineral as the Keep's own survey-clerks would draw it: the walled Keep with the Warden's hall and the mine-reeve's room; the Rim Road coming up from Sill and going on ten leagues to the Cold Pass and its survey post; the Listening Stones five leagues higher in the Rim; and below, the timbered shaft of the First Seam with its galleries, the Descent, the Duelling Floor cut into the stone with nine clamps to the floor and the tenth behind the board, the survey room holding the crossed-out entry of Y.H. 588 and its branching red mark, the Ninth Gallery with the tin lined with warm-stone, a seam-serpent's passing entered only as a change in the numbers, and the hot-lead warning of the Sweating. Cartouche dated Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, with a compass, a league scale, a convention of signs and surveyor's notes on the measure before the name, the Warden's claim, the once-a-year reading of the paper, and the insistence that no map is honest past the last pass.

maps.title: The Meal Mill — below the south bridge, Sill
maps.caption: The water-mill under the south bridge, drawn at the scale of a sack set against the hopper: the Ilm coming down from the Cross with its silt shoals and tide ripples, the timber bridge, the race taking water from above the mill and the tail returning it below, the great wheel with its paddles and spokes, the two dressed millstones under the roof, the hopper with barley going in, the meal-book kept by the miller's daughter with a barleycorn shut in its fold, the toll-bag, the sacks white with mill-dust, the grey print at the corner nobody will own, and the brown silt tideline the flood left along the foot of the leaf. The Cross and Slate Row stand faint on the north bank, High Kiln above them, Low Kiln with the Vail roof and the yard well across the water, the worked strips at the east edge. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Ash, with compass, a scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor's notes on the mill keeping one hour and the stone another, the figures that go into the meal and leave nothing on the leaf, the early note entered nil in a factor's clerk's narrow hand, the foundling left at the mill with a stone under him and no name, and the crust that travels two inches from a boy's ear. An engraved barleycorn and an engraved dressing-pick sit in the margin.

maps.title: Mud End — the peat hamlet three leagues downriver of Sill
maps.caption: The peat hamlet three leagues downriver of Sill, drawn at walking scale on the dry shelf above the marsh: nine houses and their peat stacks, the byre where the moot meets and its moot-post, sods set out to dry, the peat cuttings in the southern banks, and a landing and punt on the Ilm. The Clay Road runs west to Sill and east the fifteen leagues on to Greybank, both drawn faint at the edges for neighbourhood only; the marsh drain comes down into the river, and Reedholt stands faint among the reeds to the south. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Grain, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor's notes on the winter peat that decides who stays warm, the man taken quiet in his sleep and called merciful, and the wolves of Reedholt. An engraved peat spade sits in the margin.

maps.title: Nine Pots — the rival kiln hamlet west of Sill
maps.caption: The pottery hamlet eight leagues west of Sill, drawn at walking scale along the road of the old feud: four kilns and one shared clay pit, the potters' houses and worked strips, the moot-post, and the road east forded over the Ferr toward Sill. Stonemouth stands three leagues east where the Ferr meets the Ilm, with its lime kilns and coarse sandstone workings; the blue-grey Lead Run comes in from the west, and the Rim Road passes north on its way to Keld Keep. Sill and Greybank are drawn faint at the east edge for neighbourhood only. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Ember, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor's notes on the feud, the lime and sandstone trade, the Lead Run that makes a man thin, and a cord from the Fishstairs never carried upriver. An engraved pot counted out at Nine Pots sits in the margin.

maps.title: Reedholt — the reed-cutters' hamlet in the east marsh
maps.caption: The marsh hamlet four leagues east of Sill, drawn at walking scale: reed-cutters' huts on posts on the dry hummock, the mud-wife's hut with its grey-wool knot, the peat-dry with its drying sods and lifted tally board, peat stacks, the boardwalk over a cut with one plank gone, the peat-hut, the Reed Cut and its cut bundles, and a landing and punt on the Ilm. The river road runs above the marsh toward Sill and Greybank; the marsh road comes down from Mud End, passes the hamlet and goes off toward the Quiet Acre and the Standing Post, both drawn faint or set down in notes. The black peat and the bog-cow are written in the surveyor's margin and drawn nowhere, for a figure would make a thing stand that does not stand. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Frost, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor's notes on going into the marsh in pairs, the reed-wolf's five clicks and the man with two fingers gone, borrowed ground and standing reeves, peat and grey weighed under an apron and sealed under a Court name, and the child cutting a first bundle in the dark. An engraved reed-wolf and an engraved count-stick sit in the margin.

maps.title: Rusk's Room above the Fishstairs — Sill
maps.caption: The old man's room above the Fishstairs and below the north bridge, drawn close at the scale of a hand laid on a drawer: the floorboards and their cold, the locked drawer with its small lock left shut, a bench and the stool nobody sees him use, the pot he taps for its note, the ice-mouse-fur coat and salt-stiff hat on their pegs, and the ash in the corners unswept; the window over the steps, the stair down, the four Fishstairs steps and the out-of-line landing where a fifth should stand, the bridge over the Ilm with the fish-trade shade beneath it, the Singing Sill and its four-foot fall, the river road upriver to the Weir and the Eel House and downriver to Greybank, with the Cross and its moot-post and Slate Row drawn faint at the edges. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Ash, with compass, a hundred-pace scale, a convention of signs and surveyor's notes on the man who never sits down indoors and turns a question back on the asker, the paper read once a year on the Last Day that no surveyor has set down, and the boy who turned his head toward a pot before anybody tapped it. An engraved key with its small ward sits in the margin.

maps.title: The Bowl of Sere and the Ten Bowls
maps.caption: The hot southern capital three hundred leagues south of Sill, drawn as a factor's clerk at Greybank would copy a southern plan: no wall worth the name, but open courts each with a fire in the middle. The great Open Court holds the public bowl emptied at the third hour when an act of the Sun-Emperor is announced, and the fourth bowl that is set out at every feast and carried away full; nine other bowl-houses of the Ten Bowls stand about the courts. The Ember bowl-house is drawn with its fire-shrine fed with bought oil, its wine-press, its counting room no woman enters and a room with good light; Solene Ember was returned whole here in 799, 804 and 809. The grain mills stand on the cut to the south with their wheels and sacks, the grain strips and olive grounds beyond, the bond-quarters entered without a name, the trace of a broken wall, the burning winds and their yellow dust. The Peat Line runs along the north edge, where the southern advance stopped in Y.H. 634, with the road going on to Greybank and Sill. Cartouche dated Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, with compass, a scale in leagues, a convention of signs and surveyor's notes on the announced act, the mercy of the Spending, the burning of the debt-slates, the two kinds of returned stranger, the clerk's three times above the space and the Sere account with a place where a bowl should be emptied and is not.

maps.title: Slate Row — the Court's quarter in Sill
maps.caption: The Court's quarter, a quarter league east of the Cross, drawn at walking scale: the Clay Road passing through the Row to Greybank, the steep street climbing to High Kiln, the Ilm and its reedbeds along the south edge. The Court's room with its bench by the door, pot, draught felt at the ankles and a place in the figures where a line should stand; the assessor's narrow house of Y.H. 776; the collector's table with its slate and cold-iron tube; the barred Waiting Room where the Forty of Low Kiln were held in Y.H. 812; the Court's table at the market fringe and the printed one in twelve. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 813, the month of Tallow.

maps.title: Stonemouth — where the Ferr comes down to the Ilm
maps.caption: The quarry village five leagues upriver of Sill, drawn at walking scale where the Ferr comes down to the Ilm: the sandstone workings and the lime yard on the rising bank, the lime kilns with their smoke, the ale-room beside the kiln, the village houses, and the weigh-clerk's bench by the landing with punts on the river. The river road runs east to Sill and west over the ford to Nine Pots three leagues away; the Lead Run comes in from the west stained blue-grey from an old working, and the Rim Road passes north-west toward Keld Keep. Sill and Nine Pots are drawn faint at the edges for neighbourhood only. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Grain, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor's notes on the lime, sandstone and reed-wolf tooth that go out by water, the Ferr that makes a man thin with no figure set against it, the thirty-year habit of stopping at the end of the part when a clean coat comes up from Greybank, and the name kept in a room against the name kept on a slate. An engraved reed-wolf tooth sits in the margin.

maps.title: The Clay Yard and the Vail House — Low Kiln, Sill
maps.caption: The close ground of Low Kiln drawn at the scale a clay child walks: the Clay Yard with its slip pits and ruts, the Vail kiln-house with its hearth, loaf shelf and bed, the wheel-shed with the Debt Loft and the finger's-width-open back room, the drying racks with the space beneath the lowest, the row of houses to House Silt, the smithy, the well and the birth-flower shrine, the Slip Brook behind and the Ilm at the reedbeds. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.

maps.title: The Drawing House — the death-house two doors down the Clay Yard, Low Kiln, Sill
maps.caption: The unnamed neighbour's house two doors down the yard from Vail, drawn close at the scale of a basket set at the edge of the light: the bench by the door with its pot, the draught going along the floor before the cold is felt, four nails, four and a thumb's-width knot overhead, the grey Ash ridge a finger's width thicker than Vail's and turning the corner by the door without a break. Inside, the drawing pallet against the far wall with the pale round place on the arm, the collector with the cold iron tube wrapped in wool and the slate face downward, a hearth, the folded quilt on the other side with the warmed stone at the belly and the pot set between child and door. The Vail kiln-house, wheel-shed, smithy, drying racks, House Silt, the birth-flower shrine, the yard well and the slip pits are drawn faint for neighbourhood; the Clay Yard and Clay Road run below, west to the Cross and east to Greybank. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Smoke, with compass, a hundred-pace scale, a convention of signs and surveyor's notes on the room that bears no name, the knuckle set before the iron and the note before the figure, and the child who grew worse before the day was out. An engraved cold-iron tube in its wool sleeve sits in the margin.

maps.title: The Empty Cantons — the Quiet Acre
maps.caption: The province sixty leagues south of Sill that the Court names the Empty Cantons and the Fen call the Quiet Acre: roads rutted under turf where no wheel has gone in eight hundred years, six wells dry with their stones laid in the old order, nine doorways standing where the walls have gone with bare squares above three of them and a slate unread in one, cold hearths with white ash unswept, dry cuts dug to drain, and a twelfth doorway left out of the count. Drawn from Gedde's survey of Y.H. 812 and the Greybank annals, with the south road from Sill and Cold Acre, the way in from Greybank, the marsh road to Reedholt and the Standing Post, and the Peat Line and Sere beyond. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 814, the month of Ilmen.

maps.title: The Hearthseat on the Keel
maps.caption: The Court's city, built over the Hearth a hundred and fifty leagues south-east of Sill, drawn cool and clean as its own surveyors would file it: the Weighing Hall with the grating of cold iron over the never-out fire and the Hearth shown in cut beneath the floor; Slate Row with the College of Assessors and its second file; the Steward's room, the sealed files, the bank where measures are pressed into newborn vessels, the rooms of fewer than twenty Kept, the back rooms, the printed notice, the Hearth Road from Greybank and the way out to the Nine Wells. Surveyed and filed in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.

maps.title: The Nine Wells — on the Keel
maps.caption: The close ground of the Keel's hot springs, five leagues short of the Hearthseat, drawn in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, when the road came up frozen hard enough for a cart and the steam stood a hand high over the water. At the centre the counting stone holds nine cups cut into one stone: five worn smooth with thumbs and open, named in the well-ledger as the child's lip, the bakehouse well, the stone-warmer's, the milk well and the last open with its copper bit unspent; four stopped with lead, six through nine, whose length the warming-song leaves as a silence and a clerk puts a round nought against. The dish stands on the whitewashed lip with lime bloom worked into its grain, warm-stone grit is ground small between the cups, the grey from the Last Day lies on the fifth lip, and a reader holds his palm flat to the stone while the woman who keeps it draws water and a clerk come up from Slate Row enters a nought. Beyond, four covered springs bear a stone and a ring of cold iron with no name cut upon them, and the fifth, sealed in Y.H. 618, keeps the keeper's hanged account carried forward. The Hearth Road runs up to the Hearthseat and down to Greybank; a south way goes by report toward the Empty Cantons. Cartouche with a starred border, compass, a league scale, a convention of signs and surveyor's notes on the two counts that do not agree --- four stopped on the stone, five sealed in the books --- the reeve's claim that the fifth spring lies under the Cantons, the keeper with no licence to draw a map, the bit put in and not taken out, and the struck line at the foot in a hand nobody will own: five were left open by a hand, four were stopped by another, and the steam does not tell which hand was kinder. An engraved key on a nail in a wool sleeve sits in the margin.

maps.title: The Old Kiln and the Ash Throat — one league south of Sill
maps.caption: The collapsed kiln in the grey clay a league south of Sill, drawn as its surveyor would draw it: the fallen crown and its broken brickwork, the fire mouth on the south-east flank, the flue broken at the top, the concentric throat where the ash runs deeper than a man, the hollow in its wall from which a slate was carried north to Low Kiln, the grey banks that will not take a glaze, the surveyor's stakes and his cord, the track from Sill and the marsh way to Reedholt. A slow coil copied from the back of a slate is inked into the margin and left unread. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.

maps.title: The Smithy — Low Kiln, Sill
maps.caption: The forge east of the Clay Yard, drawn at the scale of a man standing at the bench: the long low shop with no kiln-mark over its door, the forge hearth and bellows, the anvil, the bench with its chisel notches that nobody has ever entered as a figure, the kiln behind the bench answering four pulls with the fifth missing, three collectors' cold-iron tubes on their pegs with the grips polished grey to the thumb, Keldish bars with the blue bloom no potter will glaze over, the ash pit, the trough and the slate lying face down on a shop where no man would write a sentence. The yard well, the Vail kiln-house, the wheel-shed, the drying racks, House Silt, House Reed and the birth-flower shrine stand faint at the edges; the Clay Road runs west to the Cross and east to Greybank, with the Slip Brook and the Ilm below. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Frost, with compass, a scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor's notes on the tubes that take and do not give, the pale ring left at a wrist, the count kept in wood, the iron that comes down from Keld and the counting room shut in the last war eighteen leagues east. An engraved tube and an engraved anvil sit in the margin.

maps.title: The Standing Post and the Peat Paths — the Fenmarch
maps.caption: The only Fen place a dry man is shown: the carved post and the dry boards where reeves settle fines standing up, the reeve's stone with its peat-block niche, the loose board with the reed beneath, the huts on posts, the meres and black peat, the ways east to Mud End, south to the Peat Line and north-west toward the Quiet Acre, which is set down in words and drawn nowhere. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 813, the month of Bone.

maps.title: The Tallow Works — the rendering house two leagues north-east of Sill
maps.caption: The sheep-fat works known in Sill only by the smell on a north wind, drawn at walking scale: the rendering house or fat-house with its three vats, the hot flue and the thumb-wide warm crack where the wall meets it with grey paper nests hung behind, the lamp-room with its trimmed lamps and the leaf kept under a cracked saucer, the byre where the men sit at the turning of the year, the nest-fire at the shed door with the burnt paper beside it, the sheep-folds on the rise, and the sluice run carrying ash and wash-water away south-east. The ridge road comes in from the north gate past Cold Acre, both drawn faint, and the sweet smoke goes down on a north wind toward Sill. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Bone, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor's notes on the fourth cup poured under the bench and the clerk who set it on the floor, the wasp that comes to the warmth and not the fat with twelve nests burnt and no value arising, fever first and the cold after with no figure asked for, the coal that comes up in clay on Kindling and the Long Night's cost, the nought written where a name should stand, and the second warm crack in the cold north wall that has never held a nest and is set down in words but not marked on the wall. An engraved tallow lamp and an engraved tallow-wasp sit in the margin.

maps.title: The Waste beyond the Last Pass
maps.caption: A chart of report and not of walking: the Rim and the Cold Pass at the east edge, the survey post, and beyond it the cold seams and the coastlines of cold, with the uncollected sitting upright facing the way they came. No distance past the post can be trusted. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 813.

maps.title: The Weir and the Eel Traps — one league upriver of Sill
maps.caption: The eel weir on the Ilm a league upriver of Sill, drawn at the ground the trap-keepers walk: the V of stakes and its traps, the plank walk, Orra Weir's hut and salting-racks, the hearth-maids' blessing stone, the shoals and reeds, and the river road. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.

maps.title: The Worked Strips — the barley fields east of Low Kiln, Sill
maps.caption: The ground east of Low Kiln drawn at walking scale, the chart the lived days have fallen on from the planting of Seed through the cutting and dressing of Grain to the wool-covered grain of Smoke: five long rutted plots with their furrows and a flood stone a woman swept around, the clay-heavy Slip Brook coming down behind the drying racks, the reedbeds standing grey in the ruts where the barley stood, the Ilm along the head of the chart with its landing and punt, and the river road above the strips. Low Kiln, the Vail roof and its smoke, the drying racks and the Cross are drawn faint at the western edge for neighbourhood only; the Weir lies a league upriver, Mud End and Greybank downriver, Reedholt away through the marsh. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Smoke, with compass, a hundred-pace scale, a convention of signs and surveyor's notes on the arm that knows a bundle's weight and no slate its price, the clay-heavy rise that took a woman from the end of nineteen steps and was called weather, and the empty place in the returning line where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out — described in the margin and marked nowhere, for a mark would be a figure and no figure stands. An engraved ear of barley with its top grain gone sits in the margin.

maps.title: The Vail Kiln-house — the roof over the boy, Low Kiln, Sill
maps.caption: The house known by its objects before its people, drawn at the scale of a basket set just inside the door: the boy's room with its bed, one crust in the fold and four nails, four and a knot overhead; the other room with the carried fire under ash at four and a gap, the loaf shelf with two unnamed gaps and the charcoal beneath unread, the clay jar, the charred slate and the clean dark line beside the finer grey called the thaw. Beyond it the kiln at its mouth, the wheel-shed with the cold damper of two bites, the Debt Loft and the finger's-width-open back room, the drying racks, the flagstones with the bright patch, the yard well with its bare trough and the Clay Road going west to the Cross and east to Greybank. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 813, the month of Ember.

maps.title: Vhal and the Sallow coast
maps.caption: A salt-chart of the principal Vhaleni port and the five leagues of shore east of it, drawn in the tar-and-wet-rope manner of the Council's own surveyors: the Quay with its piers, crane, moored salt boats and the pulled benches; the Council room that smells of tar and wet rope, the tide-tally house and the glass furnaces within the town; the Salt Pans outside it with their dippers at dawn and their drying salt-paper; the blue-green Glaze Cliffs stained by old lead workings, and the glass-sand pits behind them; the silt-mouthed Ilm entering from the west and the Salt Road coming up from Greybank by the coast pass. In the sea the Sallow draw runs seaward against the wind, with a brine-gull, a salt boat and a salt-thing by report, and a surveyor's notes on boat-shares passing through mothers, contracts that rot in the damp, and children warned not to lick the cliffs. Cartouche dated Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, with compass, league scale and a convention of signs.

maps.title: The War of Measures — the eastern border country
maps.caption: A surveyor's chart of the ground the measure-wars are fought over: the Ferr valley and the lower Ilm from Nine Pots and Stonemouth to Greybank and the Sallow shore. Burned kilns, a poisoned well, collectors' boats on the Ilm and a district left cold for a season. The cold is drawn as the thing that advances. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 814.

maps.title: Sarn — the bowl between Hearth and Waste
maps.caption: The known world as its own surveyors would draw it: the Rim and the cold beyond, the Sallow Sea, the Keel and the Hearth, and the nations between. Surveyed in Y.H. 812.

maps.title: The Yard Well — Low Kiln, Sill
maps.caption: The most-named uncharted stage of the daily round, drawn at the scale of a pail set down on the stone where a pail always stands: the shared well of the low houses with its little roof, uneven curb, eleven links to the water and the twelfth that hangs dry in the hand; the white frost-bloom on the north lip where the Warm went out of the stone and the thawed edge where the sun took it off; the trough skinned bare and the silt-clouded plate of ice set on the flat stone out of the path of feet. At the bucket-round a woman draws with the pail against her knee and her hand toward her sleeve, the count kept in wood and unread, while a man brings a number up out of a shut fist toward the well and puts it back, so the figure arrives nowhere. The slate lies open on the lip with the writing turned toward its owner and nobody reading it aloud; the words spoken to the boards and the well-roof stand at five shapings with no owner standing under them, and the two tellings of the counting room shut in the last war do not touch. The Vail kiln-house, House Silt and the birth-flower shrine lie faint to the west, the drying racks to the east with the space under the lowest gone around, the Clay Road running west to the Cross and east the eighteen leagues to Greybank, High Kiln over the terrace above, the clay-heavy Slip Brook and the Ilm among the reedbeds below. Cartouche dated Y.H. 814, the month of Ilmen, with compass, a hundred-pace scale, a convention of signs and surveyor's notes on the water that tasted different, the number that is kept back, the pail that goes down into weather and the plate of ice standing where the weather was told to stand. An engraved pail on a well-chain sits in the margin.

codex.title: A Bowl Not Poured, Being an Account of the Southern Empire of Sere, Set Down by Harn of Nine Pots at Greybank in Y.H. 813
codex.kind: A journeyman potter's travel account, begun on the backs of dry grain-sacks and copied forward on the back of a Court tally-roll; part itinerary, part price-list, part complaint, with the figures of a Sere counting-house clerk entered in the margin and one line added in Greybank by a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at the factor's counting house in Greybank in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, by Harn of Nine Pots, a thrower's son who went down the Peat Line in Y.H. 812 with a cart of coarse ware, two bales of wool and nine bars of Keldish iron, and came back in Ash with a purse of gold crowns that no man in the Clay Yard would change. Set down first on three dry grain-sacks and copied onto the back of a discarded Court tally-roll, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a clay tube stoppered with wool. It survives with the yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the fold, a thumb of olive oil at the head, a wine-ring at the foot, a husk of southern grain stuck fast in the gutter, one crown pressed flat between the third and fourth leaf, four corrections in the leaning hand of a Sere clerk who borrowed the leaves at the market, and a line at the back in a narrow upright hand added after the copy reached Greybank.

codex.title: A Dry Man, Being the Road-Account of Tess Marl, a Hemp-Buyer out of the Quay at Vhal, Who Went Up the Marsh Road to the Standing Post with Money for Hemp and Came Back with a Count-Stick She Could Not Read, a Knot of Grey Wool She Would Not Untie, and a Figure a Clerk Set Against a Name She Did Not Give; with the Table of What Was Offered, the Law as It Was Said to Her, the Song Said to the Boards, Two Rulings in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A buyer's road account, set down first in the leaning counting-hand on the backs of spoiled hemp-warrants at the Standing Post and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court peat-docket voided by the Long Cold; the road and the figures in the buyer's hand, the Fen sayings kept in the hearing and not translated, a knot of grey wool tied through the first leaf for the word she cannot write, the verbs put back under every borrowed correction, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward
codex.provenance: Written in Reed and Tallow of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, at the Standing Post in the Fenmarch and again on the marsh road, by Tess Marl, a buyer of hemp for a rope-house on the Quay at Vhal, who went up the Salt Road with a purse of marks and came back with a horn-notched count-stick, a phial of Fen ash unopened, and an offer she did not take; copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a spoiled warrant and sewn with tarred net-twine into a scrap of oiled sailcloth. It survives with a white salt bloom at the head off her own paper, peat worked brown into the gutter, a press of wet sedge across the second leaf, a bog-water tideline that has taken two words, a horn-shaving caught in the fourth fold, a knot of grey wool tied through the first leaf which the writer will not undo, a fish-hook nick, a thumb of tallow at the fold, a small grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, one ruling in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor's clerk, one in the charcoal of a reeve of the Post, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own

codex.title: A Tide Not Yet Seen, Being a Letter Written in the Rain and Answered in the Margin
codex.kind: A private letter on salt-paper, from the Salt Pans to the Quay at Vhal, carried out in Ilmen and returned in Silt, with the answers of the woman addressed, one correction from a Council clerk, and a word of an older law stuck fast to the leaf
codex.provenance: Written at the Salt Pans outside Vhal in the second tend of Ilmen, Y.H. 813, by Enna Salt, a salt-worker of the pans, to Vea Net of the Quay, who holds a twelfth of a boat through her mother; carried along the Salt Road by a glass carrier, rained on in Silt, and returned with answers in Vea's hand and one correction in the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the Council of Tides. Kept since in a dry tin among what the house calls nothing. The leaf survives soft at the fold, with a white salt bloom along the gutter, a thumb of tar at the head, a green bead of cliff-glass in the lower corner, a nick from a fish-hook, and one word of an old Council decree that will not come off the paper.

codex.title: Before the Name, Being an Account of the Cold Kingdom of Keld Written on the Road Down, with the Prices of Iron and Warm-Stone, the Tally of Eleven Months, the Road-Song of the Carters, and the Correction Set Over It at Greybank
codex.kind: A factor's clerk's travel account in the open courtesy of Sere, set down in gold ink on prepared paper and copied at Greybank onto the back of a spoiled Court grain-warrant; the itinerary in the long-vowelled southern hand, the prices in a tally-clerk's figures, the Keldish sayings rendered into Grathic with the hard words left hard, a mine-reeve's correction written number-first in the margin, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Court clerk, and a line at the foot that answers to no name
codex.provenance: Written in the last tend of Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, on the road down from Keld Keep by the Rim Road, by Joren Brightbowl, a junior tally-clerk in the service of the Ten Bowls of Sere, who went north in Seed with a letter of credit and forty gold crowns to buy iron, lead and warm-stone, and came back in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with three bars of iron, a pig of lead, a fist of warm-stone, and the name of nobody who had warmed it; copied at Greybank onto the back of a grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold and carried on to Sill. It survives with gold ink worked into the grain of the first leaf, the yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the fold, grey stone dust from the First Seam along the lower margin, a ring of warm wine near the song, a hard crumb of Keldish barley bread in the gutter, a bump pressed into the third leaf where a warm-stone lay under it for a night, the mine-reeve's blunt correction in the margin, the Court clerk's correction laid over the text, and a line at the foot in a hand that answers to no name

codex.title: What the Ridge Keeps, Being the Sayings of Cold Acre, Gathered at the Well and Glossed for a Child of the Six Houses Who Came Back with a Figure in Her Head
codex.kind: A curb-woman's gathering of the proverbs, pail-maxims, limb-sayings and road-refusals of the six houses of Cold Acre, set in Grathic letters on the back of a barley tally spoiled at the meal mill; the sayings in the short Cold Acre speech with the ends dropped into the well, the glosses in the writer's own charcoal thinned with well-clay, with an assessor's clerk's correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a slate-woman's line set close to the birth-flower row, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Gathered at the well that never freezes in Cold Acre, two leagues north of Sill on the ridge, through the ninety-four days of the Long Cold and into Stone of Y.H. 813, by Gedde, who keeps the curb and the clay dish and has set a pail on that stone for four-and-twenty winters; written on the back of a barley tally a wet thumb spoiled at the meal mill, in charcoal ground with well-clay, folded into oiled sacking and tied with a spent length of the well-rope; carried down the ridge road in a hunter's creel and copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a Court winter-well warrant voided by the Long Cold, where an assessor's clerk borrowed the leaves for a morning and set his hand above hers. It survives with well-clay worked into the grain at the head, a white frost-ring that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a barley awn stiff in the fold, a turnip-knife nick at the fore-edge, a pale tideline of well-water along the gutter, a thumb of tallow at the outer fold, one grey hair from a hare's back shut in the third leaf, a grey Ash print nobody will own, a twist of well-rope fibre through a hole in the first leaf which the writer will not pull out, and the line at the foot which has never been claimed

codex.title: Eight and the Flat, Being the Counting Rhyme of the Clay Yard Children at the Drying Racks, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Listening, and What a Clerk Made of It
codex.kind: A rack-woman's gathering of a children's counting game, set down in Grathic on the back of a spoiled pot-tally; the counting-out and the tapping verse in the children's own half-sung speech, the manner of the play in the writer's small hand, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor's clerk come up from Greybank, a gloss pressed in charcoal by a woman who has fired a kiln for thirty years, and a line at the foot in grey slip in a hand that has not come forward
codex.provenance: Written in Tallow of Y.H. 813 in the Clay Yard of Low Kiln in Sill, by a woman who sets the coarse pots to the drying racks and has learned her letters off a broken tally; set down in charcoal and slip on the back of a pot-tally spoiled by a wet thumb at the third rack, carried to Greybank in the satchel of a woman come to have a widow's mark confirmed and copied onto the back of a voided weigh-slip. Kept folded in the rack-woman's apron among the slips of birch she uses to mark the wet ones. It survives with slip worked into the grain at the head, a green bead of lead-glaze in the fold, a pale thumb at the second corner where a woman with the sweet sickness leaned over to read, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, a tideline where the tally went damp, a twist of grey wool through a hole in the first leaf which the writer will not untie, the clerk's correction standing above the children's words, the kiln-woman's gloss in charcoal beside the flat one, and a line at the foot in grey slip in a hand that has not come forward

codex.title: The Mud Keeps, Being the Sayings of the Fenfolk, Gathered at the Standing Post and Glossed for a Man from the South
codex.kind: A reeve's gathering of the proverbs, board-maxims, counting-words and curses of the Fenmarch, set down in Grathic letters though Fen Cant is not written; the sayings in a thick half-sung English, the glosses in the reeve's own hand, with a factor's clerk's corrections in Ledgerhand and one line at the back in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Gathered at the Standing Post in Reed and Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Nib Peat, a reeve of the Post who learned his Grathic letters off an eel-trader out of Reedholt; carried down the marsh road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a spoiled weigh-slip, so that the two barks and the slip lie sewn with eel-sinew in a folded reed wrapper under the Post's loose board. It survives with a brown peat thumb at the head, wet reed pressed across the second leaf, a bog-water tideline along the gutter, a fish-hook nick, eel slime where a trader set his hand, a grey Ash print nobody will own, and a knot of grey wool tied through a hole in the first leaf which the writer will not untie. Two corrections are in the narrow upright hand of a factor's clerk who borrowed the leaves at Greybank; one line at the back is in a hand that is nobody's.

codex.title: Four and Four and a Slack, Being the Hauling Song of the Ilm Barges, Set Down Between Greybank Quay and the Sill
codex.kind: A barge-crew's hauling song in the low-country speech, shouted in call and response on the towpath of the lower Ilm and never sung coming down with the current; written in a steersman's hand with a burnt stick on the back of a Vhaleni tide-tally, with the count as the crew keep it, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor's clerk, a line in the leaning hand of a Council tally-man, and a verse at the back in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Taken down in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 from the mouths of the men who hauled a salt barge up from Greybank to the Sill, by the steersman of that barge, who learned his letters off a glass carrier out of Vhal and has no ink on a boat; carried folded into a coil of tow-rope and copied forward at the Fishstairs. It survives with grey silt in the gutter and pressed into the rope-fibre at the fold, a tar thumb at the head, a dark streak of eel slime along the foot, a white salt bloom on one corner, a nick from a boat-hook, a green bead of lead-glaze from a pot broken on the quay, a grey Ash print nobody will own, one correction in the hand of the Court's factor's clerk, and one line at the back in a hand that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Sayings of Grath, Being the Maxims of the Clay Country, Gathered in the Clay Yard at Low Kiln and Glossed for a Child Come Back from the Bank
codex.kind: A slip-treader's gathering of the proverbs, pot-bench maxims, firing-counts and household threats of the Grathic, set down in the common tongue; the sayings spoken low and said to the ground, the pot or the fire, the glosses in the treader's own charcoal hand, with a kiln-master's correction in broad charcoal and a Court clerk's figures in a narrow upright hand, and one line at the back in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Gathered in the Clay Yard at Low Kiln in Sill through Ash of Y.H. 813 and written on birch bark in the Five Cold Days at the turn of the year by Hesta Tallow, a widow who has trodden slip for one and thirty years and holds a small kiln by the widow's mark. She set it down because she had begun to forget one of the sayings and because a child returned thin to the yard would want to know what the house used to say; bark is used because a saying that travels must go where the speaker does not, and slate is for figures that stay put. It survives folded twice and tied with a strip of grey wool, sewn at the fold with eel-sinew got from the Fishstairs, with wet clay ground into the first leaf, a chalk thumb at the head, a scorch along the lower edge where the bark lay too near the kiln mouth, a small-ale ring, a pressed sherd between the third and fourth leaf, grey Ash in the gutter, and the sweet green of lead glaze at one corner where a woman from High Kiln set her hand

codex.title: Half a Word, Being the Rope Game of the Quay at Vhal, with the Ten Counts, the Held Turn, and What a Clerk of the Council Made of the Half
codex.kind: A net-mender's setting-down of a children's rope-skipping game in the low Vhaleni speech, written on the back of a dipper's tide-tally spoiled by wet; the words in the children's own half-sung chant, the manner of the turning in the writer's hand, a correction in the narrow upright counting-hand of a clerk of the Council of Tides, a line in the leaning tallies hand of a boat's clerk, and one line at the foot in grey chalk in a child's hand
codex.provenance: Written in Ember of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, at the Quay in Vhal, by a woman who mends nets there and holds no share in anything that floats; set down with a tarred needle-point on the back of a tide-tally gone soft on the face, the figures washed off it, and kept in the coil of a mooring rope under the net-bench, where tar and salt between them kept it out of the rain. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813. It survives with a white salt bloom at the head, a tar thumb at the fold, a green bead of cliff-glass in the lower corner, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, a rope-burn along the outer edge, one corner softened by wet where a tide-name went and did not come back, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the Council clerk's correction standing above the children's words, the boat-clerk's line in the margin, and the grey chalk at the foot in a hand that will not be claimed

codex.title: Hold the Next One, Being a Letter from a Physician of Low Kiln in Sill to a Physician of the Quay at Vhal, Concerning a Girl Come Down from the Glaze Room, a Child in the Second Chill, the Fever That Cooks, and the Figure Nobody Writes; with the Answers in the Margin, a Council Clerk's Correction on the Outer Fold, and a Warming Verse in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A private letter in iron-gall thinned with barley-water and charcoal, written in Grathic on the back of a physician's charge-sheet spoiled by a wet thumb, folded thrice and sewn with a twist of grey wool; carried from Sill up the Clay Road to Greybank and from there up the Salt Road in a salt-factor's saddlebag to the Quay at Vhal, answered along the margin in the lean salt-coast hand, corrected on the outer fold at the tide-tally house, and kept since in a physician's tin among the grey rags and the tasting-spoons
codex.provenance: Written at Low Kiln in Sill in the last tend of Smoke, Y.H. 813, by Vess, a physician who learned her trade in the clay yards and not at the College of Assessors, to Orrel, a physician of the Quay at Vhal who keeps the salt-wives' book and reads the Sallow draw at dawn; carried eighteen leagues up the Clay Road and sixty-two more by the Salt Road, answered at the Quay in the first tend of Frost, Y.H. 813, and borrowed at the tide-tally house, where a Council clerk set a correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand on the outer fold. It survives sewn and salt-stiff with a thumb of tallow at the head, clay slip worked into the gutter, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner, a pale line at the margin where a finger went to a gum and stopped, salt bloom along the fold, grey Ash in the creases, one word struck through with a chisel-point and written above, a column left standing under a clerk's *No such column*, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.

codex.title: It Stands and You Go, Being a Soldier's Field Notes on the Cold-Eater Beyond the Survey Post at the Cold Pass
codex.kind: A soldier's field book on one shape, set down as the record of watches kept at the post and not as natural philosophy; the watches in Grathic with the Keldish endings struck off, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled requisitions for warm-stone, a road-song as it is said going up and never coming down, a line cut into the edge with a tally-knife in a hand that would not write, a Court clerk's correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Ash and Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Harn, one of the Warden's men set to the survey post ten leagues beyond Keld Keep, who states what he holds before he says who he is --- six and twenty, and a hand that has never been entered; set down at the end of watches in the lee of the post with a lamp shuttered against the wind and a piece of warm-stone under the coat, first on spoiled requisitions for warm-stone and then on the blank margin of a rim-seam survey sheet, sewn with wire into oiled survey-cloth and carried in the breast pocket against a flint. Copied forward at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813. It survives with frost raised out of the grain on the first leaf and gone by noon, coal smut ground into the fold off the sleeve used to hold the sheet down, a flake of warm-stone shut in the second fold that kept its heat one night on a stone floor and is cold now, a small grey stone with a face worn smooth stitched into the gutter, a thread of blue-grey from a gift-knot, a tallow drop where the lamp was set too near, a notch cut clean through a word in the edge, the charcoal rubbed thin where the wrap lay against the breast, one cut line in a tally-man's hand, one correction in the Court's upright Ledgerhand, and the line at the foot. There is no Last Day at this post and nothing has been swept.

codex.title: What the Mountain Keeps, Being the Sayings of the Keldish, Gathered at the Shaft Mouth and Glossed for a Boy Who Came Up With a Number That Was Not His Own
codex.kind: A key-keeper's gathering of the proverbs, mouth-maxims, number-rules and hard refusals of the Keldish, set in the short Rim speech with the endings struck off and written in Grathic letters because our own hand is kept for tallies; the sayings said low to the rope, the stone, the iron and the count, and to a person last, the glosses in the writer's own charcoal, with a Court survey-clerk's correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a mine-reeve's red checking point set against one figure, one cutter's line struck hard in charcoal, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Gathered at the shaft mouth of the First Seam in Keld Keep through Bone and Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, and written up in the Five at the turn into Y.H. 813 by Marn of the Keys, a woman of a key-holding family who has counted at the mouth and kept the mine-reeve's keys for nineteen years; written in charcoal on the backs of seam-tallies spoiled by slate-damp, since a figure the damp has taken cannot be entered against a man, sewn with wire into a fold of oiled survey-cloth and carried down the Rim Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with a consignment of iron, where a survey-clerk of the Court's factor copied it at Greybank onto the back of a voided requisition for lamp-oil and set his upright hand above hers. It survives with iron-red checking paint at the head off the reeve's point, which is not hers and which she has not wiped off, coal smut worked into the grain, a shaving of warm-stone shut in the second fold that is warm on the coldest morning and is never lent, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead pressed into the lower corner by a man who would not say which gallery it came from, a cold-iron filing along the gutter drawn out of the clamp-rack, a frost-fern on the head that had gone to water before she set charcoal to it, a red figure written in the margin in a hand she has not crossed out, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which is not hers and which she has not swept, and the line at the foot which nobody has claimed. There is no Last Day beneath this Keep; nothing is swept in the morning.

codex.title: The Litany of the Four Sayings, Being the Order of the Return as It Is Kept at the Collector's Table
codex.kind: The Keeping's own order of service, in seven stations, said over the dying at the draw and again at the pressing; copied from a Weighing Hall order and kept at the collector's table in Slate Row, Sill, with the rubrics of the room, the four sayings of the Court, the answers of the house, the correction of a visiting clerk and the contrary notes of a woman who used it at bedsides
codex.provenance: Copied in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, at the collector's table in Slate Row, Sill, by the clerk who keeps the order there, from an order of service brought down from the Weighing Hall in the Hearthseat; set down on the back of a spoiled district tally, sewn with wire into a board cover, and used at the draw and at the pressing. It survives with a press of cold-iron filings at the head, a lamp-black thumb, a tallow print from a draught under a door, a spot of barley, a grey Ash print along the gutter, a ring of small ale and a hair caught in the fold, with two hands of correction upon it, the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the College of Assessors who borrowed the leaf on an Account-day and the thick charcoal hand of a woman who used it at bedsides. Copied forward in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the space left the length it is and the struck line left struck.

codex.title: Measure for Measure, Being the Sayings of the Bowls, Gathered at the Ember House and Glossed for a Boy from the North
codex.kind: An under-steward's gathering of the proverbs, courtesy-maxims, press-songs and curses of Sere, written in thin gold on prepared paper in the open courtesy hand; the sayings in the long-vowelled southern speech with the ends thrown into the fire, the glosses in the same hand with less gold in it, with the leaning corrections of a bowl-house tally-clerk, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor's clerk at Greybank, and one line at the back in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Gathered in Grain and Smoke of Y.H. 811 at the Ember bowl-house in the Bowl of Sere by Dalia Ember, an under-steward who keeps the fourth bowl, for a boy come down from Greybank who sat at the lower table and did not know when to applaud; written on seven leaves of prepared paper in gold ink, the sayings in the thick gold and the glosses in the thin; carried north in a glass consignment in Ash of Y.H. 812 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold, where a factor's clerk corrected it and put a nought in the margin; carried on to Sill and copied forward in Ilmen, Y.H. 813. It survives with gold worked into the grain of the first leaf, the yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the fold, a small wine-ring at the third hour, a thumb of olive oil at the head, a husk of southern grain stuck fast in the gutter, a green-glazed shard from a northern bowl pressed into the fold, one corner scorched where the leaf lay too near a court fire, a gold crown pressed flat between the fifth and sixth leaves, the leaning corrections of the house clerk standing above the glosses, the narrow upright correction added at Greybank above both, and a line at the back in a hand that has never been claimed

codex.title: Nine to the Floor, Being a Drinking Song of the Duelling Floor in Keld Keep
codex.kind: A Keldish floor-song in three parts, taken down by the clerk who keeps the numbers at the Duelling Floor; the verses in the hard Rim speech, the corrections in the verbless hand of a Court survey-clerk, one answer from the Listening Stones, and a lowlander's verse at the foot
codex.provenance: Written in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in the room off the Duelling Floor beneath Keld Keep, on the back of a survey sheet spoiled by wet slate, the figures on the face of it gone soft; carried down the Rim Road and the Clay Road with a survey party in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank. Kept in the floor-clerk's board box among the spoil slips. It survives with coal dust at the head, a press of wet reed across the first leaf, a smear of hot lead at the fold, an ale ring, a tallow thumb, a grey Ash print along the gutter, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the Court, one line in a hand that writes very large and very slowly, and a verse added in Grathic by a clay-man who had been levied to the Cold Pass.

codex.title: Nineteen Out, Nineteen Back
codex.kind: A work song of the slip pits and the drying racks, Low Kiln
codex.provenance: Taken down on a market morning in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, from the mouths of women treading slip in the Clay Yard of Sill, by a clerk in the factor's house at Greybank whose name has been rubbed from the corner of the sheet; the copy stands on the back of a spoiled Weighing notice, folded into an apron pocket, and survives with slip-stains, a green bead of lead glaze, a thumb in tallow, and the clerk's own square hand striking out one line. The song is held to be older than the Clay Road.

codex.title: The Number Before the Name, Being the Sayings of the Keldish, Gathered Above the Shaft Mouth at Keld Keep and Glossed for a Man Come Up the Rim Road
codex.kind: A key-woman's gathering of the proverbs, tally-maxims, iron-sayings and stone-curses of Keld, set in Grathic letters on the back of a shift-tally because Keldish is cut in bone and does not travel; the sayings in the hard Rim speech with the endings struck off, the glosses in the writer's own hand, with a Court survey-clerk's correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a notch cut in the edge where a word would not come, a carter's sloping addition, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Gathered in Bone of Y.H. 812, the year the lowlands called the Thin Year, by a woman who holds the mine-reeve's keys above ground at Keld Keep, from men waiting their turn at the weigh and from the old women who count at the mouth; written in charcoal on the back of a shift-tally gone soft at the fold, cut once at the edge with a tally-knife where a word would not come, carried down the Rim Road with a cart of lead in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a spoiled weigh-slip, where a survey-clerk of the Court borrowed it and set his hand above hers. It survives folded in the key-woman's leather key-pouch, with coal smut ground into the head, an iron-red thumb at the second corner, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead shut in the fold, a warm-stone shaving that kept a little heat through a night on the stone floor, a frost-feather pressed flat that was gone by noon, a tallow print, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the knife-cut standing in the margin, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody's.

codex.title: What the Returned Say, Being the Sayings of Those Who Have Come Back, Gathered at Greybank Among the Walking Thin and Glossed for a Woman Who Has Never Been Banked
codex.kind: A keeper of the return-slate's gathering of the proverbs, cradle-maxims, borrowings and small refusals of the returned, set in Grathic letters on the back of a spoiled return-slate because the mixed speech of the bank's lower room is written nowhere; the sayings in that mixed speech with a southern word left standing where no Grathic word will come, the glosses in the keeper's own charcoal hand, the correction of a factor's clerk in narrow upright Ledgerhand, the objection of a bowl-leech come up from Sere pressed cold into the margin, a cradle-verse with a place left the length of a name, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Gathered in Ash and Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in the lower room of the bank at Greybank, from people sitting between the drawing and the pouring and from those who had come back and had nowhere else to sit; written in charcoal on the back of a return-slate spoiled by a figure entered in the wrong column and washed with barley-water, carried downriver to Sill in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied onto the back of a voided grain-warrant, sewn with wire into a fold of oiled cloth and kept under the loose board beside the cradle. It survives with cold-iron filings at the head, a tallow thumb at the fold, a ring of barley-water gone dark, a browned crust pressed flat between the third and fourth leaves, a grey Ash print nobody will own, a small square cut out with a knife where a name stood, the clerk's narrow correction standing above the keeper's words, the southern leech's cold objection in the margin, and the line at the foot which has never been claimed

codex.title: Salt, Current, and the Ebb, Being the Proverbs of the Vhaleni Set Down at the Pans and Glossed for a Landman
codex.kind: A pan-clerk's gathering of the proverbs, counting-maxims, tide-sayings and curses of Vhalen, written in the leaning counting-hand on salt-paper the writer kept dry against the rule; the sayings in the sibilant low speech with the ends of words let fall, the glosses in the writer's own hand, with a Council clerk's correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand and one line at the back in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Gathered at the Salt Pans outside Vhal in Seed and Frost of Y.H. 811 by Tavi Hull, a copyist of the dippers' tide-tallies who learned his letters in a counting house and has never held a share; written on salt-paper leaves he kept dry in a tin lined with nothing, sewn with tarred net-twine, and carried up the Salt Road with a glass consignment in Stone of Y.H. 812, where the leaves were copied at Greybank onto the back of a spoiled weigh-slip and corrected by a clerk of the Council of Tides. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with the wet corner left wet. It survives with a white salt bloom at the head, a thumb of tar at the fold, a peck-hole where a brine-gull took the leaf for a crust, a fish-hook nick, a corner softened by rain where two sayings have gone, a rope-burn along the outer edge, a grey Ash print nobody will own, and a loop of tarred twine through the first leaf which the writer will not undo.

codex.title: The Courtesy of the Bowl, Being the Proverbs of Sere, Gathered at a Name-Day in a House of the Ten Bowls and Glossed for a Child Who Is About to Be Given a Debt to Carry
codex.kind: A courtesy-woman's gathering of the proverbs, feast-sayings, name-warnings and polite refusals of the southern people, set in the long-vowelled speech of Sere and written in Grathic letters because the house hand is kept for contracts; the sayings in charcoal, which is a woman's hand and not a clerk's, the glosses in the writer's own charcoal, with a bowl-house tally-clerk's correction in thin gold above, a factor's clerk's ruling in narrow upright Ledgerhand above that, a girl of the mills in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Gathered at the name-day of a daughter of a house of the Ten Bowls in the Bowl of Sere in Ember of Y.H. 813, and set down that night by Halia Gilded, a courtesy-woman who teaches the young of that house their names and their manners before they are sent up to the Bowl; written in charcoal on the backs of glaze-tallies spoiled at the third furnace, because gold is for what a house means to keep and a saying is for the mouth; sewn with a drawn thread from the girl's name-day dress into a fold of oiled silk and kept in the lining of the teacher's sleeve. Carried north with a consignment of glass and oil in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold, where a factor's clerk set a ruling above the gold. It survives with gold dust worked into the head off the tally-clerk's cuff, yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the fold, a ring of warm wine at the second leaf, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner, a flake of quiet ash shut in the gutter, a dress-thread gone stiff with gold in the sewing, a flattened crown between the third and fourth leaves which would not change at Greybank, a pale thumb where a girl of the sweet sickness leaned to read, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, and the line at the foot which nobody has claimed

codex.title: Seven Names and the One the House Keeps, Being a Passing Game of the Lower Court at the Ember House
codex.kind: A bowl-woman's gathering of a children's passing-and-naming game in the long-vowelled southern speech, written with a burnt stick on the back of a wine-list spoiled at the third hour; the rhyme in the children's own high thin voices, the manner of the passing in the writer's small careful hand, a house tally-clerk's leaning corrections standing above it, a factor's clerk's upright correction added above both at Greybank, a gloss pressed into the margin in charcoal by a woman of the wine-press, and a verse at the foot in a northern child's hand
codex.provenance: Written in Grain of Y.H. 812 in the lower court of the Ember bowl-house in the Bowl of Sere, by a woman who washes the small bowls and is not permitted to look into one of them; set down after the third hour with a burnt stick on the back of a wine-list whose face was spoiled by a spill, and kept folded under the stack of mouth-down bowls on the lower shelf. Copied forward at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of an unissued boat-share sheet from the tide-tally house. It survives with a wine-ring at the head, yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the fold, a thumb of olive oil, a fleck of gold leaf from a contract carried past on a tray, a husk of southern grain shut in the gutter, a crack along the fold where the leaf has been folded and folded again, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the tally-clerk's hand above the children's words, the factor's clerk's hand above both, a press-woman's gloss in the margin, and the verse at the foot in a hand that has never come forward

codex.title: Six and the Seventh, Being the Rope-Skipping Game of the Weir Children, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Turns, and What an Assessor's Clerk Made of It
codex.kind: A net-mender's gathering of a children's skipping game, set down in Grathic on the back of a dried fish-bill; the counting-out and the turning verse in the children's own half-sung speech, the manner of the play in the mender's small hand, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of an assessor's clerk come up from Greybank, a gloss pressed in charcoal by the woman who keeps the blessing stone, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward
codex.provenance: Written in Reed of Y.H. 813 at the plank walk above the Weir, one league upriver of Sill, by a woman who mends the eel-nets there, on the back of a fish-bill gone stiff with silt and sun; carried downriver in the creel of a girl come to Sill and copied at Greybank in Tallow of the same year onto the back of a weighing-warrant voided by the flood. Kept folded in the net-mender's tin among the net-needles and the spent lengths of line. It survives with silt ground into the fold and worked into the fibre at the head, a ring where a dish of water stood from first grey to the going of the light, a press of wet reed across the second leaf, one fish-scale shut in the gutter, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the clerk's correction standing above the children's words, a gloss in charcoal beside the seventh, and a line at the foot in a hand that has not come forward

codex.title: Six Under the Heel, Being the Treading Song of the Clay Yard at Sill, with the Rounds as They Are Trodden and What the Factor's Clerk Made of the Count
codex.kind: A clay-yard's treading song in the Low Kiln speech, called down into the slip pit and answered by the feet and not by voices; set down in charcoal by a rack-woman who treads slip in the mornings, with the rounds in the treaders' own words, a correction in the margin by an old woman who has kept the racks thirty years, the factor's clerk's ruling in Ledgerhand above the seventh round, and a line at the back in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Silt of Y.H. 813 in the Clay Yard of Low Kiln in Sill, in charcoal on the inside of a pot gone wrong that had split from lip to foot and been set by the wall of the wheel-shed for the sweeping; the charcoal went into the grain of the clay so that no scraping would take it out. Copied forward onto the back of a kiln-setting tally gone soft with damp, carried to Greybank in the pocket of a woman come to have a widow's mark confirmed, and sewn with eel-sinew into a fold of oiled paper. It survives with bone-pale slip rubbed into the head, a wet-clay thumb at the second corner, a green bead of lead-glaze in the gutter, a brown barley crust gone stiff in the fold, a tallow print, a tideline from the Slip Brook, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the old rack-woman's correction standing in the margin, the clerk's ruling standing above the seventh round, and the line at the back that has never been claimed.

codex.title: Sold, Not Lent, Being the Account of Veno Brine, a Buyer out of the Glass Furnaces at Vhal, Who Went Up the Rim Road in Seed of Y.H. 813 with Salt, Rope and a Contract on Salt-Paper and Came Down in Ember with Iron, a Warm-Stone Gone Cold, and a Number She Did Not Enter; with the Weigh at the Keep, the Table of What Was Carried and What Came Back, the Song of the Stone Going Up, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A buyer's road account, set down first in the leaning counting-hand on the backs of spoiled tide-tallies at the shaft mouth and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court salt-warrant voided by the Long Cold; the road and the figures in the buyer's hand, the Rim sayings kept in the hearing with the endings struck off, the verbs put back underneath every borrowed correction, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward
codex.provenance: Written at Keld Keep and on the Rim Road in Seed and Tallow of Y.H. 813 by Veno Brine, a woman of the Quay at Vhal who buys for the three glass furnaces; she went up with two chests of Sallow salt, a coil of tarred rope and a contract written on salt-paper, and came down in Ember with four bars of Keldish iron, a warm-stone that had kept a fire and had gone cold, a shaving of the same stone, and a number cut in bone by a Vorr which she has not entered. Copied at Greybank in Ash of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a Court salt-warrant voided by the Long Cold, carried up the Salt Road to Vhal, and kept since in the tin among the anneal-tools. It survives folded into a strip of oiled sailcloth, soft at the fold and stiff with salt by turns: a white bloom at the head that has eaten the tails off two figures, a thumb of tar at the crease off the coil she carried home, iron-red at the second corner from the mine-reeve's checking point, a warm-stone shaving gone cold in the fourth leaf, a slip of bone with a number cut into it that no clerk of ours has matched to anything, a frost-feather pressed flat that was gone by noon, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with a knife-point, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own

codex.title: Ten at the Racks, Being the Palm-Count of the Low Kiln Girls, with the Manner of the Clapping, the Still Hands, and What a Clerk Put in the Eleventh Place
codex.kind: A rack-woman's gathering of a children's hand-clapping game, set down in charcoal on the back of a spoiled rack-tally; the count in the children's own half-sung speech, the manner of it in the writer's small hand, a correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor's clerk borrowed at Greybank, a gloss pressed in charcoal by the woman who keeps the birth-slates at the shrine, and one line at the foot in grey chalk in a hand that has learned its letters off a slate
codex.provenance: Written at the drying racks in the Clay Yard at Low Kiln of Sill in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, of an evening when the racks stood half full and the girls clapped over a tally of wet pots; carried to Greybank in the pocket of a potter gone to have a kiln-mark renewed and copied onto the back of a weigh-slip gone soft at one corner. Kept folded in the rack-shed under the loose board beside the wheel. It survives with slip dried pale in the creases at the head, a tallow thumb, a chalk score along the fore-edge where a line was drawn and rubbed out, a small-ale ring, a green bead of lead glaze in the fold, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, the clerk's correction standing above the children's words, a gloss pressed in charcoal beside the ninth line, and a line at the foot in grey chalk nobody will claim

codex.title: The Apprentice Beam, Being the Standing Rules of the Kiln-Masters of Sill for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices, Read at the Cross and Nailed Beside the Moot-Post
codex.kind: A bench-copy of the guild's standing rules in the hand of the clerk who keeps the kiln-masters' bench at the Cross; the terms set in tables, the yard's wheel-song pasted to the back, two corrections in the Thane's narrow hand, one clause crossed in a potter's charcoal, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: First gathered at Sill in Y.H. 418, the year the Clay Road was made a Court road by the treaty of the Blue Cliff, and copied forward each generation from the bench rather than from a book; this leaf written at the Cross and in the Clay Yard of Low Kiln in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, and carried through the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives folded and soft at the nail-hole, with a thumb-worn centre where a hundred men have wiped their hands before reading, a green bead of lead glaze at the head off the Thane's thumb, slip dried the colour of old bone down the gutter, a tallow spot at the wheel clause, a press of wet reed across the song from a day the bench stood in the rain, a grey print along the foot that is not mine and is not the Thane's, two small corrections in his narrow upright hand, one line struck hard in charcoal by a potter who would not put his name to it, and one line at the foot nobody will own.

codex.title: The Arm and the Cord, Being the Standing Rules of the Reed-Cutters of the Weir for the Taking, Walking, Cutting and Trying of Apprentices in the Beds Below Sill, with the Table of Walkings, the Bundle-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A cutter's leaf of rules carried in the lining of a coat against the leading rope; the rules set down in short sayings and half-sentences, the walkings and the faults in tables, the bundle-song pasted inside the cover, a knot set down in reed-ash in the margin and gone by noon, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of borrowed clerks, one line struck in charcoal by a woman who would not sign it, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
