codex.provenance: Gathered at the Weir one league upriver of Sill in Reed of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813; written by Nall of the Weir, a cutter who has kept the leading rope for nineteen years, on the back of a district tally spoiled when the river came up over it, and kept dry in the oiled lining of the coat that holds the rope. It survives with grey reed-ash at the head off the flat blessing stone, silt worked into the gutter and into the grain of the fold, the press of a wet bundle across the song, a thumb of tar off the leading rope at the head, a smear of eel slime along the second leaf, salt gone white at a wrist-print, a brine-gull's peck through one word of the last verse, a ring of small ale at the foot left by a boatman who would not drink with cutters, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that is not mine and that I have not swept, two corrections in borrowed Ledgerhand standing above my words, one charcoal line struck and written again underneath, and the line at the foot which nobody has claimed

codex.title: The Articles of the Floor, Being the Standing Rules of the Clamp-Masters of Keld Keep for the Taking, Trying, Cutting and Paying Out of Apprentices at the Duelling Floor Beneath the First Seam, with the Table of Years, the Tally of Hands, the Floor-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in a Survey-Clerk's Upright Hand, One Line Struck in Charcoal by a Cutter Who Would Not Sign It, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A clamp-room leaf of rules in the hand of the under-master who keeps the irons and the roll of hands at the Duelling Floor, written on the back of a spoiled rim-seam tally in Grathic letters with the Keldish endings struck off, hung on a spike beside the clamp-rack; the articles in the hard short Rim speech, the years and the hands in tables, the floor-song pasted inside the cover, a warm-stone shaving shut in the second fold, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Court survey-clerk, one line struck hard in charcoal, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: First gathered at Keld Keep in Y.H. 741, the year Karric VII shut the Cold Pass and the Order found it had a border it had not asked for, and copied forward from the rack and not from a book; this leaf written in Stone of Y.H. 813 by Vek of the Floor, under-master, who has kept the irons and said the count over the clamp-rack for nineteen years and carries a first way in his own forearm that aches before the thaw; carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 814. It survives hung on its spike in the clamp-room off the Duelling Floor, soft at the fold and stiff with coal smut at the head, with an iron-red thumb off the mine-reeve's checking point, a clamp-bite taken out of the upper corner, a lamp-scorch that has eaten the last word of rule 9 and left the sense standing, a warm-stone shaving shut in the second fold that is warm on the coldest morning and is never lent, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead pressed into the gutter, a frost-feather pressed flat that was gone by noon, a grey thumb along the outer fold that is not mine and not the reeve's, two corrections in the Court's upright hand, one charcoal line struck and written again underneath, and a line at the foot nobody will own.

codex.title: The Asking-Cord at the Standing Post, Being Four Riddles Tied and a Fifth Left Untied, the Knot Nobody Can Read, and the Figure a Factor's Clerk Set Above It
codex.kind: A fire-keeper's telling of a winter's riddling on the back boards at the Post, set down in Grathic letters though the questions were put in Fen Cant and are not written anywhere else; the riddles in the short nose-speech with the ends let fall into the mud, the answers tied in grey wool and read by touch, the wagers in peat-blocks laid against the hut wall, a tally nicked into the door-lintel with a fish-hook, a factor's clerk's entry in narrow upright Ledgerhand above, a slate-runner's line in the slant of a carried hand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, at the Standing Post in the Fenmarch, by Wen, who keeps the little fire on the back boards and the cord of answers that hangs beside it, from a night told over by a reed-cutter come up across the winter way; carried down the marsh road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a spoiled eel-tribute tally, sewn with eel-sinew into a fold of oiled reed and kept under the loose board with the market stick and the gathered fen sayings. It survives with a peat thumb worked into the head, a bog-water tideline along the gutter, a pressed reed across the third leaf, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, eel slime shut in the fold off a basket set down there, a glass-eel thread fine as a hair in the lower margin, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which nobody will own, a knot of grey wool tied through a hole in the first leaf which the writer will not undo, the clerk's narrow correction above the answers, the runner's sloping line below it, and the line at the foot which has never been claimed

codex.title: The Articles of the Three Years, Being the Standing Rules of the College of Assessors in Slate Row for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices in Ledgerhand, with the Weighing Rubrick and the Provost's Corrections
codex.kind: A copyist's fair copy of the College's standing articles, kept by the under-clerk who holds the second file; the three years set out in a table, the faults and their corrections in a second, the copying-song pasted inside the cover, two corrections in the Provost's narrow upright hand, one struck verb in a clerk's hand, and a line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: First gathered in the Hearthseat in Y.H. 776, the year the College built its house in Sill's own Slate Row, and copied forward from the tin at each Opening of the Slates; this leaf written by the under-clerk of the second file and carried through Y.H. 813. It survives folded inside the second file's tin, soft at the fold, with slate dust worked into the gutter, a grey collector's thumb at the head, iron-gall ink in the creases of the copyist's two fingers, a damp tide-line from the sealed-file room along the foot, a green bead of lead-glaze from a glaze-mixer come up from High Kiln, one verb struck in a hand that is not the Provost's, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Back Place, Being the Setting-Song of the Kiln Throat at Low Kiln, Sung as the Green Pots Go In, with the Rows as They Are Set, the Space at the Back That Is Gone Around with a Look, a Factor's Clerk's Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss in Green Charcoal, and One Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A setter's work song of the clay yard in the low half-sung Grathic of Low Kiln, counted in rows of three and the turning of the wrist, said down into the throat and not up into the yard; the rubrics in the setter's charcoal hand, the clerk's figures above in Ledgerhand, a glaze-girl's green gloss in the margin, and one line at the foot nobody has claimed
codex.provenance: Set down in Frost of Y.H. 813 by Senna, a woman who sets the pots into the throat of a kiln two doors below the Vail in Low Kiln of Sill and has set them through seventeen firings; written in charcoal thinned with wet slip on the back of a firing-tally spoiled by a thumb through the count, folded into four and tied with grey wool to a nail beside the damper; copied at Greybank onto the back of a voided weigh-slip. It survives with a wet-slip thumb at the head, brick dust in the fold, a wad of clay pressed flat between the second and third leaf, a scorch along the lower edge, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a sherd from the throat, a grey Ash smear along the gutter nobody will own, the clerk's figures above, the green gloss in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody has claimed

codex.title: The Bank Song, Being the Digging-Song of the Clay Yard at Low Kiln, Sung at the Face Above the Slip Brook, with the Cuts as They Are Counted, the Grey Seam Left Standing, the Overhang Kept for the Bank, a Kiln-Master's Ruling in Broad Charcoal, a Factor's Clerk's Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss from a Woman at the Tubs, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A digger's work song in the low speech of the yard, called down into the face and answered by the spade and not by voices; the verses counted in cuts going up, with the fourth cut left standing for the bank's own roof and the grey seam left uncut; the rubrics of the face in the same charcoal-and-clay hand; a kiln-master's ruling in broad charcoal, a factor's clerk's figures standing above in Ledgerhand, a gloss pressed into the margin by a woman at the tubs, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim
codex.provenance: Sung at the clay bank two doors below the wheel-shed in Low Kiln of Sill and set down in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Long Cold, by a woman who has dug that face for nine winters and has learned to tell a good cut from a grey one before the spade goes in; written with a burnt stick and clay-water thinned in the Brook on the back of a digger's docket spoiled by a wet thumb, folded twice and tied with grey wool against the frost, carried up the Clay Road with a consignment of tile and copied forward at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a factor's voided weigh-slip. It survives with a clay thumb worked into the grain at the head, a pale silt tideline from the Slip Brook along the gutter, a dry grey flake from the seam pressed in the fold, a root-hair caught across the second leaf, one word of the sixth verse softened away by water and not written in again, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl with sweetness at one mouth-corner, a sour small-ale ring at the foot, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own, a nick from a spade caught in the fold, the kiln-master's broad ruling, the clerk's figures standing above, the tub-woman's gloss, and the line at the foot

codex.title: The Articles of the Bench, Being the Standing Rules of the Hearth-Maids of Grath for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Girls at the Birth-Slates, with the Years Set in a Table, the Form of a Birth-Entry, Faults and their Correcting, the Warming-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A bench-copy of the order's standing rules in the hand of the maid who keeps the birth-flower shrine's slate-box in Low Kiln; the articles in the short half-sentences the trade speaks, the years and the faults in tables, the form of a birth-entry left blank, the warming-song pasted to the inside of the cover, two corrections in borrowed hands, a page copied again with two words left out, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed
codex.provenance: First gathered in Y.H. 782, the year every birth in Grath was made a slate-entry and the Court began to pay the maids who had kept the slates for nothing since any woman could date, and copied forward from the bench and the slate-box rather than from a book; this leaf written at the shrine beside House Reed in Low Kiln in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, carried through the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813, and read to a girl brought up from the tubs with her hands already red. It survives folded in a grey wool birth-cloth among the answered slates; beeswax from the shrine candle worked into the head, fine grey slip from the upper pit at the fold, birth-water gone brown where the leaf was doubled, grey Ash along the gutter off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying, a curl of grey wool through the tie-hole which the writer will not untie, a tallow thumb, a tideline of well-water along the foot, a green bead of lead glaze pressed in by a girl with sweetness still at her mouth, two words eaten clean away and not written in again, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot that is nobody's

codex.title: The Rules of the Birth-Cloth, Being the Standing Sayings of the Hearth-Maids of Grath for the Taking of Girls, the Warming of Stones, the Writing of Birth-Slates and the Manner of the Three Days; Kept in the Fold of a Grey Wool Birth-Cloth at the Shrine in Low Kiln, with the Table of Days, the Washing-Song Said to the Stone, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A rule-leaf of the hearth-maids' sayings in the hand of the keeper of the slate-box at the birth-flower shrine in Low Kiln; the sayings set down in charcoal and the dregs of a tallow end on the back of a spoiled birth-slate rubbing, the days and the faults in tables, the washing-song sewn into the fold, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk of the College, one in the small quick hand of a collector's clerk who wrote while the leaf was still being read aloud, and a line at the foot that nobody will claim
codex.provenance: First gathered at Sill in Y.H. 782, the year the College made every birth a Court entry and paid the maids to keep it, and copied forward from mouth to cloth and from cloth to mouth, never from a book, which is why the rule about the wrist is worn away where a hundred thumbs have tested it and the rule about the tin is as sharp as the day it was said. This leaf written at the shrine in Low Kiln in Frost of Y.H. 813 by the keeper of the slate-box, who has taken girls to births for nineteen years and has never once entered a stone. It survives folded in a grey wool birth-cloth in the box under the niche: beeswax from the shrine candle worked into the grain at the head, a tallow thumb pressed into the corner where the leaf was held down in the draught, grey Ash along the gutter off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying, a drop of birth-water gone brown in the fold and eaten into two words which have not been written in again, a round pale place where a collector's tube-wrap was set down and no hand has claimed the wrap, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl with the sweetness still at her mouth, crust-grease on the second table where a woman set down a crust for a child who would not eat, a curl of grey wool caught in the sewing of the song, one margin corrected above and one below, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never been owned

codex.title: The Sermon at the Birth-Flower, Being What Was Said Over the Slates on the Long Night of Y.H. 812
codex.kind: A sermon of the Temple of the Return preached at the birth-flower shrine in Low Kiln, with the women's answers set beside it and a clerk's corrections struck through but left standing
codex.provenance: Preached by a priest of the Temple of the Return, come up from Greybank, at the niche beside House Reed in Low Kiln, Sill, on the Long Night of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, over the birth-slates the women had laid there to lie overnight; set down two mornings after, on the Last Day, by a hearth-maid of the district in charcoal and tallow on the back of a birth-slate spoiled by a late entry, continued on the leaf of a drying tally, and kept in the fold of a grey wool birth-cloth that goes where the maids go. It survives soft at the fold with a tallow thumb at the head, a green bead of lead glaze from a girl who leaned over to see the writing, a grey Ash print along the gutter, a spot of barley grease from a crust laid down and not eaten, three corrections in the maid's own hand, one narrow hand borrowed from a clerk that takes the verbs out, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own. Copied forward in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the nought left in its place.

codex.title: The Sermon at the Bitter Well, Being What the Keeper of the Dish-Shelf Said Over the Well by the Ferr at Stonemouth on a Morning in Ash of Y.H. 813, with the Drawing-Song Left with Its Sixth Line Unsung, the Shelf in a Tally, a Factor's Clerk's Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A well-shrine sermon of the common Grathic telling preached at the niche beside the well that the road-book calls the well that was never sweetened, where the Ferr comes down to the Ilm at Stonemouth; the sayings in the flat washed speech of the washing-bench set down in Grathic, the drawing-song with the sixth line left as it is not sung, the shelf in a tally, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor's clerk come up from Greybank to weigh the winter lead, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Preached on Ash 9, Y.H. 813, by a woman of High Kiln who had kept the dish-shelf at the well for two and thirty years, whose mother went thin on the Ferr in the Long Cold and would not let her drink; written that evening by the girl who takes the quarrymen's names at the weigh-clerk's bench, in charcoal on the back of a weigh-slip spoiled by wet slate, folded with a green bead of lead glaze shut in the crease and tied with a turn of well-rope, and kept since in the niche behind the dish-shelf. It survives with lime worked into the grain at the head, a blue-grey tideline off the Ferr that has eaten two words clean off the second leaf, a ring of barley-water on the first, a grey Ash print along the gutter nobody will own, the green bead in the fold, a flake of the well's sweet crust shut in the third crease, a pale line pressed from a cup's lip in the lower corner, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor's clerk, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied once at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 814 into the factor's file of northern sayings, with the verbs put back and the sixth line left as it was not sung.

codex.title: The Blue Cliff, Being an Extract from the Road-Book of Sill Concerning the Glaze Wars, the Winter of the Ferr, and the Terms Set at the Blue Cliff in Y.H. 418, with the List of the Three Hundred, the Well-Song, and the Corrections of Two Clerks
codex.kind: A road-clerk's extract from the thane's book of distances and tolls, copied out of the moot-chest original; the year-entries in the clay-hand, the treaty clauses in a Vhaleni tally-hand gone soft with damp, the three hundred entered as a round sum with a fourth row in a hand nobody will own, the well-song taken down at Stonemouth, one struck word in the narrow upright hand of the College, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed
codex.provenance: Written at Sill in the thane's counting room off the Cross in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the road-clerk who signs himself only R. and will not say what the letter stands for; copied from a road-book kept in the moot-chest since Y.H. 418 and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives as four leaves of stout foolscap sewn with wire into a board cover rubbed bare at the corners: clay worked into the gutter, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower margin by a glaze-mixer come up from High Kiln, a ring of small ale at the head, a grey collector's thumb on the treaty clause which its owner did not wipe away, a strip of salt-paper pasted over the sixth clause and gone soft at the edge, one word struck through and written above in the College hand, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward.

codex.title: The Title of Bonds, Being the Ordinance of the Keeping for the Entering, Serving, Assignment and Reckoning of Debts, Copied into the Assessor's House at Sill with the Bond-Clerk's Margin, the Knife-Score, and a Correction in a Borrowed Hand
codex.kind: An extract from the Court's ordinances, copied out for the counter of the assessor's house in Slate Row, Sill, with the marginal hand of the clerk who keeps the bond-slate; the articles in Ledgerhand, the verbs restored beneath them, one line scored with a knife-point, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a form of entry left blank for want of a name
codex.provenance: Copied at Sill in the assessor's house built in Y.H. 776, in Ilmen of Y.H. 813, from Title the Fourth of the Ordinances of the Keeping as confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of Y.H. 418 and added to after the Rising of Y.H. 668, in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812; carried forward at the Opening of the Slates. It survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire and tied with a grown string, kept in the pigeonhole behind the counter and taken down when a debt is disputed; an iron-gall thumb at the head, a bone-pale streak of slip down the gutter, a line scored deep with a knife-point in the lower margin, a tallow thumb at the fold, a grey Ash print along the outer edge, a green bead of lead glaze in the corner, two corrections in hands that are not the writer's, and seven short lines pasted inside the cover in a hand nobody has claimed.

codex.title: The Book of Again, Being the Figures Set Against Vessels Returned to the Bank a Second, Third and Fourth Time in the Assessor's Room of Slate Row in the Hearthseat, with the Older Figure Beneath the Newer, the Remark Left Standing, Two Corrections in the College Hand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A page from an assessor's ledger in the Hearthseat; figures in Ledgerhand copied from the collectors' slates, the terse remarks in the hand that set the worth, a column of likenesses struck out by the College and drawn back underneath, one figure struck and set above in a borrowed hand, a word scraped away, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed
codex.provenance: Written in the assessor's counting room off the Weighing Hall in Slate Row of the Hearthseat, between the Weighing and the Remembering of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813; kept in a board cover under the counter and taken down whenever a whole return is disputed. It survives as two leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, with an iron-gall thumb at the head, a streak of bone-pale slip down the gutter, a tallow print where the lamp was held low, grey Ash off a returned woman's sleeve worked into the outer fold, a pale round clip-ring pressed into the third leaf, a corner scorched by a spark off the grating, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the College, one in the soft-cuffed hand of a factor's clerk out of Greybank, and a line at the foot nobody will own

codex.title: The Book of Worth, Being the Valuations Set in the Assessor's House at Sill in the Thin Year, and the Figures Set Above Them in a Second Hand
codex.kind: A page from the valuation ledger of the assessor's house in Slate Row, Sill; figures in Ledgerhand, terse remarks in the hand of the assessor who set them, one column left unfilled, and two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the College
codex.provenance: Written at Sill in the assessor's house built in Y.H. 776, in the Thin Year Y.H. 812, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates on Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813; kept in a board cover under the counter and taken down when a figure is disputed. It survives as two leaves of foolscap sewn with wire: an iron-gall thumb at the head, a streak of bone-pale slip down the gutter, a green bead of glaze in the lower corner, a tallow thumb, grey Ash worked into the outer fold, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, two corrections in the College's narrow hand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.

codex.title: The Bowl Beside the Bed, Being a Lullaby of the Bowl of Sere Sung by a Woman Who Gives Suck to a Child That Is Not Hers
codex.kind: A wet-nurse's lullaby taken down from her own mouth in the women's quarter of a great house of the Ten Bowls; the verses in the long-vowelled courtesy speech of Sere, the manner of saying them in the writer's own charcoal, a bowl-house tally-clerk's correction set above in his leaning hand, a northern bond-woman's charcoal pressed underneath, a gloss in myrrh from a woman who has given suck in three houses, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Sung in the third watch of the night in the women's quarter of a great house in the Bowl of Sere, after the household bowl had gone round at the third hour of the day and the court fires were banked, and set down in Y.H. 812 by a woman of the house who gives suck and had once kept a tally before she was bought; written in charcoal and the dregs of a myrrh phial on the back of a bowl-house linen tally spoiled at one corner, sewn with a thread of grey wool into a fold of oiled silk and kept under the cradle mat. A factor's clerk carried it north at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and copied it at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold, where the lowland name for that year, the Thin Year, was added below the southern one. It survives with a ring of warm wine at the head, yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the fold, a smear of myrrh across the second leaf, a milky thumb in the gutter that nobody will own, a green bead of lead glaze chipped from a bowl at the third hour, a curl of grey wool from a northern sleeve shut in the sewing, the tally-clerk's correction standing above, the two charcoal hands standing below, and the line at the foot which has never been claimed

codex.title: The Bowl Goes Round, Being the Drinking Song of the Women of the Washing-Bench in the House of the Ten Bowls at the Bowl of Sere, with the Order of the Bowls, the Word Under the Glaze, and the Corrections Set Over It
codex.kind: A washing-woman's drinking song, taken down from her own mouth at the basin after the court had gone; the verses in the long-vowelled courtesy of the south set down in charcoal, with the ends let fall as they are sung, the order of the bowls in the writer's own hand, the house tally-clerk's thin gold standing above, a factor's clerk's ruling in narrow upright Ledgerhand above that, a northern woman's charcoal in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Grain of Y.H. 812, in the scullery of the House of the Ten Bowls in the Bowl of Sere, by a woman of the washing-bench whose clay-name is Bowl and whose former name is under the glaze of a bowl she has never been permitted to look into; set down in charcoal on the back of a glaze-tally spoiled by a wet thumb at the third furnace, carried north with a consignment of glass and oil in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant gone soft at one corner. It survives folded in oiled silk in the fold of the washing-cloth, with a ring of warm wine at the head gone the colour of the glaze, a smear of press-oil at the second leaf, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner, a fleck of the tally-clerk's gold, a grey bead of slate-ash from the feast fire shut into the fold, a pale thumb-print where a woman with the sweet sickness leaned over to read, a thread of wool from a kitchen sleeve, one correction in thin gold, one in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor's clerk at Greybank, a gloss in the charcoal of a bought woman come down from the north, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Bowl-Leech's Book, Being Remedies for the Third-Day Tremor, the Sweet, the Fever That Cooks, the Guest That Wants Another House, the Graft That Will Not Take and the Northern Cold, Set Down in the Bowl of Sere with the Errors Left Standing
codex.kind: A bowl-leech's book of remedies in the long-vowelled courtesy of Sere, written in gold ink on the back of a spoiled glaze-tally and folded into oiled silk; the cures in a bowl-leech's hand, the objections of a physician come down from Greybank pressed cold into the margin, the corrections of a factor's clerk in narrow Ledgerhand, a song for the third day with a place left where the seventh name stood, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in the Bowl of Sere between Grain and Smoke of Y.H. 812, the year the northern measures came south cheap, by Ilyra Vey, a leech attached to the house of Vey who held the third-day hand through nineteen returns; begun on the back of a glaze-tally spoiled in the pressing of a public bowl, written in gold ink on four leaves of glazed paper gummed into a fold of oiled silk, carried north with the glass in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a discarded rent-roll gone soft. It survives in a dry tin in a room with good light in the Greybank counting house, with gold worked into the creases of the first leaf, a ring of warm wine at the head, myrrh rubbed into the grain, a green bead of cliff-glass pressed into the lower corner, a grey bead of public-bowl ash caught in the gutter, a pale crescent of tallow-wasp resin at the foot of the remedies, a line that runs out toward the gutter and stops, a small square where a word was cut away with a knife and not written back, three objections in the cold margin hand of the physician, corrections in the upright Ledgerhand of the factor's clerk, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: Of the Theft of Warmth, the Cold-Iron Brand and the Unclosed Account, Being Title the Sixth of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied into the Court's Room at Slate Row in Sill with the Brand-Clerk's Margin, the Marks Entered in the Hands of Those Who Wore Them, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: An extract from the Court's ordinances, written out for the counter of the Court's room in Slate Row, Sill, with the marginal hand of the clerk who keeps the brand-book and hands the irons to the officer; the articles in Ledgerhand, the marks set down beneath them in the hands of the persons who wore them, a table of offences, a form of entry left blank, the ring-song as it is said at the counter, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed
codex.provenance: Copied at Sill in the Court's room in Slate Row in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates on Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, from Title the Sixth of the Ordinances of the Keeping as confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of the Blue Cliff in Y.H. 418 and added to after the Rising of Y.H. 668, in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year. It survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, kept in the drawer under the counter where the brand and the clip lie together in a cloth; an Ash thumb at the head, iron filings worked into the gutter, a pale ring of skin-grease at the foot where a branded wrist was laid on the leaf, a tallow thumb beside it, a green bead of lead glaze in the corner, a bare square where a word was scraped away with the point of the clip-key, a damp tide-line from the Waiting Room, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own.

codex.title: The Litany of the Browned Crust, Being the Prayer of the Return as the Bread-Women of Low Kiln Keep It on the Last Day
codex.kind: A bread-woman's litany of the Return, said over the Last Day loaves before the bread is cut and while the grey is still lying in the corners; the rubrics in the hand that mixed the dough, the stations in the words they are spoken in, the answer given by the room, a clerk's correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand set above the verbs, a woman's note written in charcoal and flour, and a line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written on the Last Day of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in a bakehouse in Low Kiln below the sill of Sill, on the back of a flour-tally spoiled by a wet thumb; copied forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, onto the inside leaf of the meal-box in which the bread is kept warm in Stone. It survives folded in oiled sacking under the loaf shelf, with a bone-pale flour thumb at the head, a browned crumb pressed into the fold, a scorch where the oven mouth took the upper corner, a ridge of grey Ash along the gutter from a corner that was not swept, a green bead of lead glaze from a girl come down from the Cross, a tallow print where the lamp was held low, a thread of grey wool from a cradle blanket, a damp from the dough bench, a bare square where a word was scraped away, one correction in a borrowed hand, and one line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Bundle and the Cord, Being the Standing Rules of the Reed-Cutters of Reedholt and the Weir for the Taking, Keeping, Trying and Paying Out of Apprentices at the Reed Cut, with the Years in a Table, the Faults in a Second Table, the Counting-Song Pasted to the Back, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, One Line Struck in Charcoal by a Cutter Who Would Not Sign It, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A cut-leaf of the trade's standing rules in the hand of the cutter who keeps the board at the dry, written on the back of a spoiled peat-tally and sewn with eel-sinew into oiled sacking; the rules in the short sayings of the east marsh, the years and the faults in tables, a knot tied in the margin where no Grathic word will come, the counting-song pasted to the back, two corrections in borrowed hands, a charcoal line struck and written again underneath, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim
codex.provenance: First gathered at Reedholt in Y.H. 601, the year the marsh road was made a cart way to Greybank and the cutters found they had a price to argue about; copied forward from the board at the dry and not from a book. This leaf written at the Reed Cut and at Reedholt in the east marsh in Reed of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813. It survives folded in oiled sacking under the loose board at the dry, sewn with eel-sinew, with a peat thumb ground into the head, a bog-water tideline that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, dried sedge pressed across the third, a knot of grey wool tied through a hole in the first leaf which the writer will not untie, a second knot tied low with teeth where the hand that made it could not see, a small pale round place where a collector's cuff was laid, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, the song soft with handling at the back, two corrections in borrowed hands, one line struck hard in charcoal and written again under it, and a line at the foot nobody will own

codex.title: The Carried Forward, Being a Page from the Roll of the Dead in the Bank at the Hearthseat, with the Measures Pressed into Newborn Vessels, the Figures Unspent, and the Line Which Is Never Closed
codex.kind: A page from the bank's own roll, kept under the counter by the clerk who writes the dead; figures in Ledgerhand set from the district slates, the remarks in the hand that carries a name forward, two corrections in borrowed hands, a column struck by the College and drawn back, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in the bank at the Hearthseat on the Keel in the last tend of Stone, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, through the Five and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813; kept under the counter in a board cover and taken down when a figure is disputed or a kinsman comes to close an account, which no kinsman has yet done. It survives as two leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, with an iron-gall thumb at the head, slate dust worked into the gutter, a tallow print from the lamp, a pressed grey Ash print from a district bundle laid on the counter, a small square of bare paper where a name was scraped away, a corner gone soft from the cold of the sealed-file room, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Chamber Found Warm, Being an Extract from the Chronicle of the Hearth Concerning the Lighting, the First Returns, the Three Offices, the Fixing of the Deduction and the Four Sealed Wells; with the Line as the Copyists Smoothed It, the Kindling Verse, and Two Hands of Correction
codex.kind: A Hearthseat annalist's extract from the low chronicle kept in the Weighing Hall, being the first hundred and twenty years after the lighting; the year-entries in a small close clerk's hand, the line of the lighting in four successive copies set side by side, the offices entered in the order they were founded, the deduction set out against the notice that carries it, the kindling verse taken down from the keepers at the grating, one struck word restored from underneath, and two corrections in borrowed hands
codex.provenance: Written in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Senn, a keeper of the low roll in the Weighing Hall of the Hearthseat, who signs with his name and not with the office, and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813. Copied from the low chronicle begun in the roll-room in Y.H. 120 and carried forward at each Opening since; the original is kept in the lower drawer beneath the fire-tongs and shown to no one below the rank of keeper. It survives as eight leaves of the thin ruled roll-paper sewn with iron wire into a slate-coloured board cover, soft at the fold: slate dust worked into the gutter, a coal pressed into the wax of the sewing by a keeper who had no business pressing it, a scorch along the third leaf where it lay against the grating, a tallow thumb at the head, a flake of cold-iron scale in the lower margin, grey Ash in the crease of the fourth leaf which no keeper sweeps during the Five, one word struck through and restored from underneath in the writer's own hand, a correction in the narrow upright hand of the College and one in a temple hand that writes without verbs, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.

codex.title: The Chronicle of Grath, Being an Extract Concerning the Choosing and the Confirming of the Thanes of Clay, from the Kiln-Masters' First Naming to the Present Thane at the Cross; with the Table of Confirmations, the Treaty Years in Which No Thane Was Asked, the Levies Called in a Thane's Name, the Moot-Song, Three Corrections in the Narrow Hand of Greybank, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A clerk's extract from the Chronicle of Grath, kept in the chronicle chest in the thane's house at Sill and not in the moot-chest below the Cross, which holds the town's year-book and the thane's road-book and is another kind of book; the year-entries in a broad clay-hand with the verbs left in, the thanes set in a table of choosing and confirming, the treaty years entered in the margin where the chest puts what the Court did not ask, the levies set against the notice in a column no clerk has signed, the moot-song taken down from a man who would not give his day's wage, three corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor's clerk come up from Greybank, one charcoal line left by a hearth-maid of Low Kiln, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at Sill in the thane's house in the last tend of Ash, Y.H. 813, by the clerk of the chronicle, who signs with the office and not with a name and has put the verbs back where he found them taken out; copied from the Chronicle of Grath begun in the year of the Blue Cliff and carried forward at each Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 814. It survives as six leaves of foolscap sewn with wire into a board cover gone soft at the hinge: brick dust ground into the head off the High Kiln terrace, clay worked into the gutter and not swept out, a shaving of raw slip shut in the second fold, silt from the sill dried pale along the foot, a tallow thumb at the head, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a glaze-mixer who leaned to read the song and went off with the sweetness still at her mouth, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first entry to the last, a short square of bare paper where a word was scraped away and no other put in, three corrections in the narrow upright hand of Greybank, one charcoal line left by a hearth-maid who would not give her name, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the clerk did not make and has not swept, and the line at the foot which has never been claimed

codex.title: The Clamp and the Bowl, Being an Account of the Southern Empire of Sere, Set Down by Veth, a Hired Clamp out of Keld Keep, Who Went Down the Peat Line in the Service of a Factor of the Sunbowl Houses and Came Back with His Measure Unchanged and a Figure He Could Not Spend; with the Order of the Name, the Road That Counted Nothing, the Four Bowls, a Table of Hire, the Clamp-Song as It Is Said Going Down, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A hired soldier's road account, set down first in charcoal on the backs of three spoiled requisitions for warm-stone and cut in the edge with a tally-knife where charcoal would not hold, then copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold; the figures in a number-first counting hand learned at the shaft mouth, the southern sayings kept in the hearing and not made into proverbs, the hard Rim endings struck off where Grathic letters would not carry them, the verbs put back under every borrowed correction, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward
codex.provenance: Written in Grain and Smoke of Y.H. 813 in the Bowl of Sere and at a provincial bowl on the south road, by Veth of Keld Keep, a clamp for hire who went down in Reed with a letter for a house of the Ten Bowls and an iron clamp at his belt and came back in Ash with the same number in his arm, three gold crowns he could not change, and a sliver of lead glaze in the seam of his coat; copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 814 onto the back of a voided grain-warrant and carried up the Rim Road to the Keep. It survives folded into a tin lined with a shaving of warm-stone now gone cold, soft at the fore-edge and sour with the burning winds; yellow dust ground into the sewing, a ring of warm wine at the third hour, olive oil at the thumb, a curl of burnt paper from a slate that had gone into a court fire shut into the second fold, iron filings off a clamp filed at a gate, a shaving of warm-stone cold in the gutter, a square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with a knife-point, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own

codex.title: The Clap at the Gap, Being the Hand-Counting Game of the Children of the Cross at Sill, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Hands, the Verses as They Are Clapped, a Factor's Clerk's Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, an Old Woman's Gloss in Charcoal, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A keeper's gathering of a children's hand game, set down in Grathic on the back of a market board spoiled by a wet thumb; the verses in the children's own half-sung speech, the manner of the play in the keeper's small hand, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor's clerk from Greybank, a gloss pressed in charcoal by a woman who has swept the Cross since before the Glaze Wars, and a line at the foot in a hand that has not come forward
codex.provenance: Written in Bone of Y.H. 813 at the reading block under the moot-post at the Cross in Sill, by Halla of the Step, who keeps the step clean of slate dust and sells barley water on Account-days; set down because a factor's clerk come up from Greybank to check the winter grain asked what the children counted when they clapped there on ordinary mornings, and wrote it down with the clapping taken out and a figure put where the ninth sound stood. Written in charcoal on the back of a market board gone soft in the rain, folded into four, carried to Greybank in a woman's satchel and copied onto the back of a voided weigh-slip. It survives with slate dust ground into the head, a barley-water ring through the second leaf, a chip of coarse tile shut in the fold, a frost-feather pressed flat that was gone by noon, a grey Ash print nobody will own, a twist of grey wool through a hole which the writer will not untie, the clerk's figures above the children's words, the old woman's gloss in charcoal beside the gap, and one line at the foot that has never come forward

codex.title: The Clay-Yard Book of Remedies, Being What a Hearth-Maid of Low Kiln Sets to the Second Chill, the Sweet Sickness, the Kiln-Burn, the Cord That Will Not Fall and the Cold That Stays, Written Down in Grathic with the Errors Left Standing
codex.kind: A midwife's and healer's book of remedies in the Grathic clay-yard manner, the cures in a hearth-maid's hand with the verbs left in, the objections of a physician come down from Greybank pressed in the margin, the corrections of a College clerk in Ledgerhand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Low Kiln in Sill between Ash of Y.H. 811 and Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the Long Cold and the Thin Year, by Hedda of the Clay Yard, a hearth-maid who caught children in the slip pits and laid out the dead of the kiln terraces for twenty-six years; begun on the back of a glaze-house tally spoiled by a fall of slip, folded into four and carried in the breast of her apron against a square of birth-cloth washed so often there is no birth left in it, and copied at Greybank in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, onto the back of a rent-roll gone soft. It survives with a thumb of tallow at the head, grey Ash worked into the gutter, brick dust ground into the fold, a wet smear of slip that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a ring of barley-water, a scorch where a spark off the kiln caught the corner, a long hair the colour of wet wool caught in the seam, objections in the hand of a Greybank physician, corrections in the narrow upright hand of a College clerk, and a line at the foot nobody will own.

codex.title: The Glass Eel, Being a Trapper's Field Notes on the Eel of the Lower Ilm and the Silt Below the North Bridge
codex.kind: A hunter's field book on one beast, set down as the record of nights at the trap and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled fish-tallies, an eel-song as it is sung, a Greybank skin-buyer's price pressed in the margin, two rulings in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the factor's clerk, and one line in pale ink from a hearth-maid at the Fish Blessing
codex.provenance: Written in Ilmen of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in the first warm days after the Long Cold, by Tibb of the Fishstairs, who sets eel-traps at the Weir and fishes the silt below the north bridge; set down at the end of nights with a tallow lamp guttering in a clay dish, first on the backs of fish-tallies spoiled by river water and then on two folds of oiled eel-skin, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a clay tube stoppered with wool. Copied at Greybank in Smoke of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a salt warrant voided by the damp. It survives with dried eel slime along the fore-edge, grey silt worked into the gutter, a white salt bloom at the head blown up from the Sallow, a lamp-scorch on the second leaf where the dish overturned, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, one eel-scale pressed flat in the fold, a tar thumb at the head, a brown tideline where the river stood on it through a night, a green bead of lead glaze from a woman who leaned to see the tally, a grey Ash print nobody will own, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the factor's clerk at Greybank, a price in the blocky hand of the skin-buyer, a line in pale ink from a hearth-maid, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own

codex.title: The Clicking in the Reed, Being a Hunter's Notes on the Reed-Wolf of the East Marsh
codex.kind: A reed-cutter's field book on one beast, set down as a record of hunts and not a book of natural philosophy; the calls and the counting-song in Grathic, the tally in charcoal and reed-sap, with a Stonemouth tooth-buyer's corrections in Ledgerhand in the margin
codex.provenance: Written in the hunting month of Bone, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a reed-cutter of Reedholt who went into the east marsh with a spear and a knot of cord, and who hunts still; copied forward in Bone, Y.H. 813. Set on the backs of Stonemouth weigh-slips gone soft with damp and on two folded sheets of birch bark, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a bark wrap under a loose board of the hunter's hut. It survives stained and used: a tooth-grey smear along the fore-edge where the book was wiped on a sleeve after a kill, a press of wet reed across the first leaf, a brown peat thumb at the tally, a small round mark where a buyer set a two-mark piece down and left it, and a line of figures in the narrow hand of the Stonemouth weigh-clerk who counted and paid for the teeth. The hunter has answered that clerk in the foot and has not struck a word of his out.

codex.title: The Cold Acre Book of Remedies, Being Remedies for the Well-Cold, the Threshing Cough, the Turnip-Knife Cut, the Sweet Line, the Second Chill, the Birth-Flower and the Member Gone Dark, Set Down on the Ridge with the Errors Left Standing
codex.kind: A ridge-wife's and midwife's book of remedies in the Cold Acre speech, written in Grathic letters learned off a man who came up to have his mark confirmed; the cures in a healer's hand on the back of a barley tally spoiled at the meal mill, the objections of a physician come down from Greybank pressed into the margin, the corrections of a factor's clerk in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a slate-woman's line set close to the third-night row, a well-song with the place where the twelfth should stand left as it is sung, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at Cold Acre, two leagues north of Sill on the ridge where the one well has not frozen in any winter the oldest on the ridge can name, between Tallow of Y.H. 812 and Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the Long Cold and the Thin Year, by Renna of Cold Acre, a ridge-wife who has set the bones of the harvest and caught the children of the six houses for nine-and-twenty years; begun on the back of a barley tally from the meal mill that a wet thumb spoiled, folded into oiled sacking and carried in the breast of a wool apron against a square of birth-cloth, and copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a discarded rent-roll. It survives with well-clay worked into the grain at the head, a frost-ring that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a barley awn stiff in the fold, a nick from a turnip knife at the fore-edge, a tideline of well-water gone pale along the gutter, a thumb of tallow at the outer fold, a green bead of High Kiln glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl with the sweetness at one mouth-corner, objections in the cold margin hand of the physician, corrections in the upright hand of the factor's clerk, a slate-woman's line set close to the third-night row, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: The Cold in One Foot, Being a Hunter's Field Notes on the Silt-Leach of the Lower Ilm and the Ferr Shallows
codex.kind: A hunter's field book on one beast, set down as the record of wades and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled eel-bills, a blessing verse as it is said on the bank, one ruling in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the factor's clerk at Greybank, a line in the pale ink of a hearth-maid, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Ember and Grain of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a hunter of the Fishstairs who waded the shallows of the lower Ilm and the Ferr for eels and for leeches, and was paid by the dozen; set down at the end of wades on the bank with a tallow end in a dish and the cold still in one foot, first on the backs of eel-bills gone soft with river water and then on two folds of birch bark, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a coat pocket against a twist of tallow. Copied forward at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold. It survives with grey silt worked into the head, an iron-brown tideline along the gutter from the Ferr, a press of wet sedge across the first leaf, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a woman who leaned to see the tally, a cuff-grey smear where a collector set his slate down and took it up again, a singe where the tallow caught the third leaf, a grey Ash print nobody will own, one ruling in the clerk's Ledgerhand, one line in the pale ink of a hearth-maid, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: The Cold-Iron Letter, Being a Letter from the Smithy at Low Kiln to His Sister at the Greybank Quay, Concerning the Tubes He Is Sent to Mend, the Iron That Comes Down from Keld, and the Figure Nobody Writes; with the Answers in the Margin, a Clerk's Correction in Ledgerhand, and a Counting Song in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A private letter on a strip of oiled packing-paper, written in charcoal and iron-gall, folded thrice and tied with a bit of wire; carried downriver from Sill to Greybank on an eel barge, answered in the margin, corrected on the back at the factor's house, and kept since in a dry tin among the quay's iron tallies
codex.provenance: Written at the smithy east of the Clay Yard in Low Kiln, Sill, in the last tend of Silt, Y.H. 813, by Harn, a smith who mends kiln irons, barrow irons and the collectors' cold-iron tubes, to Nessa his sister, who keeps the iron tally at the Greybank quay; carried eighteen leagues downriver on the eel barge, answered in her hand along the margin, and borrowed at the Court's factor's house, where a clerk set a correction on the back in Ledgerhand. It survives folded and wired in a tin of iron tallies, the charcoal rubbed thin at the folds, a thumb of brick-dust at the head, a tallow mark at the outer fold, a grey Ash print along the gutter where the writer's cuff passed, a smear of cold-iron scale at the foot, a strip torn from the second fold, one word struck through with a chisel-point and written again underneath in the recipient's hand, and a line on the back in a hand nobody has claimed.

codex.title: The Kingdom of Cold Iron, Being the Road-Book of Garl, a Potter of Nine Pots, Who Took a Cart of Coarse Bowls up the Rim Road to Keld Keep in the Thin Year and Came Back with Two Iron Clamps, a Warm-Stone Gone Cold, and a Figure on a Slate That Was Not the One He Gave; with the Reckoning of the Road, the Manner of the Weigh, the Song of the Descent, the Cup Nobody Takes, Two Borrowed Corrections, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A potter's road-book, set down first in charcoal on the backs of spoiled pot-warrants at the mouth of the shaft and copied at Greybank onto the back of a clay-and-tile docket voided by the Long Cold; the days in the potter's own hand, the prices in a sloped tally hand, the sayings of the Keep kept in the hearing and not translated, the verbs put back under every borrowed correction, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward
codex.provenance: Written in Ash and Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, at Keld Keep and again at Nine Pots, by Garl, a potter of the rival kiln hamlet eight leagues west of Sill, who took nine coarse bowls and a letter up the Rim Road to trade for iron and came back in Stone with four bowls whole, two in pieces, two iron clamps, a warm-stone that had kept a fire and had now gone cold, and a figure on a slate; carried down the Rim Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a voided docket. It survives folded into a strip of well-worn harness leather: coal smut worked into the head, iron-red from the mine-reeve's checking point at the second corner, a chip of Ferr lead in one gutter and a bead of Ninth Gallery lead shut in the fold which are not the same lead and have never been joined, a warm-stone shaving gone cold in the fourth leaf, a frost-feather pressed flat that was gone by noon, a tallow print at the head, a square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with a knife-point, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, a Court survey-clerk's correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own

codex.title: The Cold Place in the Wall, Being a Soldier's Field Notes on the Seam-Serpent of the First Seam Beneath Keld Keep; with the Song as It Is Not Sung, the Deep Tally, a Survey-Clerk's Ruling in Ledgerhand, a Vorr's Answer, and One Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A soldier's field book on one beast, set down as the record of a watch kept over the deep shaft and not as natural philosophy; the sayings in the hard Keldish speech with the endings struck off, the watch-song with the number left as it is not spoken, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled rim-seam rubbings, one ruling in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Court survey-clerk, one line in the broad slow hand of a Vorr come up from the Stones, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Bone and Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by Dren, a man of the Warden's watch set over the shaft mouth at Keld Keep, who states his number before his name and has never gone down the Descent; set down at the end of watches in the lamp-room at the head, first on the backs of rim-seam rubbings spoiled by wet slate and then on three leaves of rough survey paper sewn with wire into a board cover gone soft at the seam, carried down the Rim Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with a survey party's clamps and copied at Greybank onto the back of a voided weigh-slip. It survives with coal smut ground into the head off the writer's own sleeve, iron-red at the second corner off the mine-reeve's checking point, a smear of hot lead at the fold that has burnt one word clean through, a frost-feather pressed flat between the second and third leaves which was gone by noon, a warm-stone shaving gone cold shut in the fourth fold, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first watch to the last, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, one ruling in the narrow upright hand of a Court survey-clerk, one line in the broad slow hand of a Vorr, and the line at the foot

codex.title: The Collector's Day-Book, Being the Measures Drawn in Sill and the Clay Towns from the Last Market of Stone in Y.H. 812 through the Five to the Opening of the Slates in Y.H. 813, with the Embers, the Deduction, and the Note the Vessel Gave
codex.kind: A page from an officer's own pocket day-book; figures in Ledgerhand copied from the slate, the remarks in the hand that held the cold iron tube, a column of notes struck out by the College and drawn back by the officer, one figure struck and set above in a borrowed hand, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written on the road between Sill and Greybank in the last tend of Stone, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, through the Five and into Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates; carried in an oiled-paper wrap in the officer's coat, beside the tube in its wool sleeve. It survives with grey at the head of the ember column, iron filings worked into the gutter from the tube's wrap, a tallow thumb at the foot, a streak of bone-pale slip, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a damp tide-line from the Waiting Room, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the College, and one line at the foot nobody will own.

codex.title: The Cord Kept Dry, Being a Letter from a Mother at the Quay to Her Daughter on the Eve of Her Marriage, Concerning the Share That Passes Through Women, the Man Come Aboard, the Eight Sacks, and the Knot No Tally-Man Has Counted
codex.kind: A private letter on the back of a Council tide-draw spoiled by rain, written in charcoal gone over in iron-gall where the salt had got into the grain, folded four times and sewn with eel-sinew into a scrap of oiled sailcloth; carried up the Salt Road in a glass-carrier's coat to Greybank, answered along the margin in a younger hand, borrowed at the tide-tally house where a Council clerk set a correction on the outer fold in the leaning hand the damp has nearly taken, and kept since in a dry tin among the boat's share-cords
codex.provenance: Written at the Quay in Vhal in the last tend of Grain, Y.H. 813, by Vessa of the Quay, who holds a share in a salt boat through her mother and dips at the pans when the weather turns, to her daughter Luli, who is to be married on the flood to Daro, a man come aboard off the coast road; set down on the back of a tide-draw the Council left out in the rain, answered in the margin at Greybank on the daughter's way north, corrected on the outer fold at the tide-tally house, and kept folded and sewn in a dry tin among the boat's share-cords. It survives with a white salt bloom at the head, tar at the second fold, a fibre of wet net-cord pressed across the third crease, a green bead of Glaze Cliffs glass caught in the stitch, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, a ring of brine, a grey print along the outer fold that neither woman made and neither has swept, one word eaten away by the damp with the space left standing, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody has claimed

codex.title: The Cost of Carrying, Being a Winter Worth-Night at the Heaped Measure in Greybank, with Four Costings Put to the Barley Dish, the Factor's Clerk's Figures Entered Over Them, and the Grain in the Crack That Would Not Burn
codex.kind: An ale-keeper's telling of one night's contest, set down for the settling of an argument the granary never settled and not for the improvement of the reader; the costings in the words they were spoken, the sayings put to the dish and not to the room, the stake in grains of barley laid in a cracked dish, the tally in charcoal on the back of a grain-warrant voided by the granary's second count, the factor's clerk's figures entered above in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a carter's gloss in broad charcoal, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, at the alehouse called the Heaped Measure on the Clay Road in Greybank, where the road comes in from Sill and turns uphill before noon to the factor's table; set down by the woman who keeps the house, the fire and the barley dish, on the back of a grain-warrant spoiled by a second count, and copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a voided carriage-receipt, sewn with wire into a fold of oiled sacking and kept in the tin beside the lamp-wick, where nothing else in this house is kept dry. It survives with a thumb of wet clay at the head, a tallow thumb at the fold, a barley grain shut fast in a crack of the dish pressed into the paper, a press of frozen wool across the first leaf, a dark ring where small ale stood from the first costing to the last, a browned crust gone soft in the gutter, frost raised out of the paper on the climb up the Clay Road, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own, the charcoal rubbed thin where the warrant was carried in an apron, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor's clerk, one gloss in the broad charcoal of a carter, and the line at the foot which has never been claimed

codex.title: The Count in the Bone, Being the Sayings of the Vorr, Gathered at the Listening Stones and Glossed for a Man Who Wanted Them Translated
codex.kind: A keeper of the Keldish survey's gathering of the sayings, refusals, counting-maxims and death-words of the Vorr, set in Grathic letters on the back of a spoiled rim-seam rubbing because Vorr speech is not written and a notch cut in bone travels worse down a road than a letter; the sayings in the slow long-vowelled Rim speech, the glosses in the writer's own hand, with a Court survey-clerk's correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, one answer in the very large, very slow hand of a Vorr, a clamp-master's line in charcoal from the Duelling Floor, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Gathered over three Long Sittings in Bone and Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, at the Listening Stones five leagues above Keld Keep, by a keeper of the survey who had leave to sit within sight of the stones and was never allowed to touch the stone a Vorr keeps; written on the back of a rim-seam rubbing gone soft with wet slate, sewn with wire into a fold of oiled survey-cloth and carried down the Rim Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813, where a survey-clerk of the Court's factor at Greybank corrected it. It survives with grey dust of a blighted seam rubbed into the head, the same dust the Vorr mark their counting-stones with and do not sell, coal smut at the fold, a shaving of warm-stone that kept its heat one night on a stone floor and is cold now, a frost-feather pressed flat which was gone by noon, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead shut in the sewing, a tallow print beside which the doubled last joint of a finger has left its mark, a clamp-scratch across two glosses, a grey Ash print nobody will own, and the line at the foot which has never been claimed

codex.title: The Country Outside, Being the Account of Orven, a Carter out of Stonemouth, Who Took Lime to Keld Keep and Walked Past the Survey Post With a Warm-Stone in His Coat and Came Back Without the Reason; with the Reckoning of the Days That Held, the Table of What Was Given and What Was Taken, the Song of the Sitting Dead, Two Corrections in the Narrow Hand of a Factor's Clerk, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A carter's road-book, written first in charcoal on four strips of birch bark beyond the last pass and copied at Greybank onto the back of a lime-warrant voided by the Long Cold; the days in the carter's own hand with the lost ones left standing as gaps, the figures of the road in a sloped tally hand, the sayings of the country set down in the hearing and not translated, the verbs put back under every borrowed correction, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward
codex.provenance: Written beyond the Cold Pass and at Keld Keep in Ash and Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by Orven, a carter of Stonemouth who hauled lime up the Rim Road and went on past the post with a warm-stone in his coat; copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a voided lime-warrant and carried down the Ilm to Sill. It survives as five leaves of rough survey paper sewn with wire into a board cover gone soft at the seam: frost raised out of the grain on the climb and gone by noon, lime dust from the quarry worked into the gutter, a tallow thumb at the fold, a small grey stone from beyond the post sewn into the lower corner, a flake of warm-stone gone cold in the fourth leaf, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the factor's clerk at Greybank, one date scraped away with a knife-point, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own

codex.title: The Country That Empties, Being an Account of the Southern Empire of Sere Set Down by Tavi Salt, a Tally-Clerk of Vhal, Who Went Down with Glass and Salt and Came Back with Crowns He Could Not Spend; with the Prices of the South, the Four Bowls, the Song of the Wine-Press, Three Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A travelling tally-clerk's account, kept dry in a tarred tin and written first on salt-paper, then copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold; the figures in a sloped tally hand, the southern sayings kept in the hearing and not translated, the verbs put back underneath every borrowed correction, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward
codex.provenance: Written in Grain and Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in the Bowl of Sere and at a provincial bowl on the south road, by Tavi Salt, a tally-clerk out of the tide-tally house on the Quay at Vhal, who went south in Reed with two chests of Cliffs glass and a consignment of Sallow salt for a house of the Ten Bowls and came back in Ash with three gold crowns, a jar of wine whose contract had perished on the Salt Road, and a green-glazed bowl that cracked on the second morning at home. Copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a voided grain-warrant and carried up the Salt Road to Vhal. It survives soft at the fore-edge and sour with salt, with a white bloom at the head, a tar thumb at the fold, yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the sewing, a ring of warm wine at the third hour, a thumb of olive oil, myrrh worked into the grain, the fibre of a wet rope pressed into the second leaf, a green bead of Cliffs glass flattened into the lower corner, a gold crown pressed flat between the fourth and fifth leaves, a husk of southern grain stuck fast in the gutter, a scorched corner, one small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with a knife-point, three corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own

codex.title: The Song of the Cradle Kept Overnight, Being a Lullaby of the Waiting Room in Slate Row at Sill, Sung to a Child on the Night Before Its Banking, with the Manner of It, the Verses as the Maid Keeps Them, a Collector's Clerk's Correction Set Above in the Narrow Hand, a Mother's Gloss Pressed into the Margin, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A hearth-maid's lullaby of the last watch, set down in the low Grathic of the district; the verses said to the cradle and not to the child, the refrain kept by the room's own order of reaching, the correction of a collector's clerk standing above in the narrow upright hand, a mother's charcoal pressed into the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim
codex.provenance: Sung in the Waiting Room off Slate Row in Sill in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, the winter after the Long Cold, by a hearth-maid who keeps the birth-slates and has sat with the collected overnight for nine winters; set down because a collector's clerk come up from Greybank stood in the doorway with a slate under his arm and asked what the maids said to the children before the drawing, and wrote the answer down while she was still saying it, with the doing taken out and a figure put where a cradle should stand. Written in charcoal and the dregs of a tallow end on the back of a night-watch sheet spoiled by a wet thumb, the figures on the face of it gone soft, folded into a grey wool birth-cloth and kept in the fold of the maid's apron; carried up the Clay Road and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold, where the lowland name for that year was written below the southern one. It survives with a tallow thumb worked into the head, a crust-grease print on the second leaf, a ring where a cup of barley water stood from the first verse to the last and went cold without being drunk, a small pale round where a collector's tube-wrap was laid and nobody will own the wrap, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which a cuff left going through the room and nobody will own the cuff, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner, a thread of grey wool caught in the sewing, one word eaten clean away by damp and not written in again, the clerk's correction standing above, the mother's gloss pressed in below, and the line at the foot which has never been claimed

codex.title: The Book of the Open Table, Being the Figures Entered at the Court's Table Set at the Fringe of the Cross in Sill on the Three Account-Days of Ember, with the Bell Told Beside the Bell Heard, the Figure Read Beside the Figure Paid, and the Place Where a Number Went That Nobody Entered
codex.kind: A Court assessor's clerk's day-book kept at the table set in the open air at the Cross; figures in Ledgerhand, terse remarks in the hand that touches the top slate before it looks at the woman waiting, one column struck by a College clerk and drawn back underneath, noughts set beside blanks in a borrowed hand, and a line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at Sill at the Court's table at the Slate Row fringe of the Cross on the Account-days of Ember, Y.H. 813, the year after the Thin Year --- Ember 10, 20 and 30 --- and carried forward into the first tend of Grain; kept in the bottom drawer of the table under a loose slate and taken down when a figure is disputed, which on these three days it was not. It survives as one leaf of foolscap folded to the pocket, with an iron-gall thumb at the head, grey Ash worked into the outer fold, a tallow print where the lamp was held low, a pale streak of slip down the gutter, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a brown barley crust gone stiff in the fold, a pale round ring where a cold iron tube was set down and taken up, a damp tide-line from a board standing overnight in the rain, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, a column struck and drawn back, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the College, noughts set by a hand that is not mine, and one line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Cup at the Wall, Being the Drinking-Song of the Shift at the Shaft Mouth of Keld Keep, Sung Sitting When a Man Has Been Walled Into the Deep Seam; with the Passing by Number, the Place Kept at the End, a Survey-Clerk's Figure Set Above, a Leech's Objection from the Ninth Gallery, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A woman of the count at the mouth's drinking-song and walling-lament, set down in Grathic letters because Keldish is cut in bone and does not travel; the verses in the hard clipped Rim speech with the endings struck off, the rubrics in the writer's small charcoal hand, a Court survey-clerk's correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand above the lines, a leech's objection in a leaning hand pressed into the gutter, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Set down in Bone of Y.H. 812, the year the lowlands called the Thin Year, at the mouth of the First Seam beneath Keld Keep, by a woman of the count who has taken the numbers at the weigh for twenty-two years and puts the warm-stone into a boy's hand after the knife; written in charcoal on the back of a shift-tally spoiled by a wet thumb and a fall of hot-lead dust, carried down the Rim Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with the winter's lead and copied at Greybank onto the back of a voided weigh-slip, where a survey-clerk of the Court borrowed it and set his figure above hers. It survives in the count-woman's tin beside the nails, with coal smut ground into the head, an iron-red thumb at the second corner, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead shut in the fold, a shaving of warm-stone that held its heat one night on the stone floor and is cold now, a frost-feather pressed flat which was gone by noon, a ring of sour ale at the foot where the last cup stood, slate dust in the gutter, the clerk's correction above the verses, the leech's objection beneath them, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Cup in the Dark, Being Five Tellings of the Return at the Alehouse Called the Wet Wool in Low Kiln, Set Down the Morning After While the Dead Were Named in the Street
codex.kind: A housekeeper's record of a Long Night, written by daylight because nothing could be written in the dark; the order of the tellers in the house's hand, the tellings in the words they were told, a charcoal count of the cups, a clerk's figures entered over them and a carter's gloss beneath, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written on the Remembering, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, at the alehouse called the Wet Wool in Low Kiln of Sill, by the woman who keeps the room and takes the kiln hands' washing; set down from the dark of the Long Night before, on the back of a drying-tally spoiled when a wet hem went over it, in charcoal and pipe-clay, the house keeping no ink, sewn with a strand of grey wool into a fold of oiled sackcloth and kept in the meal crock behind the door, where nothing is kept dry. It survives with white pipe-clay ground into the head, a thumb of tallow, a ring of small ale gone dark, the press of a wet wool sleeve across the first leaf, a crust of frost along the outer edge gone soft, grey Ash worked into the gutter, the charcoal rubbed thin where a hand has gone over it, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor's clerk come up from Greybank on the next market morning, one gloss in the thick charcoal of a carter, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody's.

codex.title: The Day Tally of the First Seam, Being the Heads That Went Down and the Heads That Came Up at Keld Keep Through Bone of Y.H. 812, with the Iron Raised, the Lives Entered at Eleven Months, the Sweating Stopped Early, and the Place Where the Mountain's Number Is Held
codex.kind: A page from the mine-reeve's own day-tally book, kept by his counting-clerk at the mouth of the shaft; figures in Ledgerhand, the remarks in the clipped Keldish speech set down terse and without endings, the reeve's iron-red checking point set against two lines, a column of what came up in the men struck by a Court survey-clerk and drawn back underneath, one round nought put in the held place by a factor's leaning hand, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at the shaft mouth of the First Seam in Keld Keep through Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by the clerk who keeps the mine-reeve's day tally, carried up with the winter's iron in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 when the Rim Road opened, and copied at Greybank onto the back of a voided lamp-oil requisition. It survives sewn with wire into a fold of oiled survey-cloth: coal smut ground into the head off the reeve's sleeve, iron-red checking paint at two figures and along the margin, a warm-stone shaving shut in the fold that is warm on the coldest morning, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead in the lower corner, a cold-iron filing in the gutter out of the clamp-rack, a frost-fern raised out of the paper on the climb over the Cold Pass, a clamp-scratch across two columns, a thumb in coal dust nobody will claim, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed. There is no Last Day beneath this Keep; nothing is swept in the morning.

codex.title: The Sermon at the Dish-Niche, Being What a Man Who Came Back Thin Said at the Shrine of the Return in Sill on the Morning After the Weighing of Y.H. 812, with the Skimming-Song, the Dish-Row, a Factor's Clerk's Correction, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
