codex.kind: A lay sermon of the Temple of the Return preached at the shrine of the Return off the Cross in Sill, at the niche where households set a dish of water overnight for them whose measure has been banked; the sayings in the low Grathic of the town set down in the shelf-keeper's charcoal, the skimming-song with the gap left the length of a dish being wiped, the dishes in a shelf-tally, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor's clerk come up from Greybank, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Preached on the morning after the Weighing, in the five days outside the months, of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a man of the shrine who had come back thin from the north two winters before and had kept the dish-shelf since, to the women who came up from Low Kiln with their dishes after the year's figures had been read; written that evening by the woman who keeps the shelf and the shrine's door, in charcoal and the dregs of a tallow lamp on the back of a spoiled levy notice gone soft at one corner, folded twice and tied with a thread of grey wool, and kept in the niche behind the shelf where the marked clay dishes stand. It survives with a tallow thumb worked into the head, a crescent of dry river silt along the gutter from a morning the leaf lay on the shrine step, a chip of pale dish-clay shut in the fold, a thread of grey wool through the tie, a ring where a dish of water stood from the first voice to the last, a bead of beeswax with a grey hair caught in it, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the clerk's correction standing above the sayings, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a voided grain-warrant, with the verbs put back and the empty place left empty.

codex.title: The Dish of Salt, Being a Guessing-Night at the Head of the Quay in the Long Cold, Four Questions Put to the Brazier, the Answers Said to the Dish, and What a Council Clerk Made of the Morning
codex.kind: A room-keeper's account of one winter night, set down for the settling of a wager and not for the improvement of the reader; the questions in the words they were spoken, the wagers in pinches of salt in a dish, the tally taken off the dish at dawn, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Council clerk, a salt-wife's gloss pressed into the margin, and a line at the foot in a hand that nobody will claim
codex.provenance: Set down at the head of the Quay in Vhal in Stone of Y.H. 811, the Long Cold, when the coast pass was shut and no cart came down from Greybank in nine days, by the woman who keeps the brazier room there; copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a spoil Council salt warrant, sewn with tarred thread into a fold of oiled sailcloth and kept in a tin above the brazier, which is the only dry place in the house. It survives with a white salt bloom in the gutter, a thumb of tar at the head, a wine ring near the fourth question, wet wool pressed across the first leaf, a crust of frost along the outer edge, a green bead of cliff-glass folded into the second fold, a fish-hook nick, a grey print nobody will own, the clerk's correction standing above the room's words, the salt-wife's gloss standing in the margin, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody's.

codex.title: The Drawing Book, Being the Measures of the Sill District Entered at Greybank in the Last Tends of Stone, Y.H. 812
codex.kind: A page from the tally-book of the Court's collector's clerk at Greybank; figures in Ledgerhand, with the officer's remarks in the hand that made the draw
codex.provenance: Written in the factor's house at Greybank in Y.H. 812, the year the clay towns call the Thin Year, by the clerk who keeps the tally for Sill and the villages about; the officers are entered on the leaf and the clerk is not. Copied forward at the Opening of the Slates in Y.H. 813. It survives as a quire of paper soft at the fore-edge in a tin on the factor's shelf: a grey thumb at the head of the ember column, a streak of slip down the gutter, a green bead of glaze in the lower corner, a drag of Ash along the foot, one figure struck through and set above in a second hand, and a line at the foot which the factor's clerk did not write.

codex.title: The Drawing Table, Being the Standing Rules of the Collectors of Sill and Greybank for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices at the Table in Slate Row and on the Clay Road, with the Table of Years, the Wrapping-Song Pasted Inside the Wool Sleeve, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A table-copy of the collectors' standing rules in the hand of an old officer who keeps the wool sleeves and the roll of hands behind the collector's table in Slate Row; the articles in short road sayings, the years and the faults in tables, the wrapping-song pasted inside a wool sleeve, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a College clerk, one in the soft-cuffed hand of a factor's clerk at Greybank, three lines in the thick charcoal of a hearth-maid come up from Low Kiln, and a line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: First gathered at Greybank in Y.H. 719, the year the factor's house began to keep a roll of hands beside its roll of measures, and copied forward from the sleeve and not from a book, which is why the rule about the grey is rubbed nearly through at the corner and the rule about the wool is as sharp as the day it was set down; this leaf written in Smoke of Y.H. 813 by a collector who has drawn on the Clay Road for twenty-six years and keeps the table's sleeves and its roll of hands, after the Thin Year and the Opening of the Slates. It survives folded small enough for a coat pocket, carried in the wool sleeve of a tube that has never once drawn the warmth out of the paper: grey worked under the nails at the head, iron filings ground into the gutter off the tube's wrap, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl at the Cross with the sweetness still at her mouth, frost-crisp along one edge from a morning on the Rim Road, a tallow thumb, a damp tide-line from the Waiting Room along the foot, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away and no other put in its place, two corrections in borrowed hands, three lines in the margin, and a line at the foot nobody will own

codex.title: The Price of a Dry Foot, Being the Market of the Standing Post and the Dues of the Boardwalks, the Peat Paths and the Marsh Roads, Cut on Count-Sticks and Copied into the South's Letters
codex.kind: A board-man's tally of the marsh's prices and road-dues, cut as notches in a count-stick and written on oiled reed for a factor who cannot read a notch; the figure told below set above the figure taken here, one place left smooth and not noughted, the verbs put back where a borrowed hand took them out, two corrections in other hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at the Standing Post in the Fenmarch by Wade, who cuts the reeves' sticks there and learned his south's letters off a peat-tally clerk at Greybank, though he keeps his own accounts in notches; begun in Reed of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, after the Long Cold, carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and written up again at the Reed Cut of that year. It survives as one strip of oiled reed and two leaves of birch bark sewn with eel-sinew, folded and kept in a dry tin under the loose board at the Post; with a cross-notch cut at the head for a fine paid, a dry-mud thumb, a bog-water tideline along the gutter that has taken two figures clean off, a cross-cut from a reeve's point, a reed-wolf's tooth nick at the second corner, eel slime at the foot, the dark wet mark of a board laid across the third leaf, a grey Ash smear nobody will own, one knot of grey wool tied through a hole in the first strip which the writer will not untie, two corrections in borrowed hands, and one line at the foot nobody will claim.

codex.title: The Dry Tally at Reedholt, Being the Market of the East Marsh in Bits, Sticks and Kind, with the Dues of the Marsh Road, the Boardwalks and the Cuts, Kept Under an Apron and Copied at Greybank
codex.kind: An eel-trader's tally of what the east marsh fetches and what the ways between its villages take, the figures named into an apron and not across a table, peat weighed at the dry set beside the same peat weighed at the quay, with a column left as a place and not a nought, two corrections in borrowed hands, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Kept by Meg Sedge, who buys eels on the marsh road and weighs peat at the dry in Reedholt, in the east marsh four leagues east of Sill; set down first in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, after the Long Cold, and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, onto the back of a spoiled peat-tally at Greybank. It survives folded into oiled sacking under a loose board at the dry, sewn with eel-sinew, with a peat thumb ground into the head, a bog-water tideline that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, dried eel slime at the fore-edge, a fish-hook nick at the head, a grey Ash print along the gutter nobody will own, a press of wet sedge across the third leaf, a knot of grey wool tied through a hole in the first leaf which the writer will not untie, a small pale round place where a collector's cuff was laid, two corrections in hands that are not the writer's, and one line at the foot nobody will claim.

codex.title: The Litany of the Ebb, Being the Order of the Return as the Quay of Vhal Keeps It
codex.kind: A litany of the Return said over the salted boat at the turning of the ebb, the dipper reading from the bollard and the women of the boats answering; with the rubrics of the quay, seven stations and their answer, a Council clerk's correction, and two sayings at the foot that will not agree
codex.provenance: Written at the Quay in Vhal in Grain of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Ova Rill, a dipper of the Salt Pans under Neri Sail, on the back of a tide-tally spoiled by a wet thumb in the tide-tally house; borrowed on a market morning in Ash and corrected by a clerk of the Council of Tides; copied forward in Silt of Y.H. 813 into a quire of salt-paper kept in a dry tin among what the house calls nothing. It survives soft at the fold and furred with white salt, with a tar thumb at the head, the print of a wet rope along the gutter, a nick from a fish-hook, a green bead of cliff-glass pressed into the lower corner, a peck from a brine-gull that took the corner and not the word, and one line of the fourth station eaten away by damp, which the writer has not tried to write again.

codex.title: The Eel-Wife's Book, Being Remedies for the Cold in One Foot, the Glass-Eel's Clamp, the Bone in the Throat, the Fish-Knob Cut, the Child Come Up Drowned, the Sweet at the Mouth, the Birth-Flower and the Third-Night Chill, Set Down at the Fishstairs Below the North Bridge with the Errors Left Standing
codex.kind: A fish-midwife's and healer's book of remedies in the short wet speech of the Fishstairs, written in Grathic letters so a factor's daughter might read it; the cures in an eel-wife's hand on the back of a fish-bill spoiled by brine, the objections of a physician come down from Greybank pressed into the margin, the corrections of a factor's clerk in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a second hand in charcoal at the foot of the remedies, a counting song with the place where the twelfth should stand left as it is sung, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at the Fishstairs in Sill between Ash of Y.H. 812 and Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the Long Cold and the Thin Year, by Vessa of the Fishstairs, who dressed the hands of the eel-women below the north bridge and caught their children in the fish-sheds for two-and-twenty years; begun on the back of a fish-bill that a spill of brine took clean, folded into oiled sacking and carried in a tin among the net-needles, and copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a weigh-slip voided by the damp. It survives with river silt worked into the grain at the head, a grey tideline of dried eel slime down the fold which has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a fish-scale pressed flat into the lower corner, a brine ring gone white on the third, a thumb of tar, a green bead of High Kiln glaze pressed in by a girl with the sweetness at one mouth-corner, a scorch where the stall lamp caught the fourth leaf, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which nobody will own, three objections in the cold margin hand of the physician, the clerk's upright hand above the cures, a second hand in charcoal below them, and the line at the foot

codex.title: The Eleven Months, Being the Sayings of the Under-Vessed of Keld, Gathered at the Shaft Mouth and Glossed for a Man Who Has Never Been Bought
codex.kind: A windlass-man's gathering of the proverbs, month-words, rope-maxims and bitter small sayings of the bought hands of the First Seam, set in Grathic letters though the sayings come in four tongues; the sayings in the short speech of the deep, the glosses in the writer's own charcoal, a mine-reeve's red cross, a Court survey-clerk's correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a southern word left standing where no northern word would come, one note in a clamp-master's coal, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Gathered at Keld Keep in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Orv of the Rope, a windlass-man who has lowered and raised men at the shaft mouth for two and thirty years, from bought hands waiting their turn at the weigh and from those who sat by the lamp-room door with a month left in them; written in charcoal on the back of a spoiled month-tally, cut once at the edge with a tally-knife where a word would not come, carried down the Rim Road with the first carts of Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a voided grain-warrant. It survives folded into a tarred rope-glove, with coal smut ground into the head, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead shut in the fold, iron filings caught in the gutter off the clamps, a warm-stone shaving that kept a little heat through a night on the stone floor, a frost-feather pressed flat that was gone by noon, a tallow thumb, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the knife-cut standing in the margin, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody's

codex.title: The Eleven Weeks, Being an Extract from the Chronicle of the Keeping Concerning the Rising in Low Kiln and the Forty-One, with the List Set Against the Corners That Were Not Swept
codex.kind: A chronicler's extract from the annals of the Keeping, copied from a Hearthseat original; the year-entries in Ledgerhand, Pell Varr's list entered as it stands, the answer of the hearth-maids kept in the margin, one song carried out of Low Kiln, and two hands of correction, one of which no hand will own
codex.provenance: Written at the Hearthseat in the College of Assessors in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the keeper of the chronicle of the Keeping, who signs nothing and calls himself only the continuator; copied from an original of Y.H. 669 kept face down in the roll-room and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives as five leaves of foolscap sewn with wire into a board cover, kept in the chronicle drawer under the narrow window that looks toward the Keel: an iron-gall thumb at the head, a soot print where a leaf was held too near the Hearth grate, a drip of tallow gone hard as a fingernail, slate dust in the gutter, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the continuator did not make and will not sweep, one line struck through and written again underneath in his own hand, and one correction in the narrow upright hand of the College which takes the verbs out.

codex.title: The Ember House Book of Bowls, Being Remedies for the Feast-Sickness, the Sweetness at the Gum, the Mill-Cough, the Bowl-Burn, a Graft That Wants, the Quiet on the Third Day, the Name Inside the Bowl and a Cut from a Bowl-Shard, Set Down in the Slave Quarters with the Errors Left Standing
codex.kind: A house-leech's and midwife's book of remedies in the manner of the Sunbowl houses, written in northern letters so a factor's daughter might read it, with the long southern vowels left in the words that will not fit; the cures in a house-leech's hand on the backs of spoiled feast-orders, a physician's objections come down from Greybank pressed into the margin, the corrections of a factor's clerk in a hand with a little gold in it, a song for the third watch with a place where the old name would stand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at the Ember bowl-house in the Bowl of Sere between Ash of Y.H. 811 and Ilmen of Y.H. 813, in the years the northern factors call the Thin Year and the Long Cold, which in Sere were two good harvests and a high price for measures; by Halia of the Ember House, a house-leech who caught the children of the quarters and laid out the bowls at the feasts for three-and-twenty years. Begun on the backs of feast-orders spoiled by wine, sewn with silk into a fold of clean linen and carried in the sleeve against a small green bead of broken glaze; carried north by a factor and copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a discarded price-list. It survives with a thumb of lamp-oil at the head, a wine tideline that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a flake of gold in the gutter, a chip of green glaze pressed into the lower corner, a scorch where a spark off the open court fire caught the third leaf, a long black hair bound with a bronze bead caught in the fold, a pale round greased print where a bowl-surgeon laid his pad, objections in the cold margin hand of a physician, corrections in the upright hand of a factor's clerk, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: The Empty Oar, Being a Quay-Tale Told at the Rope-End in the Ash, with the Wager of a Quart, the Seat That Was Counted Full, the Tide-Clerk's Figure Set Over It, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A salt-man's tale told in a laid-up winter, set down for the settling of a wager and not for the improvement of the reader; the rules of the house in the hand that keeps it, the tale in the words it was told, the question in the words it was put, the night's score in charcoal on the bench end, the tide-clerk's entries set above in a hand the damp has begun to run, a boat-woman's gloss in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Ash of Y.H. 813, the dark month, at the alehouse called the Rope-End on the Quay in Vhal, by the man who keeps the house, the quart and the bench the laid-up galley-men sit on; told to him by a man off a salt galley who had rowed the pulled benches seven years and come back with hands that would not close. Set down in charcoal on the back of a spoiled tide-draw, the wet already into one corner, carried up the Salt Road in the first cold of Stone and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the damp, where a tide-clerk borrowed the leaf and set his figures above the telling. It survives folded in a strip of hemp tied with eel-sinew and kept in the tin behind the door, where nothing else in this house is kept dry: salt raised white in the fold, tar at the head where a thumb held the leaf in the draught, a ring where a quart stood from the first word to the last, the press of a wet sleeve across the second leaf, grey Ash along the gutter which the writer did not put there, a curl of hemp in the sewing, one correction in the narrow upright hand of the tide-clerk, a gloss in the small close hand of a woman who holds a share through her mother, and a line at the foot which nobody has claimed

codex.title: The Line of Figures and the Line of Squares, Being an Extract from the Chronicle of the Cantons
codex.kind: An annalist's extract from the chronicle of the Keeping, being the account of the Empty Cantons; copied from a Hearthseat original and set beside a surveyor's field note, a Fen song, and two hands of correction in the margin
codex.provenance: Written at Greybank in the factor's house in the last tend of Stone, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, by the keeper of the annals there (the office stands on the roll, the hand does not); copied from an original kept face down in the roll-room of the Hearthseat. It survives as four leaves of foolscap sewn with wire into a board cover, kept in the annals drawer beside the winter tallies: a brown iron-gall thumb at the head, slate dust in the gutter, a tar print from the quay along the fore-edge, a dried Fen reed folded between the second and third leaves, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, one correction in the narrow hand of a clerk of the College and one in a hand nobody will own.

codex.title: The Litany of the Emptying, Being the Order of the Return as the Third Bowl of Sere Keeps It at the Burning of the Slates
codex.kind: A litany of the Return said in the open court at the end of the feast, while the wine is warm and one household's debt-slates burn; the keeper of the fire reading from the bowl's lip and the bowl answering by emptying its cups; set down by the keeper of the court fire with the rubrics of the court, eight stations and their answer, the burning said between the stations, the correction of a factor's clerk from Greybank in narrow upright Ledgerhand, the notes of a woman returned three times, and a line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in the court of the house of Ardel in the third bowl of Sere in Grain of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Vessa Ardel, keeper of the court fire and reader of names at the feast, on the back of a wine-tally spoiled by a warm thumb in the bowl's counting room, the third-day hand unsteady and the wine of the public bowl gone cold on it; carried north with the grain factor's convoy in Smoke and corrected at Greybank in Ash of Y.H. 812 by a clerk of the factor's office; copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 into a quire kept in a dry tin under a fold of myrrh cloth. It survives soft along the fold and scorched at the upper edge, with a ring of warm wine at the head, myrrh worked into the grain, a grey grain of Ash from the public bowl pressed into the fold, a green smear at the lower corner from the thumb of a girl with the sweetness of the glaze still on her mouth, a leaf of gold beaten thin between the last two leaves, a hair, a line of wine that ran out toward the gutter and stopped, the eight stations and their answer, one correction in Ledgerhand, the margin in a warm sloped hand, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward

codex.title: The Ending Put Back, Being a Letter from the Wine-List at the Ember Bowl-House in the Bowl of Sere to a Woman of the Grain Mills South of the City, Concerning a Spoiled Sheet, a Name Whose Last Syllable the House Would Not Enter, the Gold Hand in the Physician's Book, and a Girl at the Presses with a Line at Her Gum; with the Wine-List as Kept and as Entered, a Press-Song with Its Last Line Put Back, Three Corrections, an Answer in Charcoal, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A private letter on the back of a wine-list spoiled at the third hour, written in burnt stick and charcoal, folded twice and carried five leagues south on a mill cart; answered along the margin in the hard Grathic letters, corrected at the house in the leaning hand of the tally-clerk and above that in the narrow upright hand of a factor's clerk, and kept since under the stack of mouth-down bowls on the lower shelf
codex.provenance: Written in Grain of Y.H. 813 at the Ember bowl-house in the Bowl of Sere by Neva, a northern bond-woman who keeps the wine-list outside the barred counting room, to Hedda of the grain mills south of the city, who set a charcoal correction under the gold hand in the house-physician's book and would not give her name; carried south on the mill cart at the turning of Grain, answered in the margin at the mills, borrowed by the house tally-clerk at the next feast and corrected, then folded back under the bowls. It survives with the yellow dust of the burning winds worked into the first fold, a wine-ring at the head from the third hour, a thumb of olive oil at the outer crease, a fleck of gold leaf from a contract carried past on a tray, a husk of southern grain shut in the gutter, a scorch where the burnt stick lay down while a bell was rung, a drop of myrrh from the fire-shrine gone hard at the foot, the three corrections standing one above another, the answer pressed hard at the ends of words, and a grey Ash print nobody will own along the outer fold.

codex.title: The Fifth Breath, Being the Firing Song of the Kilns of Low Kiln, Kept at the Damper with One Verse Held Back for the Watch
codex.kind: A firing-woman's watch song of the clay yards of Sill, pricked with a kiln-needle into soft clay and fired with the pots, so that the words are burnt into the body of a tile and cannot be struck out; the Grathic in the women's own half-sung manner, said to the fire and not to a person, with a Court clerk's copy on the back of a Greybank weigh-slip in Ledgerhand above it, and one line at the back in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Cut into a tile in the Clay Yard of Low Kiln by Wenna, a firing-woman of the third kiln, in Ember of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, and fired with a standing load, the words going into the throat green and coming out hard; the tile was set in a niche of the damper-shed where the watchers put their hands to warm them, and is kept there still. In Ilmen of Y.H. 813 a clerk of the factor at Greybank made a copy on the back of a spoiled weigh-slip, being a man who cannot leave a figure alone, and struck at the copy what he could not strike at the tile; the two lie folded together in a fold of oiled sacking. It survives coal-black in the gutter, with slip dried bone-pale in the letter-cuts, a thumb in slip at the head, a green bead of lead glaze melted into one corner in the firing and sweet to this day, a burn-pit where a coal fell, grey Ash along the base that comes off on a finger, and a hairline crack that goes around the word *fifth* and does not cross it. The clerk's hand stands above the copy and the women's words under it, as the fire keeps above and below in one kiln.

codex.title: The Fifth Eel, Being the Trap-Drawing Song of the Weir Above Sill, Sung at First Light as the Baskets Come Up, with the Four That Go to the Creel, the One That Goes Back over the Rail, a Girl's Gloss Pressed into the Margin, a Factor's Clerk's Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A work song of the eel-weir, counted in the lifts of the basket and on the knuckles of the left hand; the verses said down into the basket and not up to the bank, the fifth said and never sung; the rubrics of the boards in the writer's own charcoal, a girl with a creel's gloss in thick charcoal, a Greybank clerk's figures standing above in Ledgerhand, and one line at the foot nobody will claim
codex.provenance: Sung on the plank walk at the Weir, one league upriver of Sill, since before the Fish Blessing was kept on the flat stone, and set down in Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the thaw year, in the trap-hut where the eels are salted, by a woman of the Weir who has drawn the baskets for nine-and-twenty years and would put no name to the leaf; written in charcoal thinned with eel-slime on the back of a spoiled salt-tally from the Fishstairs, folded twice and tied with a strip of grey wool, carried in the breast of her apron against a square of sacking gone soft with salt; copied forward at Greybank onto the back of a weigh-slip gone stiff with brine. It survives with slime dried grey into the grain at the head, salt white at the fold where her wrists touched it, a silt tideline along the gutter, an eel-scale pressed flat in the lower corner, a bone the length of a thumbnail between the third and fourth leaf, a reed-fibre caught in the seam, a tar thumb nobody will own, the girl's gloss in the margin, the clerk's figures standing above, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: The Fifth in the Trace, Being the Tale the Old Carter Told at the Bent Nail on a Night the Rim Road Was Shut, with the Keeper's Margin, a Survey-Clerk's Correction, and the Line Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A wayhouse keeper's record of one tale told aloud in the cold months, set down from the mouth for the settling of an argument the road never settled; the tale in the carter's own Grathic, the keeper's glosses in the hand she keeps the lamp by, the tally of a cart's iron in charcoal on a way-bill gone soft with snow-melt, a Keldish survey-clerk's ruling entered over it in narrow upright Ledgerhand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, at the wayhouse called the Bent Nail on the Rim Road six leagues short of Keld Keep, by the woman who keeps the house and the lamp and will not let a slate lie on her table; set down first on the back of a factor's way-bill spoiled by snow-melt and then on a strip of birch bark, sewn with wire and kept in a tin beside the lamp wick, where nothing else in this house is kept dry. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 when the road opened and the first iron carts came down. It survives with coal smut ground into the head, a frost-feather pressed flat between the second and third leaves that was gone by noon, a press of wet wool across the first leaf, a bent nail shut in the fold that came out of the keeper's own door, a small-ale ring, a grey Ash print along the gutter that is not hers, the charcoal rubbed thin where the way-bill was carried in a coat pocket, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a survey-clerk of the Court who came up from Greybank with the thaw, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody's

codex.title: The Book of the Figure Set Above, Being the Figures Struck and Written Over in the Collectors' and Assessors' Books of Sill, Greybank and the Hearthseat, with the Hands That Set Them, the Terse Remarks Left Underneath, the Correcting-Song, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A page from the correction-register of an under-clerk of the College of Assessors in Slate Row of the Hearthseat; the struck figures and the figures written over them copied in the narrow upright hand, the remarks in the hands that made the draws, the verbs put back underneath where they were taken out, one column struck and drawn back again, and a line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Slate Row of the Hearthseat in the last tend of Ash, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813; copied from the correction-leaves of the collector's table at Sill, the factor's house at Greybank and the College's own benches, the upper hand in each case kept apart from the lower and both left standing. It survives folded into a quire of spoiled Weighing notices, kept in the under-clerk's tin beside the second file: iron-gall worked into the head, slate dust ground into the gutter, iron filings from a tube's wool wrap caught in the fold, a tallow thumb at the foot, a streak of bone-pale slip along the fore-edge, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a red clip-score across two rows, a damp tide-line from the sealed-file room along the foot, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, three corrections in borrowed hands, and one line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Sermon at the Fire-Shrine, Being What the Bowl-Priest Said Over the Four Bowls at the Ember House on a Name-Day in Smoke of Y.H. 812, with the Pouring-Song Left as It Is Sung, the Bowls in a Wine-List, the Gold Hand Above, a Bond-Woman's Charcoal Beneath, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A sermon of the Spending preached at the fire-shrine of the Ember bowl-house in the Bowl of Sere; the sayings in the long-vowelled courtesy of the south set down in Grathic letters by a northern bond-woman of the wine-press, the pouring-song with the fourth silence left as it is sung, the four bowls in a wine-list table, one correction in the thin gold of the house tally-clerk, one in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor's clerk at Greybank, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Preached by Valen Openhand, the Bowl-Priest, come down from the open court of the Bowl of Sere to the small fire-shrine within the Ember house, on the name-day of the house's youngest daughter in Smoke of Y.H. 812, when the burning winds stood and the fourth bowl was set out as it is set out at every feast; written that evening by a northern bond-woman who keeps the wine-list at the house press, in charcoal on the back of a wine-list spoiled at the third hour, folded into oiled silk and kept within the clay bowl in which the shrine's fire is carried at the turning of the year. It survives with gold dust worked into the head off the clerk's cuff, yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the fold, a ring of warm wine on the second leaf, an olive thumb at the head, a grain husk stuck fast in the gutter, a flake of myrrh from a burial cloth shut in the crease, a scorched corner where the leaf lay near the fire, a shard of green northern glaze pressed into the lower corner, a gold crown flattened between the third and fourth leaves, the gold correction standing above the charcoal, the Greybank hand set above both, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied at Greybank in Ash of Y.H. 812 into the factor's file of southern sayings, with the verbs put back and the fourth silence left the length it is sung.

codex.title: The Firing Cup, Being the Drinking Song of Low Kiln at the Draw, with the Order of the Cup, the Verses as They Go Round, a Kiln-Master's Correction in Broad Charcoal, a Clerk's Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss from the Woman Who Keeps the Birth-Slates, and One Verse at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A kiln-house drinking song for the end of a firing, taken down from the mouths of the yard in the low half-sung speech of Grath; the cup passed hand to hand and no man pouring for himself, the verses said to the kiln mouth and not to the company, a kiln-master's broad charcoal set above, a factor's clerk's figures in narrow upright Ledgerhand above that, a hearth-maid's small careful gloss in the margin, and a last verse in a hand nobody will claim
codex.provenance: Set down in Low Kiln of Sill in Ember and Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, at the draw of the Vail kiln and three firings after, by Tessa of the Racks, a woman who turns the drying racks two doors up the Clay Yard and keeps the firing cup; written in charcoal and tallow on the back of a kiln tally spoiled by a wet thumb, sewn with iron wire into a fold of grey sacking and kept in a meal crock behind the lowest rack. Carried up the clay road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold. It survives soft at the fold and gritty with slip, with a grey curl of fired clay at the head, a thumb of tallow, a brown crust-grease print on the second leaf, a ring of small ale gone sour where the cup stood from the first verse to the last, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner where a girl with sweetness at her mouth leaned over to see the writing, a scorch where the leaf lay too near the kiln mouth, grey Ash along the gutter that nobody will own, a twist of grey wool through a hole in the first leaf which the writer will not untie, two corrections set one above the other, a gloss in the margin, and a verse at the foot in a hand that has never come forward

codex.title: The First Book of the Chronicle of the Keeping, Being an Extract Concerning the Finding of the Chamber Already Warm, the First Returns of Y.H. 3, the Setting Up of the Three Offices, the Printing of the Figure One in Twelve, the Four Wells Sealed, and the Line of Empty Squares; with the Kindling Song, the Table of the Founding Years, Two Corrections in the Upright Hand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A keeper's extract from the oldest volume of the chronicle of the Keeping, being the first book, which lies nearer the fire than any other book in the Hearthseat; the founding years in the oldest and smoothest Ledgerhand, the rough first entries showing through under it where the ink has gone brown, the figure set on the notice in a clean round hand, the three offices entered as a list of rooms and duties, the kindling song taken down from a woman who had sung it at the grate for forty years, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the College, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward
codex.provenance: Written at the Hearthseat in the Weighing Hall, beside the grating of cold iron, in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the keeper of the first book, who appears on no roll and signs only *the office of the first book*; copied from the volume kept in a box on the inner side of the Hall since before the College was built, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives as five leaves of thick vellum gone brittle at the head from the heat that comes up through the grating, sewn with iron wire into a board cover warped out of true: the ink at the head the colour of weak tea and the ink in the gutter still black, soot from the grate worked into the grain of the first leaf, a coal gone cold shut in a nail-hole of the cover which nobody will say came from the first fire, slate dust along the fold where a surveyor laid his slate and was told to move it, a tallow thumb at the second corner, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first copying to the last, a square of bare vellum where a word was scraped away and not written back, the figure struck and written again beneath in the keeper's own hand, two corrections in the upright College hand, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the keeper did not make and has not swept, and the line at the foot

codex.title: The First Measure, Being the Collector's Own Leaf for the Hearth Drawing in Low Kiln on Stone 12 of Y.H. 812, with the Embers, the Deduction, the Note the Room Gave, the Child Worse Before Dusk, and the Figure Read Twice at the Cross; Written in the Hand That Carried the Tube and Corrected in Two Others
codex.kind: A page from a collector's pocket ledger; figures in Ledgerhand copied from the day-slate, the remarks terse and in the hand that unwrapped the wool and held the tube, one column struck by a College clerk and drawn back beneath his words, a passive verb set above each of mine, one sentence written over by a factor's man, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in the Clay Yard of Low Kiln and in the death-house two doors down from the Vail kiln-house on Stone 12, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, the day of the Hearth Drawing; copied forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and carried in the oiled-paper wrap in the collector's coat beside the tube in its wool sleeve. It survives with grey worked under the nails at the head, iron filings ground into the gutter off the tube's wrap, a tallow thumb where the lamp was held low, a bone-pale streak of slip from a thrower's forearm, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a pale round ring where a cold tube was set down on the leaf, the circle of a milk-cup pressed into the second fold, a damp tide-line along the foot out of a house where a pot was broken at the door, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with the tube's edge, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of a College clerk, one in the leaning hand of a factor's man from Greybank, and one line at the foot nobody will own

codex.title: Of the Five Days Outside the Months, Being Title the Third of the Ordinances of the Keeping: the Kindling, the Weighing, the Long Night, the Remembering and the Last Day; with the Table of Days, the Things Not Entered, the Fire-Carrying Verse, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: An extract from the Court's ordinances, written out for the counter of the Court's room in Slate Row, Sill, with the marginal hand of the clerk who keeps the five-day slate; the articles in Ledgerhand and the verbs restored beneath them, the days and the things not entered in a table, the carrying-verse as it is said under the covered pot, one line scored with a bread crust, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed
codex.provenance: Copied at Sill in Slate Row in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, from Title the Third of the Ordinances of the Keeping as set down in the first years and confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of Y.H. 418, added to after the Rising of Y.H. 668, in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year; survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire in a slate-coloured board cover, kept in the drawer under the counter between the bell-cord and the tallow end and taken down when the months leave off: a tallow thumb at the head, grey Ash worked into the outer fold, a scorch along the first leaf where a covered pot was set down, a bead of lead glaze, a brown score where a crust was laid, a damp tideline along the foot, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own

codex.title: The Sermon at the Flat Stone, Being What Was Said Over the Traps on Ilmen 15 of Y.H. 812, with the Old Words Left in Knots Because Fen Cant Will Not Write
codex.kind: A sermon of the Weir preached at the blessing stone on the north bank at the Weir, one league upriver of Sill; the saying in Grathic, the three old lines held in the margin as knots of grey wool, with the tally-keeper's corrections, a Court clerk's in Ledgerhand, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Preached at the Fish Blessing by an old woman of the Weir who had stood at the stone at thirty blessings, over the traps lifted and set on their sides on the plank walk, on Ilmen 15, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year; written that evening by a woman of the Weir who keeps the eel tally and has no slate-name, on the back of a weigh-slip spoiled by a wet figure out of Greybank, and sewn with eel-sinew into the folded reed wrapper that holds the knot-accounts in the Eel House. It survives with a salt crust at the head where a flat hand was set to brush the grit from the cut, a silt tideline along the gutter from a morning the plank walk stood under water, eel slime on the second leaf, a fish-hook nick nobody will own, a grey Ash print from a cuff at the stone, three knots left over right with the tail under against the three old lines, and a fourth knot tied through a hole in the first leaf for a word the preacher would not give out. Copied once at Greybank in Silt, Y.H. 812, and again in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the knots left as they were tied.

codex.title: Of the Body Found, the Uncollected Dead, and the Ash Gathered Where No House Sent for the Collector, Being a Standing Order of the Keeping Copied into the Court's Room at Slate Row in Sill with the Margin of the Clerk Who Enters the Found; with the Table of Findings, the Form Left Blank, the Covering-Song Said Over the Face, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: An extract from the Court's ordinances, written out for the counter of the Court's room in Slate Row, Sill, with the marginal hand of the clerk who keeps the found-slate; the articles in Ledgerhand and the verbs restored beneath them, the findings and what was found with them in a table, the form of a finding left blank, the covering-song said low over the face, one line scored away with the edge of a boot-heel, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed
codex.provenance: Copied at Sill in the Court's room in Slate Row in Stone of Y.H. 813, the deep-winter month, from a standing order of the Keeping sent down to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of Y.H. 418 and set down in this form in the years after the Rising of Y.H. 668, added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812; carried forward at each Opening of the Slates. It survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, kept in the tin beside the found-slate under the counter where the clip and the brand lie together in a cloth: a grey Ash thumb at the head, black peat worked into the gutter off a finder's boot, iron filings from a tube-wrap laid on the counter and never used, a stale crumb of barley bread at the second fold, the pale ring of a pot set down and not broken, a curl of grey wool through the tie-hole, a green bead of lead glaze pressed in by a girl who came to ask about a body and did not ask, one word scored with a boot-heel in the lower margin, a washing-water tide-line along the foot, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Fourth Name, Being a Letter from a Room with Good Light in Greybank to a Sister of the Ember House in the Bowl of Sere, with the Three Deaths Set Down, the Bowl-Song, a Factor's Correction in Ledgerhand, and the Answer Left in the Margin
codex.kind: A letter between two women of one great house, the one written in the open courtesy of Sere and the other answered in the same warm hand; a tally of three names against three deaths, the feast-song in verse, the correction of a factor's clerk laid over both, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Grain of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in a room with good light in the counting house at Greybank, eighteen leagues east downriver of Sill, by Solene Ember, returned whole in Y.H. 799, 804 and 809, to her sister of House Ember in the Bowl of Sere; written on the back of a spoiled grain docket from the Court's granaries, the third-day hand unsteady and the wine of the public bowl gone cold on it. Carried south with the grain factor's convoy in Smoke, answered in the margin at the Bowl in Ash, and brought north again with the glass in Ilmen of Y.H. 813. Kept since in a dry tin in the room with good light, under a fold of cloth that smells of myrrh. It survives with a ring of warm wine at the head, myrrh worked into the grain, a grey bead of Ash from a public bowl pressed into the fold, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a greenish mark where a ring lay on the leaf, a line that runs out toward the gutter and stops, the three deaths set down in a small table, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk of the factor's office, the sister's answer in a warm sloped hand in the margin, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.

codex.title: The Fourth Phial, Being a Letter from the Licence-House at Greybank to a Hearth-Maid of Low Kiln, Concerning the Ash That Is Sold to Stop a Voice, the Greyed Hand That Dispenses It, the Woman Who Came Back on the Ninth Day, and the Blank Where Her Name Should Stand; with the Answer in the Margin, a Correction in Ledgerhand, a Corking Verse in a Hand Nobody Will Own, and a Line at the Foot
codex.kind: A private letter on the back of a licence for the buying of quiet ash spoiled by a wet thumb at the signing, written in iron-gall and pressed charcoal, folded three times and tied with the strip of grey wool that came off the stopper-bag; carried eighteen leagues down the Clay Road in a pot-carter's empty bread-basket, answered along the margin at Low Kiln, borrowed at the Court's table set at the fringe of the Cross where a clerk set a correction on the back, and kept since in the licence-house tin among the corks and the grey rags
codex.provenance: Written at the factor's house in Greybank in the second tend of Grain, Y.H. 813, by Renna, keeper of the licence for quiet ash, to Oda, a hearth-maid of Low Kiln in Sill who had taught her the three-day warming before she went up the road; carried down the Clay Road by a pot-carter going empty, answered at Low Kiln in the third tend of Grain, borrowed at the Court's table at the Cross where a clerk of the assessor set a correction in the neat upright Ledgerhand. It survives folded and tied with the wool strip, with a grey thumb at the head where a stopper was set down unsealed, a cork-shaving caught in the second fold, a rain-line along the gutter from the carter's basket, a small-ale ring on the third leaf, a tallow print at the outer fold, one word eaten clean out of the verse where the damp took it, the clerk's correction standing above and the two hands of the women underneath, and one line at the foot that nobody has claimed

codex.title: The Fourth Poured Out, Being the Drinking Song of the Lamp-Women at the Tallow Works, Sung at the Turning of the Year with a Heel-Tap Under the Bench
codex.kind: A lamp-woman's drinking song, taken down from her own mouth at the fat-house and set in the low half-sung speech of the works; the verses with the ends let fall as they are sung, the order of the pouring in the writer's own charcoal, a gloss pressed in the margin by a hearth-maid come up from Sill, the verbs taken out of two lines by a factor's clerk in narrow upright Ledgerhand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Sung at the turning of the year in the fat-house two leagues north-east of Sill, where sheep fat is rendered and the tallow poured into lamps, and set down in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the woman who keeps the lamps there, on the back of a tallow-chandler's tally gone soft at the fold; written in charcoal and the dregs of a tallow-dip, sewn with a wick into a fold of grey wool and kept in the lamp-room under a cracked saucer. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a Court grain-warrant spoiled at one corner by the damp at Greybank. It survives with a thumb of tallow at the head, a scorch where a wick-end touched the second leaf, a ring of stale small ale near the refrain, a smear of bone-meal across the third leaf, a pressed sheep's-ear mark in the gutter, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own, a gloss in the thick charcoal hand of a hearth-maid, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor's clerk, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Furnace Articles, Being the Standing Rules of the Furnace-Masters of Vhal for the Taking, Keeping, Trying and Paying Out of Apprentices at the Three Glass Furnaces, with the Table of Heats, the Tally of Hands, the Gathering-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A furnace-leaf of rules in the hand of the under-master who keeps the pipes and the anneal at the third furnace; the rules in the short sayings of the Quay, the heats and the hands in tables, the gathering-song pasted inside the cover, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Council clerk, one line struck in charcoal by a furnace-master, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: First gathered at Vhal in Y.H. 627, the year after the rising at the furnaces of Y.H. 626, when the masters found that a trade which could melt sand could also refuse to work, and set the rules down so that a refusal would have a place to be entered; copied forward from the anneal shelf and not from a book. This leaf written in Grain of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by Riva of the Third Furnace, under-master, who has kept the pipes and taken the young at the gather for two and twenty years; carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813. It survives on Council salt-paper furred white at the head and soft at the fold, with the lower edge gone over into a clear bead of glass under twenty years of anneal heat, so that the last two rules read best held up to the light, which is how furnace work is read; a thumb of tar at the fold off the pipe-rest, the press of a wet gathering-cloth across the song, a nick from a glass-cutter's point, a ring of vinegar from a tasting cup set down by a girl who would not eat, a green bead of cliff-glass pressed into the second fold by a girl with the sweetness still at her mouth, a grey thumb along the outer fold that a factor come up from Greybank called Ash, which in Vhal is a thing that must be bought and sold, and nobody bought this one; two corrections in the Council's upright hand, one charcoal line struck and written again beneath, and a line at the foot nobody will own.

codex.title: The Gallery Leech, Being Remedies for the Sweating, the Stone-Cough, the Clamp-Bite, the Hand Gone Rope-Coloured and the Cold That Stays, Set Down Under Keld Keep
codex.kind: A mine-leech's book of remedies in the Keldish measure-first manner, set down in Grathic letters with the counts notched into the board cover in iron; the cures in a gallery-leech's hand, the objections of a clamp-master pressed in coal, the corrections of a Court survey-clerk in Ledgerhand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at Keld Keep in the First Seam between Y.H. 808 and Y.H. 812, the Long Cold and the Thin Year, by Dren of the Ninth Gallery, a leech who tended the clamp-hands and the stone-cough of the deep workings and went up and down the shaft by the same rope for nineteen years; written on the back of a survey sheet spoiled by a sweating in the Ninth Gallery and on four strips of birch bark, sewn with iron wire into a board cover and carried in a coat pocket against a splinter of warm-stone. Copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a discarded tally-roll. It survives with coal dust ground into the head, a clear stain of lamp-oil down the fold that has made two words transparent, iron filings caught in the gutter off the Duelling Floor, a scorch where a lamp-spark took the corner of the second leaf, the splinter of warm-stone sewn into the cover which keeps the whole book a little warm, a ring of frost on the third leaf from the climb over the Cold Pass, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Court survey-clerk, one note in the blocky coal-pressed hand of a clamp-master, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.

codex.title: The Gate Account at Sill, Being the Year's Render of the South Bridge and the Road-Rail, with the Market Price of Every Load That Crossed It Set Beside the Moot's Figure, and the Tolls of the Roads Laid Under
codex.kind: A bridge-keeper's year-book, written for his own sureties and never posted; the prices cried at the Cross set against what a load was worth at the rail, the dues of the roads that come down to Sill set against the sum the moot expected to receive, the verbs put back where a clerk took them out, one surety's note in a second hand, and a line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at the toll-house beside the south bridge in Sill by Tarrow, keeper of the bridge and the road-rail, in the last tend of Stone, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, and rendered to the moot at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813; copied back into the quire in Reed of that year. It survives in a tin box under a loose board of the toll-house floor, stitched with eel-sinew: bridge tar at the head, river silt worked into the gutter, a pig bristle pressed flat in the second leaf, a white salt bloom along the fore-edge, a green fleck of lead glaze brought down on the High Kiln wind, grey Ash in the fold, a tallow thumb, a small bare square where a figure was scraped away, the moot clerk's correction in a narrow hand, a surety's note in a leaning one, and a line at the foot which nobody has claimed

codex.title: The Gate-Slate of Keld Keep, Being the Prices Current at the Shaft Mouth and the Dues of the Rim Road and the Cold Pass, Cut in Chalk by the Reeve's Tally-Man and Never Washed Clean
codex.kind: A tally-man's cutting on a slate propped against the gate-post within the shaft mouth, being a market list of iron, lead, coal, warm-stone, clamps and hired lives set against what the same things fetch in the lowlands, with the road-dues cut beneath; scored in red by the mine-reeve, written over in a Greybank factor's narrow hand, and left with one line at the foot that nobody will own
codex.provenance: Cut first in Bone of Y.H. 812, the year the lowlands called the Thin Year, and cut forward in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, when the Rim Road opened and the first carts came up with the winter's iron. Kept at Keld Keep in the lee of the gate-post, wiped at the end of each tend with a wet sleeve and never made clean, so that the figures of former years show through the current ones the way old repairs show through a vessel. It survives with coal smut ground into the head, an iron-red cross from the mine-reeve's point, slate dust in the gutter, a warm-stone shaving shut in the fold, a bead of lead out of the Ninth Gallery, a frost-feather along the lower edge, a clamp-scratch across two columns, a thumb in coal dust nobody will claim, one correction in a factor's narrow upright hand, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.

codex.title: Title the Seventh, Being the Ordinance of the Keeping Concerning Blent-Work, the Grafting of Beast-Clay into Human Wall, and the Measure of the Donor, Copied into a Back Room Behind the College in Slate Row of the Hearthseat with the Graft-Clerk's Margin, a Sere Surgeon's Correction, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: An extract from the Court's ordinances, written out for the use of the back rooms behind the College of Assessors in the Hearthseat, with the marginal hand of the clerk who keeps the graft-book; the articles in Ledgerhand, the verbs set back beneath them, two tables, a form of entry left blank, the graft-song as it is said over the bench, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed
codex.provenance: Copied in Slate Row of the Hearthseat in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, from Title the Seventh of the Ordinances of the Keeping as set down in the Hearthseat after the Rising of Y.H. 668 and added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year; it survives folded under a warm-stone in the back room behind the College, three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, with iron-gall in the creases of two fingers, warm-stone dust ground fine as meal in the gutter, a pale crescent of grease where a pad of beast-clay was laid, a green bead of lead glaze chipped from a bowl out of Sere, a grey Ash print along the outer fold, a small square of bare paper where a word was cut away with a knife, a tide-line along the foot from the sealed-file room, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own.

codex.title: The Granary Years, Being an Extract from the Chronicle of the Factor's House at Greybank Concerning the Raising of the Granary in Y.H. 726, the Doubling of the Grain Levy, the Ninety-Four Days, and the Row of Empty Sacks; with the Cart-Song, the Table of Loads, Two Corrections in the College Hand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A factor's annalist's extract from the granary chronicle, copied out of the loft-book; the year-entries in a sloping tally hand, the two figures set against the notice, the loads entered as a round sum with the rows underneath it in the gutter, the cart-song taken down at the quay, one figure struck and written again beneath, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the College, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward
codex.provenance: Written at Greybank in the factor's counting house in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the keeper of the granary chronicle, who signs nothing and calls himself only the continuator of the sacks; copied from a loft-book kept in a tin box above the second floor since Y.H. 726 and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives as six leaves of stout foolscap sewn with wire into a board cover gone soft at the hinge: barley dust worked into the grain of the first leaf, a husk stuck fast in the gutter, a weevil shut in the second fold, the lower corner gnawed by a mouse so that two words are gone clean off the third leaf, a white bloom of Sallow salt at the head that comes and goes with the weather, a tallow thumb, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first load to the last, the figure for the four loads struck through and written again underneath in the writer's own hand, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the College, and a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the continuator did not make and has not swept

codex.title: The Grave-Dog, Being a Soldier's Field Notes on the Bone-Hound at the Bone Orchard Beyond Sill's North Gate; with the Watch-Song as It Is Sung, a Tally of Graves and Phials, a Ruling in Ledgerhand, a Line in Pale Ink, and One Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A soldier's field book on one beast, set down as the record of a watch kept over the thin-return graves and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on the backs of burial dockets gone soft with rain, a watch-song as it is sung, a ruling in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk of the Court's factor at Greybank, a line in the pale ink of an Ash-runner written on a scrap of salt-paper, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Ash and Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by Gant, one of the Thane of Clay's men set over the north road, in the watch-shed at the Bone Orchard a league beyond Sill's north gate, with a tallow end, a short spear and a spade; set down first on the backs of thin-return burial dockets spoiled by rain and then on two folds of birch bark sewn with eel-sinew, carried in a coat pocket under the arm; copied forward in Bone of Y.H. 813. It survives with grave-clay ground into the head, a grey Ash thumb along the fore-edge where the leaf was wiped on a sleeve, a small round mark where a five-bit piece was set down and left, a dry grave-flower pressed flat in the second fold, a tideline along the gutter where a pail went over, a scorch where the watch-lamp caught the fourth leaf, the charcoal rubbed thin where the wrap was carried against the thigh, one ruling in Ledgerhand standing above the words it corrects, one line in pale ink on salt-paper gone soft at a corner, and the line at the foot

codex.title: The Green at the Mouth, Being a Letter from the Glass Furnaces at Vhal to the Glaze Room at High Kiln in Sill, with the Answer Written on the Back in Another Hand, a Proportion Set Down in Charcoal, a Correction in Ledgerhand, and a Mixing Song Nobody Will Claim
codex.kind: A private letter on a sheet of Council salt-paper softened by the spring damp, written in iron-gall and the point of a cliff-glass bead, folded four times and sewn with eel-sinew into a scrap of oiled sailcloth; carried up the Salt Road after the flood by a salt-factor's man, borrowed at the factor's house at Greybank, answered at High Kiln in Seed, and kept since in a glaze-room tin among the tasting-spoons
codex.provenance: Written at Vhal in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 by Wenna, a glaze-mixer's daughter of High Kiln who went down the Salt Road to work the glass furnaces, to Gessa her mother, who keeps the Glaze Room in High Kiln, Sill; carried eighty leagues up the Salt Road and through the coast pass in Silt of Y.H. 813, after the water went off the road, borrowed at Greybank where a Council clerk set a correction in Ledgerhand, and answered at High Kiln in Seed of Y.H. 813. It survives sewn into oiled sailcloth, with a green thumb at the head, a bead of cliff-glass pressed into the second fold, a bloom of salt along the gutter, a ring of vinegar on the third leaf, a smear of lead glaze at the foot, two words eaten clean away by damp, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Council clerk, the answer in the mother's charcoal hand on the back, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.

codex.title: The Grey Eel, Being a Quay-Tale of a Riddle Night Fourteen Winters Back, Told at the Fire in Ash, with the Questions as They Were Put, the Wager in Marks, a Factor's Clerk's Entry Set Over It, a Surveyor's Gloss in the Margin, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A fire-keeper's telling of a winter contest, set down for the settling of a question about a prize nobody claimed and not for the improvement of the reader; the tale in the old tally-man's words, the riddles in the words they were put, the wager in a column of marks, the clerk's figures entered above them, a gloss in another hand come back over the pass, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Ash of Y.H. 813 at the Grey Eel, an alehouse at the lower end of the quay at Greybank, by Hedda, who keeps the fire behind the bar and mends nets in the afternoons when the quay is shut; told to her by Varr, who kept the quay tally for thirty years and now sits by the door with his hands on his stick, in the words he told it, which are the words of a man telling a thing he has told twice and would rather not tell a third time. Set down on the back of a spoiled quay-tally leaf in charcoal thinned with small ale, folded and sewn with eel-sinew and kept in the tin behind the fire, where the house keeps nothing else. It survives with a tallow thumb at the head, a press of wet wool across the first leaf, a small-ale ring gone dark where a quart stood from the first question to the last, a spot of barley grease, grey Ash worked into the gutter, frost raised out of the paper on the carry up from the quay, one correction in the narrow upright hand of the factor's clerk, a gloss in the sloping hand of a Keldish surveyor who could not get back over the pass, and one line at the foot which nobody has claimed

codex.title: Of the Grey in the Corners, the Last Day, and the Burning Called Dealt With, Being the Court's Standing Order for the Sweeping of the Last Day, Copied into the Court's Room at Sill with the Sweep-Clerk's Margin, the Places in a Table, the Form of Entry Left Blank, the Sweeping-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: An extract from the Court's ordinances, written out in the Court's room in Slate Row in Sill for the households of the district; the articles in Ledgerhand with the verbs restored beneath them, the places and the faults in tables, the form of the entry left blank, the sweeping-song pasted inside the cover, two corrections in borrowed hands, a scorch off a household lamp, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed
codex.provenance: Copied at Sill in the dark month of Ash, Y.H. 813, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by the under-clerk who keeps the last-day slate in the Court's room in Slate Row, from the standing order sent down from the Hearthseat to the factor at Greybank, sent down in Y.H. 418, set down after the Rising of Y.H. 668 and added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year; kept against the Last Day in the drawer under the counter beside the bell-cord, and written to be carried forward at the Opening of the Slates. It survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, with grey Ash off my own thumb at the head, tallow gone white where the lamp stood through a watching, a browned crumb of barley bread pressed into the second fold, a curl of grey wool through the tie-hole off a cradle blanket carried over a threshold, a pale ring where a pan of washing-water stood, bone-coloured slip along the outer edge from a swaddling cloth, a green bead of lead glaze pressed in by a girl come up from High Kiln with the sweetness still at her mouth, a scorch where a spark off the household hearth caught the third leaf, a washing-water tide-line along the foot, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot that nobody will own

codex.title: The Sermon at the Grey Mouth, Being What an Old Kiln-Woman Said Under the Fallen Arch of the Old Kiln on the Morning the Watch Turned a Man Back from the Ash, in Bone of Y.H. 812, with the Grey-Song Left as It Is Sung, the Row of Jars in a Sherd-Tally, a Factor's Clerk's Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A kiln-mouth sermon of the common Grathic telling, preached at the niche under the lip of the Old Kiln one league south of Sill; the sayings in Grathic, the grey-song with the place where the fifth line should stand left as it is sung, the jars in a sherd-tally, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor's clerk come out from Greybank to measure the winter clay, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Preached on Bone 12, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by an old kiln-woman who had swept the mouth of the Old Kiln for seven and twenty winters, on a morning when the Thane's watch turned a man back from the throat and the man left his crust on the lip and went; written that evening by the keeper of the niche, in charcoal and with the point of a broken sherd on the back of a kiln-docket spoiled by rain, folded into a grey wool kiln-cloth and kept in a tin under a loose firebrick at the mouth, out of reach of the watch. It survives with soot worked into the head and the gutter, grey clay dried pale in the creases and under one nail, a frost-crisp along the fore-edge where the leaf lay a night outside the arch, a wet ring where a dish of barley-water stood from the first voice to the last, a green bead of High Kiln lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl with the sweetness still at her mouth, a grey Ash print along the gutter off a cuff nobody will own, a copper bit shut in the fold, the charred end of a tallow dip, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor's clerk come out from Greybank to measure the winter clay, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied once at Greybank in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the empty place left empty.

codex.title: The Guess-Shed of Nine Pots, Being the Riddle Fight of the Long Frost, the Wagers Counted in Sherds, and the Loaf That Was Not Paid
codex.kind: A pot-mender's winter record, set down for the settling of a wager and not for the improvement of the reader; the rules in the hand the shed keeps, the riddles in the words they were spoken, the wagers in broken sherds in a jar, the tally of one night set against a Sill carter's tally, the correction of a factor's clerk in Ledgerhand, a gloss pressed into the margin in charcoal, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim
codex.provenance: Written in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year after the Long Cold, in the shared drying shed at Nine Pots (four kilns and one clay pit, eight leagues west of Sill, in standing feud with Sill over the road), by Heddi of Nine Pots, a woman who mends cracked pots with slip and keeps the shed and its fire through the cold months; copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a spoiled glaze-tally from the third firing, sewn with wire into a fold of oiled sackcloth and kept in the jar by the covered bench at the pit's head. It survives with bone-coloured slip ground into the head, a green thumb of glaze at the fold, tallow in the gutter, a crust of frost along the outer edge, a press of wet wool across the first leaf, a potsherd folded into the gutter where a figure should stand, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor's clerk come up from Greybank, a gloss in the thick charcoal hand of a Sill carter who borrowed the leaf on a market morning, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody's

codex.title: The Gull That Carries, Being a Boat-Soldier's Field Notes on the Brine-Gull of the Sallow Coast and the Glaze Cliffs
codex.kind: A soldier's field book on one beast, set down as the record of watches kept over a boat's warm-store and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in the Vhaleni tide-words written in Grathic letters, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled tide-tallies, a Quay song as it is sung, two rulings in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk of the tide-tally house, a line in the pale ink of a salt-pan dipper, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by one of the Council's men set over the night-store of a salt boat out of the Quay at Vhal, who wrote at the end of a watch with a tallow end in a pot and the Sallow coming up under the hull; carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Ilmen of Y.H. 813. Set down first on the backs of tide-tallies spoiled by sea-water and then on four folds of salt-paper stiffened with tar, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a tarred wrap in a coat pocket. It survives with a white salt bloom at the head, tar at the fold, a Sallow tideline along the gutter, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, a brown spot the size of a fingernail on the second leaf where a boy's blood fell, the charcoal rubbed thin where the wrap was carried against the thigh, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the tide-tally clerk who borrowed the leaves at the tally house, one line in the pale ink of a dipper written on salt-paper gone soft at one corner, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: The Half Knot, Being the Rope-Skipping Game of the Quay at Vhal, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Turns, the Eleven Lines, the Half Kept at the Untied Place, and What a Council Clerk Made of It
codex.kind: A rope-woman's gathering of a children's skipping game, set down in Grathic letters on the back of a Council tide-draw spoiled by rain; the verses in the children's own half-sung Quay speech, the manner of it in the writer's tarred small hand, one gloss pressed in charcoal by a woman who dips at the pans, a Council clerk's correction in the leaning hand that has gone soft with damp, and one line at the foot in grey chalk in a hand nobody will claim
codex.provenance: Written at the Quay in Vhal in Ilmen of Y.H. 813, on the evening of a flood after the Long Cold had gone off the coast, by a woman who mends the nets and coils the tow-ropes for the boats that tie under the tide-tally house; set down on the back of a Council tide-draw gone soft at one edge and sewn with eel-sinew into a fold of oiled sailcloth; carried up the Salt Road with a consignment of glass in Ember and copied at Greybank onto the back of a voided weigh-slip. Kept in a tarred tin under a coil of rope beside the tide-tally house. It survives with a white salt bloom worked into the grain at the head, a tar thumb at the fold, a fibre of wet rope pressed into the second leaf, a brine-gull's peck through one word of the sixth line, a fish-hook nick at the head, a rent where the old rope frayed across the lower corner, a green bead of cliff-glass pressed in by a girl with sweetness at one mouth-corner, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, the pan-woman's gloss in charcoal, the Council clerk's correction standing above the children's words, and a line at the foot in grey chalk

codex.title: The Half Share, Being the Quay's Drinking Song for a Man Come Aboard
codex.kind: A Vhaleni drinking song for the coming-aboard feast and the spring launching, taken down in Grathic letters from a mouth that has no word for guest; the verses on salt-paper squared at the edges, with three lines the damp has made void by the Council's own law, a factor's clerk's correction in Ledgerhand, a dipper's note in charcoal, and one verse in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Set down at Vhal on the Sallow coast in Ember of Y.H. 807 by Vessa of the Quay, a woman who held a boat-share from her mother, for the coming aboard of a man whose name she did not enter, because a name entered is a name held; carried up the Salt Road in Frost of Y.H. 810 in a dry tin and copied at Greybank onto the back of a spoiled harbour tally; copied forward in Stone of Y.H. 812 with the damp-void lines left void. It survives with a white salt crust along the gutter, a ring of red wine that has eaten one word clean through, a fibre of wet rope pressed into the second fold, a green bead of Glaze glass, a fish-hook nick at the head, and a thumb printed in salt where the writer signed, because a boat on this coast is signed in salt and not in ink. One correction is in the narrow upright hand of a factor's clerk who borrowed the sheet at Greybank; one note is in charcoal and is a dipper's; the verse at the foot is in a hand nobody will own.

codex.title: The Half Turn, Being the Skipping Game of the Quay Children at Vhal, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Turning, the Verse They Do Not Skip While the Crier Calls the Turn, a Council Clerk's Figures on Salt-Paper Gone Soft, a Gloss in Charcoal from a Woman Who Mends Nets, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A children's skipping game gathered on the Quay at Vhal and set down in Grathic letters for a man who wanted a figure; the counting-out and the four whole shares in the children's half-sung Quay speech, the manner of the play in the writer's small hand, the kept half left as a half and never called a fifth, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Council clerk on salt-paper the damp has since eaten, a gloss pressed in charcoal by a net-mending woman, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim
codex.provenance: Set down at Vhal on the Sallow coast in Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a woman of the Quay who mends nets and has turned the rope for three councils of children; written in charcoal thinned with brine on the back of a dippers' tide-tally spoiled by rain and sewn with eel-sinew into a fold of oiled sailcloth, carried up the Salt Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a voided weigh-slip. The original survives in a dry tin among a boat's things at the Quay, with a white salt bloom along the gutter, a tar thumb at the head, a salt-stiff fibre of the painter across the second leaf, a green bead of cliff-glass pressed into the lower corner by a girl with sweetness at one mouth-corner, a brine ring at the foot, a white brine-gull feather shut in the fold, a tide-line that has taken one word off the third share and has not given it back, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own, the Council clerk's figures eaten down to a figure and half a verb, the net-mender's charcoal gloss, and the line at the foot

codex.title: The Sermon at the Hand-Stone, Being What a Miller of Sill Said Over the Note at the Singing Sill on the Morning It Came a Week Early in Silt of Y.H. 813, with the Early-Note Tally, the Low-Note Verse, a Factor's Clerk's Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
