codex.kind: A sermon of the meal mill preached at the shrine of the hand-stone above the Singing Sill, below the north bridge at Sill; the sayings in Grathic, the low-note verse with the gap left as it is sung, the early notes in a meal-book tally, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor's clerk come up from Greybank, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Preached on Silt 7, Y.H. 813, by a miller of Sill who had ground at the meal mill under the north bridge for two and thirty years, on the morning the stone gave its note a week before its hour and the yard said the water ran fast under the skin and then said weather; written that evening by his daughter, who keeps the mill's meal-book, on the back of a leaf spoiled by a wet figure out of the Glaze Room, folded into the toll-bag with a barleycorn shut in the crease. It survives with white mill-dust worked into the head and the gutter, a brown silt tideline along the foot from a morning the leaf went down to the Fishstairs in a woman's apron, a wet ring where a cup was set on it, a grey Ash print nobody will own, a barleycorn in the fold, one small nick from a millstone dressing-pick, one correction in the clerk's hand that takes the verbs out and numbers the early note nil, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied once at the Fishstairs in Seed, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the nought left in its place.

codex.title: The Held Palm, Being the Clapping Game of the Quay Children at Vhal, with the Counting-Out, the Half That Stands, and What the Tally-man Made of It
codex.kind: A share-woman's gathering of a children's clapping-count, set down in Grathic letters on the back of a boat-share sheet gone soft with damp; the counting-out and the clapping verse in the children's own half-sung salt-coast speech, the manner of the play in the writer's small hand, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk come down from the tide-tally house, a gloss pressed into the margin by a dipper who reads the Sallow draw at dawn, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward
codex.provenance: Written in Ember of Y.H. 813 at the Quay in Vhal, by a woman who keeps the mothers' share-lines and mends the rope that holds the salt galleys, on the back of a share-sheet spoiled by a wet tend, the figures on its face gone soft and the salt-paper rotten at one corner. She set it down because a man from the tide-tally house came down the boards and asked what the children counted when they clapped, and was given a count and not a figure; he went away and sent a clerk, which is what happens to a count in this country. Kept folded in a coil of spent tow-rope under the Quay bench among the beads and the net-needles. It survives with a white salt bloom across the head, a tar thumb at the first corner, a press of wet rope across the second leaf, a gritting of glass from the furnaces in the fold, a fish-scale shut in the gutter, a tideline along the foot where the sheet went damp, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the clerk's correction standing above the children's words, a dipper's gloss in charcoal beside the half, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim

codex.title: The Held Rope, Being the Counting Game of the Fishstairs Children at the Out-of-Line Landing, with the Choosing, the Manner of the Turns, the Verse of the Hold, and What a Court Clerk Entered Over It
codex.kind: A woman of the fish-trade shade's gathering of a children's skipping game, set down in Grathic on the back of a weigh-slip blown down from the Cross; the choosing and the verses in the children's own half-sung speech, the rules in the writer's charcoal hand, a correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Court-table clerk, a gloss in the charcoal letters of the girl who holds the rope, a line from the Weir in the hand of a woman who counts in wool, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Set down in Seed of Y.H. 813 at the fish-trade shade below the sill in Sill, of an evening when the eel boats were out and the children skipped on the flat place at the foot of the Fishstairs; copied forward in Reed of Y.H. 813 onto a second slip when the first went soft at the fold. The slip came originally from the Court's table at the Cross and was trodden into the shade, which the writer thought a proper beginning for it. It survives folded into a twist of oiled cloth under the outer tub at the shade: eel slime worked into the grain at the head, silt along the fore-edge and a tideline through the second leaf, a fish scale pressed flat in the fold, the smoke-smudge of a coal from a banked fire on one corner, a nick from a fish-hook, a bloom of salt on the leaf that lay nearest the creel, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, the clerk's correction standing above the children's words, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Holding Book of the Waiting Room at Slate Row in Sill, Being the Vessels Kept Overnight Between the Drawing and the Pouring, with the Embers Standing, the Note Each Gave in the Dark, the Loss by Morning, and the Figure Carried Up the Clay Road at First Light
codex.kind: A leaf from a collector's own night-book, kept behind the collector's table; figures in Ledgerhand copied from the day-slates, the remarks in the hand that fed the room's dish and turned the pallets, one column struck by a College clerk and drawn back beneath his words, a verb corrected in a second hand, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at Sill in the Waiting Room behind the collector's table in Slate Row, in the firing month of Tallow, Y.H. 813, the year after the Thin Year, between the first Account-day and the second; sent up the Clay Road at first light with the figures and left folded under the bench at the turning of the tend. It survives as one leaf of foolscap folded small enough for a coat pocket, with grey Ash worked into the outer fold, a tallow thumb at the head, iron filings in the gutter from the tube's wool sleeve, a bone-pale streak of slip along the foot, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a damp tide-line from the flagstones where a barrow stood overnight, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of a College clerk, and one line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Song of the Hollow Seat, Being the Wheel-Shed Work Song of Low Kiln, Counted in Turns of the Wheel and Said into the Clay
codex.kind: A wheel-woman's work song of the Clay Yard, counted in the turns and not in the pots; the verses in the low Grathic of the yard, said down into the lump and not up into the air; the manner of the turns and the unsung last verse in the wheel-woman's charcoal hand; a glaze girl's gloss pressed into the margin in thick charcoal; the corrections of a College clerk borrowed at Greybank in Ledgerhand standing above; and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Sung at the hollow wheel-seat of the wheel-shed in Low Kiln of Sill since before the Glaze Wars and set down in Ember of Y.H. 813, the kiln month, by a woman who has turned at that wheel for one-and-thirty years and has begun to lose the use of her right thumb; written in charcoal and tallow on the back of a drying-rack tally spoiled by a fall of slip, folded into four and carried in the breast of her apron against a square of sacking gone soft at the seam, and copied forward at Greybank onto the back of a factor's weigh-slip gone stiff with salt. It survives with wet slip worked into the grain at the head, brick dust ground into the fold, a tallow thumb at the second corner, a green bead of lead-glaze in the lower corner, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, a ring the colour of weak barley-water, a long hair the colour of wet wool caught in the seam, a pot-shard pressed flat between the third and fourth leaves, the clerk's figures standing above the verses, the glaze girl's gloss in the margin, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: The Articles of the Hopper, Being the Standing Rules of the Millers of Sill for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices at the Meal Mill on the Ilm, with the Table of Grinds, the Faults in a Second Table, the Dressing-Song Pasted Inside the Meal-Book, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A mill-leaf of rules in the hand of the under-miller who keeps the hopper and the roll of hands; the articles in the short sayings of the river bank, the grinds and the faults in tables, the dressing-song pasted to the inside of the meal-book, a barleycorn shut in the fold, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor's clerk, one line in a carter's thick charcoal, a girl's gloss underneath, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed
codex.provenance: First set down at Sill in Y.H. 726, the year the factor at Greybank raised his granary and doubled the grain levy, when a mill that had carried its rules in the dust was made to write them so that a due could be argued with; copied forward from the hopper board and not from a book, which is why the rule about the handful is worn smooth where a hundred thumbs have lifted it and the rule about the foundling is as sharp as the day it was cut. This leaf written in Stone of Y.H. 813, the year after the Thin Year, by the under-miller who keeps the hopper and the roll of hands, and kept folded in the toll-bag on its nail behind the mill door. It survives with white mill-dust worked into the head and the gutter, a brown silt tideline along the foot from a morning the leaf went down to the Fishstairs in an apron, a barley awn stiff in the second fold, a barleycorn shut in the crease that has not sprouted, a wet ring where a cup was set down and taken up before it was seen, a nick from a millstone dressing-pick at the fore-edge, a thumb of tallow off the hopper strap, a thread of grey wool caught in the sewing where a foundling's fold was mended, the sweet green of lead glaze pressed in by a girl come down from High Kiln, a grey print along the outer fold that nobody will own, two corrections in the factor's upright hand, one line in a carter's charcoal added at the bridge, a girl's gloss under it, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: Of the Joining of Vessels, the Marriage Slate, the Number of Pourings, and the Vessel Unsafe to Marry, Being Title the Eleventh of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied into the Assessor's House at Sill with the Joining-Clerk's Margin, the Form Left Blank, the Joining-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: An extract from the Court's ordinances, written out for the counter of the assessor's house in Sill's Slate Row, with the marginal hand of the clerk who keeps the joining-slate; the articles in Ledgerhand and the persons restored beneath them, the returns and the faults in tables, a form of joining left blank, the joining-song pasted inside the cover, a word left out where an older hand struck it, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed
codex.provenance: Copied at Sill in the assessor's house built in Y.H. 776, in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, from Title the Eleventh of the Ordinances of the Keeping as set down in the first years after the Rising of Y.H. 668, amended in Y.H. 651 by the striking of a phrase, confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of Y.H. 418, and added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year; carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813. It survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire and tied with a grown string, kept in the joining-slate's box behind the counter and taken down when two people come to stand as one house: an iron-gall thumb at the head, a streak of pale slip down the gutter, a thread of grey wool tied through the tie-hole, a brown crust-mark at the second fold, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner, a cold-iron scratch the length of a clip in the margin where no clip is used, a washing-water tide-line along the foot, a bare place the length of a word struck before this leaf was copied, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Song of the Rooms, Being the Lament of One Kept Near the Fire in the Hearthseat, with the Manner of It, the Words as the Room Keeps Them, and the Correction Set Over Them at the Weighing
codex.kind: A lament of the Kept, taken down by the keeper of the room-book in the Hearthseat; the verses in the soft Court speech of the warm passage, the refrain in the room's own order of reaching, the coal-woman's charcoal set underneath, the Steward's clerk's correction standing above, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Set down in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in the rooms beside the Weighing Hall on the Keel, by a junior clerk of the College who keeps the evening slate and signs nothing, calling herself only the keeper of the room-book; written on the back of a measure-slip spoiled by a wet thumb at the Weighing, carried down the Clay Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant gone soft at one corner. It survives in the room-book's board cover in the Steward's room: a flake of scale from the grating at the head, a thumb of tallow, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, a ring where a cup of water stood from the first verse to the last and went cold without being drunk, a thread of grey wool from a Kept sleeve caught in the fold, the coal-woman's words below the lines and the clerk's verbless correction above them, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: Of the Nine Wells, the Sealing, the Keys and the Drawing Without Authority, Being Title the Eighth of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied for the Steward's Room in the Hearthseat with the Key-Clerk's Margin, the Notch of a Key in the Paper, the Tellers' Verse, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: An extract from the Court's ordinances, written out for the Steward's room beside the Weighing Hall; the articles in Ledgerhand and the verbs restored beneath them, the wells and their seals in a table, a table of offences and their correcting, a form of key-receipt left blank, the tellers' verse as it is said in the passage, one line scored with the notch of a key, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed
codex.provenance: Copied at the Hearthseat in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, from Title the Eighth of the Ordinances of the Keeping, four of the Nine Wells sealed in the first hundred and twenty years and a fifth in Y.H. 618, with additions in Y.H. 782 and the Thin Year; carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813. It survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, kept in the Steward's room under the key-slate and taken down when a key is entered: a tallow thumb at the head, warm-stone dust ground into the gutter, a green mineral stain off a spring-lip at the fold, a cold-iron scratch the length of a key in the lower margin, iron-gall in the creases of two fingers, a damp tide-line from the sealed-file room along the foot, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Kneading Song, Being the Working-Song of the Clay Yard at Low Kiln, Sung Over the Lump on the Beating-Bench Before It Goes to the Wheel, with the Thumps Counted, the Fourth Kept as the Turning of the Lump, the Hidden Pocket Pressed Out, a Kiln-Master's Ruling in Broad Charcoal, a Factor's Clerk's Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss from a Woman of the Firing Work, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A worker's song in the low hard speech of the yard, said down into the lump and not across the bench; the verses counted in thumps of the heel going into the clay, with the fourth kept as the turning of the lump and not entered, and the little room of air pressed shut before the lump goes to the wheel; the manner of the working in the writer's own charcoal, the kiln-master's ruling in broad charcoal, a factor's clerk's figures standing above in Ledgerhand, a gloss pressed into the margin by a woman of the firing work, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim
codex.provenance: Sung over the beating-bench two doors below the slip pits in the Clay Yard at Low Kiln of Sill and set down in Smoke of Y.H. 813, the second firing-month, by a woman who has worked the lump at that bench for twelve seasons and knows a hollow by the sound of the heel going in and not by any word spoken over it; written in charcoal thinned with slip-water on the back of a working-docket spoiled by a wet thumb, folded twice and tied with a curl of eel-sinew against the dust, carried up the Clay Road with a consignment of coarse tile and copied forward at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 814 onto the back of a factor's voided weigh-slip. It survives with a clay thumb worked into the grain at the head, a pale tideline from the Slip Brook along the gutter that has taken the edge off one word of the fifth verse, a curl of eel-sinew caught across the second leaf, a grey flake from the bench pressed in the fold, a hair from a horse's forelock caught where the docket lay in the cart, a dark pinprick where a wire cut through the fourth verse and showed the speck the song is about, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl with sweetness at one mouth-corner, a sour small-ale ring at the foot, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own, the kiln-master's broad ruling, the clerk's figures standing above, the firing woman's gloss in the margin, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: The Knot Not Untied, Being a Letter from Wenna at the Standing Post to Her Brother Holl at Mud End, Concerning a Stand That Ended Otherwise, a Peat Block Kept Loose Against the Niche, a Term of Bought Breath Owed at the Line, and the Bringing Back of Salt; with the Answer Written Along the Margin on the Return of the Peat Cart, a Factor's Clerk's Correction on the Back, and a Song Said to the Boards
codex.kind: A private letter on the back of a Sill weigh-slip read twice and not paid, folded small and lashed with eel-sinew, sent down the mud road in a peat cart and handed back up by the same cart three mornings later; the writer's words in a reed-pen over a washed-out figure, the answer in a hard salt-stiff hand along the margin, a knot tied through a hole where a word would not come, a factor's clerk's correction on the back in Ledgerhand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at the Standing Post in the last tend of Seed, Y.H. 813, by Wenna, a board-woman of the Post who lays the peat blocks in the niche at the foot of the reeve's stone, to her brother Holl, who keeps the eel baskets at the landing at Mud End, three leagues downriver of Sill. Carried down the mud road under a carter's boot and returned three mornings later with the answer in the margin and a little salt gone damp in the fold; borrowed at Greybank by a clerk of the factor who set his correction on the back, and kept since under the loose board in a folded reed wrapper with the Post's sayings and the dry stick of market rates. It survives with a peat thumb ground into the head, a bog-water tideline that has taken two words off the second page, dried eel slime at the fore-edge, a fish-hook nick, a pale round place where a collector's cuff was laid, grey Ash pressed into the outer fold which the writer did not put there and has not swept, a knot of grey wool tied through a hole in the first page which she will not untie, and one line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Knotted Answer, Being the Order of the Return as the Reed-Midwives Say It Face Down in the Peat, with the Child Named Before the Collector Comes, the Answer Tied in Grey Wool, a Factor's Clerk's Correction, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A litany of the Return said face down on the peat-dry at the Reed Cut, the mud-wife saying it to the ground and the answer tied in knots instead of spoken; set down in Grathic letters learned off an eel-trader, though Fen Cant is not written, the sayings in the thick half-sung speech of the marsh with the ends bitten off, the rubrics of the dry, seven stations and their knot, a bog-tally of names said into the ground before the collector came, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor's clerk come out from Greybank, an eel-trader's margin, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward
codex.provenance: Written in Reed of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, at the peat-dry beside the Reed Cut by Lett Peat, a reed-midwife of the east marsh, who signs the leaf with a knot in grey wool and not with a name, in charcoal on the back of a bog-tally spoiled by a wet figure; folded into oiled sacking with a knot-stick shut in the crease and kept in the thatch of the drying shed, taken out only when a child is born before the collector's boat is seen. Borrowed in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 by a clerk of the factor's house come out from Greybank to count the winter thin returns, who set his hand above hers; read over by an eel-trader out of Reedholt, who put four lines in the margin in a leaning hand gone soft with eel slime. It survives with peat worked into the grain at the head in a brown thumb, a press of wet sedge across the first leaf, a bog-water tideline along the gutter, the loan-knot tied through a hole in the first leaf, a horn-shaving from the count-stick in the second crease, a fish-hook nick, an Ash print off the cuff of a man who sells it, a ring of small ale, and the clerk's correction standing above the words it corrects

codex.title: The Lament of the Pulled Bench, Being the Song the Women of the Quay Sing Over the Oars at Vhal, with the Manner of It, the Verses as the Oar-Keeper Keeps Them, the Council Clerk's Correction Set Above, a Boat-Mother's Gloss in Charcoal, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A lament of the bench-women of the Quay, set down in the Vhaleni tide-words in Grathic letters by the woman who keeps the oar-store; the verses in the thick half-sung speech of the Quay, the refrain kept by the oars, a Council clerk's correction in the leaning hand on salt-paper gone soft with damp, a boat-mother's gloss pressed into the margin in charcoal, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim
codex.provenance: Written at the oar-store on the Quay at Vhal in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Ulla Brine, a woman of the Quay who counts the oars in at the ebb and out at the flood and mends the leather sleeves at the rowlock; set down because a clerk of the tide-tally house come to count the galley stores asked what the women sang when the boats came in off the pull, and wrote the answer down while she was still saying it, with the doing taken out and a term set where a place should stand. Written first on the back of a tide-tally spoiled by sea-water and then on folds of salt-paper stiffened with tar, sewn with eel-sinew and kept in a tarred tin under the oar rack; carried up the Salt Road at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and copied at Greybank onto the back of a factor's voided weigh-slip. It survives with a white salt bloom at the head, a tar thumb at the fold, a fibre of wet rope pressed into the second leaf, a brine ring gone sour at the foot, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, a green bead of Cliffs glass in the lower corner, a shaving of worn oar-wood laid in the fold where a sixth verse should stand, a grey Ash print along the margin that nobody will own, the Council clerk's leaning hand going soft with the damp, the boat-mother's charcoal gloss, and one line at the foot that has never come forward

codex.title: The Land That Is Lent, Being the Account of Orra, a Pack-Woman out of Sill, Who Went Down the Marsh Road in the Reed of Y.H. 812 with Clay Pipes, Needles and Salt Herring and Came Back with Rushes, a Knot of Grey Wool She Will Not Untie, a Reed-Name She Will Not Say Aloud, and a Figure Read Over Her in the South but Paid in the Mud; with the Roads and Their Dues, the Table of What Was Asked and What Was Given, the Standing-Song as It Is Sung Face Down, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A pack-woman's road-account, set down first in charcoal on the backs of dried herring wrappers and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court tallow-warrant voided by the Long Cold; the days in the pack-woman's own hand, the figures in a sloped tally hand learned at the Cross, the sayings of the mud kept in the hearing and not translated, the verbs put back under every borrowed correction, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward
codex.provenance: Written in Reed of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, on the marsh road out of Reedholt and at the Standing Post in the Fenmarch, by Orra, a pack-woman of Sill who carried small wares down to the fen and came back with rushes, eel-sinew, a knot of grey wool and a name she would not write; copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a voided tallow-warrant and carried up the Clay Road to Sill in an oiled-sacking wrapper under the loose board of a landing. It survives as three leaves of soft reed-paper sewn with eel-sinew and folded in oiled sacking: a peat thumb worked into the head, a bog-water tideline along the gutter that has taken two figures clean off, a wet reed pressed flat across the second leaf, a clay-pipe stem snapped in the fold, a salt-herring scale at the foot, a reed-wolf's tooth nick at the second corner, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, a knot of grey wool tied through a hole in the first leaf which she will not untie, two corrections in borrowed hands, one word scraped away with a knife-point, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own

codex.title: The Landing Tally, Being the Dues of the Fishstairs Below the North Bridge in Sill and the Measures Set to the Clerk at the Out-of-Line Step, with the Figures Called, the Figures Not Called, and the Order of Reaching Entered Beside Them
codex.kind: A page from a collector's clerk's pocket ledger; figures in Ledgerhand, the remarks terse and in the hand that holds the slate, one column struck by the College and drawn back underneath, a numbering in a borrowed hand where the writer left a place, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Kept at the Fishstairs landing below the north bridge in Sill from the Opening of the Slates on Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, through the Account-days of Reed in the Thin Year; written by the clerk set at the out-of-line step (the office stands on the roll, the hand does not), carried in the inner coat pocket where the slate's strap has worn a place opposite the wrist and the cuff has gone grey from washing. It survives soft at the fold, with dried eel slime along the fore-edge, grey silt worked into the gutter, a white salt bloom at the head, a green bead of lead-glaze in the lower corner, a pale round ring pressed into the paper where a cold tube was set down, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, corrections in the narrow upright hand of the College, a numbering in a hand that is not the College's, and one line at the foot nobody will own.

codex.title: Of the Last Bed, the Drawing at the Mouth, and the Pot Broken at the Door, Being Title the Tenth of the Ordinances of the Keeping: with the Last-Bed Tally, the Form Left Blank, the Pot-Breaking Verse Said at the Threshold, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: An extract from the Court's ordinances, written out for the gate of the Bone Orchard outside Sill with the marginal hand of the clerk who keeps the last-bed slate there; the articles in Ledgerhand with the verbs restored beneath them, the tally in a table, the form of entry left blank, the pot-breaking verse said at the threshold, one word scored away with the edge of the cold-iron tube, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed
codex.provenance: Copied at the Bone Orchard gate in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, from Title the Tenth of the Ordinances of the Keeping as confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of Y.H. 418, set down after the Rising of Y.H. 668 and added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year; it survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, kept on a nail in the gate-room and taken down when a household sends for the collector: a grey Ash thumb at the head, a tallow watch-candle thumb beside it, the pale ring of a pot set down at the second fold, cold-iron filings from a tube-wrap worked into the gutter, a streak of pale slip along the outer edge, a green bead of lead glaze in the corner, a thread of grey wool through the tie-hole, one word scored out with the tube's edge, a washing-water tide-line along the foot, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own

codex.title: Of Quiet Ash, the Licence to Buy, and the Greyed Hand, Being Title the Fifth of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied into the Factor's House at Greybank with the Licence-Clerk's Margin, the Scrape of a Phial-Cork, and a Correction in a Borrowed Hand
codex.kind: An extract from the Court's ordinances, written out for the counter of the factor's house at Greybank, with the marginal hand of the clerk who keeps the licence-book; the articles in Ledgerhand and the verbs restored beneath them, a table of offences, a form of licence left blank, one line scored with a phial-cork, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed
codex.provenance: Copied at Greybank in Seed of Y.H. 813 from Title the Fifth of the Ordinances of the Keeping as first licensed in Y.H. 683, fifteen years after the Rising, and added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812; carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813. It survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, kept under the licence-book in the factor's counting house: a grey Ash thumb at the head, salt bloom along the gutter from the Sallow wind off the quay, a tar thumb at the fold, iron-gall in the creases of two fingers, a scrape where a phial-cork crossed the lower margin, a green bead of cliff-glass, a damp tide-line along the foot, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own.

codex.title: The Lie of the Ground, Being an Account of the Empty Cantons, Which the Court Names So and the Fen Calls the Quiet Acre, Set Down by a Well-Sinker out of Cold Acre Who Went South with a Survey Party in the Thin Year and Came Back Before the Thaw with Nothing to Tell Except the Lie of the Ground; with the Measure of Six Wells, the Nine Doorways, the Song of the Dry Road, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A well-sinker's field account, set down first in charcoal on the backs of three spoiled well-tallies and a Court lime-warrant and copied at Greybank onto the back of a granary docket voided by the Long Cold; the measurements in a rough travelling hand with the rope's figure set above the eye's, the sayings of the country kept in the hearing and not translated, the verbs put back under every borrowed correction, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward
codex.provenance: Written in the Cantons and at Cold Acre in Ash and Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by Gedde, a well-sinker of Cold Acre who keeps the ridge wells from freezing and had never sunk a dry one until he went south, hired with a survey party out of the factor's house at Greybank to measure the old wells; carried back up the south road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a granary docket voided by the Long Cold. It survives folded into a well-rope coil in a dry tin: a white dust like bone meal worked into the fold from the hearths, grey silt in the gutter off the road, a chip of slate pressed into the lower corner with a mark on it that is not a figure, a thumb of tallow at the head, a length of well-rope fibre caught in the sewing, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with a knife-point, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that the writer did not make and has not swept, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own

codex.title: The Light in the Clay Cup, Being a Letter from the Tryworks Two Leagues North-East of Sill to a Woman Who Keeps the Lamp-Row in the Low Houses, Concerning a Thin Rendering After the Long Cold, the Smell on a North Wind, the Price of a Quart of Fat, and the Question of Who Pays for a Burning; with the Answer in the Margin, a Clerk's Correction in Ledgerhand, and a Lamp-Song in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A private letter on the back of a tallow-weight chit spoiled by a wet thumb, written in iron-gall over charcoal that would not take on the fat, folded thrice and tied with a hemp wick; carried down the north-east road from the Tallow Works to Low Kiln in the cover of a pail, answered along the margin in a second hand, borrowed at Greybank where a factor's clerk set a correction on the back in Ledgerhand, and kept since in a dry tin among the wicks and the spoiled weights
codex.provenance: Written at the Tallow Works, two leagues north-east of Sill, in the last tend of Bone, Y.H. 813, by Orra, a woman who renders sheep fat, to Lett, who keeps the lamp-row in the low houses below the sill; carried down in the last week of Bone and answered in the margin at Low Kiln in Ash of the same year, borrowed on the Clay Road at the factor's house at Greybank, and kept in the tin beside the wicks. It survives with a thumb of raw tallow worked into the grain at the head, a grey Ash print along the gutter which nobody will own, a hemp wick through the tie-hole, a bloom of salt on the outer fold off a cuff that had been at the pans, a scorch where the leaf lay too near the try-pot, a brown crust spot at the second fold, the clerk's correction standing above the words, the verbs standing underneath it, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody has claimed

codex.title: The Stonemouth Book of Remedies, Being What a Dresser of Stone Sets to the Lime-Burn, the White Cough, the Fall from the Bank, the Ferr-Thin, the Lead-Rat's Bite, the Birth-Flower and the Child That Comes Cold, Written in the Dust of the Lime Yard with the Errors Left Standing
codex.kind: A quarry-leech's book of remedies in the Stonemouth manner, set down on the back of a spoiled lime-warrant with the counts cut in the margin by a tally-point; the cures in a stone-dresser's hand, the objections of a physician come down from Greybank pressed blue-grey into the gutter, the corrections of a College clerk in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a bank-master's line in chalk at the foot of the remedies, a washing-song with the odd ones left standing, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at Stonemouth, where the Ferr joins the Ilm five leagues upriver of Sill, between Stone of Y.H. 811 and Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the Long Cold and the Thin Year, by Ivo of Stonemouth, a dresser of coarse sandstone who has set bones and caught children in the lime yard for three-and-twenty years; begun on the back of a lime-warrant spoiled by a wetting, cut at the edge with a tally-point, folded into oiled sailcloth and carried downriver at the Opening of the Slates, then copied at Greybank in Smoke of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a discarded weigh-slip. It survives with lime worked into the grain at the head, a blue-grey tideline off the Ferr that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a reed-wolf's tooth pressed into the lower corner by a buyer who paid two marks and did not stay to see it written, a ring of barley-water, a grey Ash print from a cuff nobody will own, a strip of salt-paper pasted over one correction and gone soft at the edge so that the correction shows through, three objections in the cold margin hand of the physician, the clerk's upright hand above the cures, the bank-master's chalk at the remedies, and the line at the foot

codex.title: The Sermon at the Listening Stones, Being What Om of the Long Sitting Said Against the Fourth Stone on the Hearth Drawing of Y.H. 812, with the Sitting-Song Left with Its Number Unsaid, the Sittings in a Stone-Tally, a Mine-Reeve's Clerk's Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A sermon of the Long Sitting preached at the shrine of the Standing Stones five leagues above Keld Keep, where the Vorr sit and come away with numbers; the sayings in the short one-sentence speech of the Vorr set down in Grathic, the sitting-song with the number left as it is not spoken, the sittings in a stone-tally, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a mine-reeve's clerk who learned his letters out of a Court primer, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Preached on Stone 12, Y.H. 812, the Hearth Drawing of the Thin Year, on a morning when the wind came over the Cold Pass and snow stood in the joints of the stones, by Om of the Long Sitting, a Vorr who had sat at the Stones since his fortieth year; written that evening by the woman who keeps the stone-shelter and counts the warm-stone issued to sitters, in charcoal on the back of a survey-sheet spoiled by a lead-rub, folded with a warm-stone chip shut in the crease and tied with a turn of iron wire, and kept since in the tin at the shelter among the tally-stones. It survives with pale lead dust worked into the head off the survey rubbing, cold stone grit in the grain, a warm-stone chip in the fold, a tallow thumb at the head, iron filings caught in the gutter, a grey Ash print along the foot from a cuff nobody will own, a wet ring where a tin of melted snow stood from the first voice to the last, a pressed lichen shut in the second crease, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a mine-reeve's clerk come up from Keld Keep to take the winter count of warm-stone, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied at Greybank in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, into the factor's file of northern sayings, with the verbs put back and the number left as it was not spoken.

codex.title: The Litany Before the Grating, Being the Prayer of the Keepers of the Hearth-Fire at the Weighing, with the Voice's Corrections and a Junior Keeper's Margin
codex.kind: A litany of the Return said by the keepers of the Hearth-fire in the Weighing Hall, the Voice reading and the keepers answering through the bars; set down by a keeper of the third watch who signs with a coal-cross, with the rubrics of the grating, the eight stations and their answer, the Voice's struck corrections, the second watch's note, and a line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in the Weighing Hall in the Hearthseat on Weighing of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the junior keeper of the third watch, on the back of a spoiled slate-copy of the year's first measure, and corrected by Hesta Clay, Voice of the Return, before the Remembering; carried through the Opening of the Slates and copied forward in Ash of Y.H. 813 into a quire kept in the iron box under the grating ledge. It survives soft along the fold and scorched at the upper edge, with coal-dust worked into the creases of the first leaf, a lamp-black thumb, iron filings caught in the gutter from the grating hinge, a spot of tallow off the watch lamp, a hair, a grey Ash print from a cuff that had been in the residue room, and a small coal in the fold that nobody will own.

codex.title: The Litany of the Deep, Being the Order of the Return as the Surveyors of the First Seam Say It Over the Walling-In at Keld Keep
codex.kind: A litany of the Return read from the walling-slate at the mouth of the First Seam, before the mortar is mixed and while the dead one still faces the deep seam; with the rubrics of the mouth, eight stations and their answer, the walling-slate for the season, a Court survey-clerk's correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a widow's margin, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Senn, who keeps the walling-slate at the mouth of the First Seam at Keld Keep and has never been down the Descent, on the back of a walling-tally spoiled by a thumb of iron filings and a spill of lamp oil; folded into the flap of the slate satchel and kept on the nail beside the mouth, taken out only when there is a wall to make; borrowed at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 by a survey-clerk of the Court who set his hand above hers. It survives with clamp-filings ground into the head, pale lime from the walling mortar along the gutter, a thumb of tallow at the fold, a spot that came over the Cold Pass and has been water twice and frost twice, two words gone where the lamp oil ran across the fifth station, a notch cut at the edge with a tally-knife where a word would not come, the clerk's correction standing above the words it corrects, a widow's hand in the margin, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward

codex.title: The Litany of the Ground Pot, Being the Order of the Return as the Four Kilns of Nine Pots Keep It at the Opening of a Firing
codex.kind: A litany of the Return said to the clay at the shared pit and again over a child born under the fourth kiln, the tally-woman reading from the firing-tally and the women of the kilns answering; with the rubrics of the pit, eight stations and their answer, a road-clerk's correction come up from Sill, a woman's notes written in slip, and a line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at Nine Pots in Ember of Y.H. 813, the year after the Thin Year, by Tessa of the Fourth Kiln, keeper of the firing-tally at the shared clay pit, on the back of a tally spoiled by a wet slip-thumb in the tally-shed; carried down to Sill on Account-day in a cart of coarse ware and corrected there by a clerk of the Court's table in Slate Row, who had come up about the road; copied forward in Frost of Y.H. 813 into a quire wrapped in oiled sacking and kept in a hollow of the pit under a flat stone. It survives with bone-pale slip in every crease, brick-red kiln dust along the fore-edge, a broken sherd pressed into the fold with a cupworm's bore through it, a green bead of lead glaze from a girl come up from the Cross, a press of wet wool across the second leaf, a small ale ring gone dark, the clerk's upright hand above the talk, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed.

codex.title: The Litany of the Peat Raft, Being the Return as the Reed-Cutters of the Fenmarch Say It at the Cutting, with the Rubrics of the Bank, Seven Stations and the Answer Said to the Water, the Knot Tied After the Fourth, a Factor's Clerk's Correction, Two Hands in the Margin, and the Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A litany of the Return said over a peat raft going out into the reedbed, the reader at the cut and the row answering to the water; set down in charcoal and peat by a woman who keeps the reed-cut outside Reedholt, with the manner of it, seven stations, the verse at the loosing, one correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, two hands in the margin, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Reed of Y.H. 813, the year after the Thin Year, at the reed-cut outside Reedholt in the Fenmarch, by a woman of the cut who signs with a knot of grey wool and not with a name; written on the back of a fen peat-docket spoiled by bog-water, carried up the marsh road through Mud End and copied at Greybank in Ash of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a voided thin-return docket, sewn with eel-sinew into a fold of oiled reed and kept under the loose board at the Standing Post. It survives with peat worked brown into the head, a bog-water tideline along the gutter that has taken two words clean off the fourth station, a press of wet sedge across the second leaf, a knot of grey wool tied through a hole in the margin which the writer has not untied, a fish-hook nick at the upper corner, a shaving of horn caught in the fourth fold, a brine ring gone white on the third leaf, a tallow thumb, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the clerk's correction standing above the words it corrects, two hands in the margin, and a line at the foot which has never been claimed

codex.title: The Litany of the Rows, Being the Order of the Return as the Women of the North Road Say It Over the Small Graves at the Bone Orchard, with the Manner of It, Eight Stations and Their Answer, the Verse Said While the Pot Is Broken, a Ruling in Ledgerhand, a Mother's Note in Charcoal, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A litany of the Return said at the setting-down of a thin-return child, when the collector has been and the body is carried out by the arm that knew the household; the prayer is for the clay and not for the child, which is already in the account. Set down in the voice of the woman who lays the small ones in the rows, with the rubrics of the orchard, station and answer, the breaking verse, one narrow correction in the Ledgerhand of a clerk of the factor at Greybank, four lines of thick charcoal from a woman who had set a child down, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Set down in Ash of Y.H. 813, the Thin Year, by a woman of Low Kiln who has laid the small ones in the rows at the Bone Orchard a league beyond Sill's north gate for nineteen years; she signs with the foot of a broken pot and not with a name. Written in charcoal and tallow on the back of a thin-return burial docket spoiled by rain, folded into a fold of grey wool and carried in the breast of a coat, which is why there is ash in every crease; copied forward once at the Fishstairs in the same year in another hand, with the verbs left standing. It survives with grave-clay ground into the head, cold-iron filings from a tube-wrap worked along the gutter, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the pale ring of a pot set down and lifted, a dry grave-flower pressed flat in the second fold, a silt tideline where a pail went over on the watch-shed step, a tallow thumb, a ring of small ale gone dark, a barley awn stiff in the fold, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the factor at Greybank, four lines of thick charcoal from a woman who had carried, and the line at the foot, which has never been claimed

codex.title: The Litany of the Second Cutting, Being the Order of the Return as the Number-Cutters of Keld Keep Keep It Over the Returned Arm
codex.kind: A litany of the Return said at the shaft mouth over a man come back thin from the bank, before the old numbers are cut out of the forearm and the new cut in; the cutter reading from the arm and the order answering by number, with the rubrics of the Keep, nine stations and their answer, the silence of the Vorr left standing, a factor's clerk's correction in Ledgerhand, the margin of a woman cut twice, and a line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the cutter of numbers at the Descent in Keld Keep, who has set two counts where her name would stand, the first cut at thirteen and the second after the bank, on the back of a survey sheet spoiled in the First Seam; carried down the Rim Road in Stone of Y.H. 812 with a lead cart, corrected at Greybank in Kindling of Y.H. 812 by a clerk of the factor's office, and copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 into a quire kept in a tin at the shaft mouth. It survives with coal smut ground into the head, an iron-red cross from the mine-reeve's point, a warm-stone shaving still warm in the fold, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead, a frost-feather pressed flat between the third and fourth leaves and gone by noon, a clamp-scratch across the answer, grey Ash on the outer fold, a thumb in coal dust nobody will own, the nine stations, one correction in Ledgerhand, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath

codex.title: The Litany of the Third Pouring, Being the Order of the Return as a House of Nine Pots Keeps It When a Woman Comes Back for the Third Time, with the Manner of It, Seven Stations and the Answer Said to the Cloth, the Three Knots Counted Out, a Factor's Clerk's Correction in Narrow Upright Ledgerhand, a Bowl-Leech's Cold Objection, a Daughter's Charcoal, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A prayer of the Return said in a potter's house at Nine Pots on the evening a woman is brought back for the third time, the woman of the house reading from a folded birth-cloth and the household answering to the knots; written in charcoal on the back of a spoiled clay-docket, with the rubrics of the house, seven stations and their answer, the pourings set in a table with the figure entered and the figure that came back, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor's clerk out of Greybank, the pressed objection of a bowl-leech come up from the south, a daughter's thick charcoal in the margin, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at Nine Pots, eight leagues west of Sill, in Tallow of Y.H. 813, the year after the Thin Year, by the woman of a potter's house who keeps the birth-cloth, and signed with three knots of grey wool and not with a name; carried down the Clay Road to Sill on the evening of an Account-day and borrowed there by a clerk of the factor at Greybank, who set his hand above hers and put a nought in the fourth place; kept since in the fold of the grey wool cloth on the pot-shelf, taken out after the evening figure has been read and put back before the lamp is trimmed. It survives with clay worked brown into the head, a bone-pale streak of slip down the gutter, the print of a wet pot's foot at the third fold, a tallow thumb, a grey Ash print nobody will own, a cold-iron shaving out of a tube's wool wrap, a thread of grey wool from the cloth which comes back after every shaking, a browned crust pressed flat between the fifth and sixth leaves, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, the clerk's correction standing above the words it corrects, the leech's cold objection in the margin, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward

codex.title: The Long Night Riddles, Being a Contest Held with the Fire Banked under Slate Row in the Hearthseat, with Four Questions Put in the Dark, the Fifth Answered by a Voice Nobody Could Place, the Warm Places Read by Touch at First Grey, a College Clerk's Figures Set Above at the Remembering, and One Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: An alehouse keeper's record of a night with no light, set down for the settling of an argument about a voice and not for the improvement of the reader; the rules in the hand that covers the hearth, the questions in the words they were put in the dark, the answers as they came back out of it, the score read by the warmth of hands on the bench at first grey, the figures of a College clerk entered above afterwards, a coal-woman's gloss pressed into the margin in broad charcoal, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim
codex.provenance: Written at first grey on the morning of the Remembering, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, at the alehouse called the Covered Fire in the lane under Slate Row in the Hearthseat, by the woman who keeps the room and covers the hearth at dusk; set down from what she remembered of the voices before the fire was uncovered, because what is spent in the night is not entered in the morning. Written in lamp-black thinned with small ale on the back of a notice of the Five spoiled when the damp took the clean figure off one corner, folded and sewn with wire into a fold of oiled sacking and kept under the dish beside the banked hearth; copied forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, onto the back of a College term-sheet voided by a wet thumb. It survives with a thumb of tallow at the head, lamp-black in the grain of every word, a ring where a cup of water stood from the first question to the fifth and went cold without being drunk, a grey Ash print off a Kept room's skirting board worked into the gutter, a scorch where a spark off the grating caught the second leaf when the fire was uncovered, the pale ghost of the printed figure showing through one corner, a press of wet wool across the first leaf off a man who held the door and did not let go when he was through, the charcoal rubbed thin where a sleeve went over it in the dark, a damp tide-line out of the sealed-file room along the foot, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the College of Assessors, a gloss in the broad charcoal of the woman who carried the dish up from the Hall on Kindling, and a line at the foot which nobody has claimed

codex.title: The Song of the Cut, Being a Mother's Lullaby of the High Rim, Sung to the Cradle Board at Keld Keep; with the Number Before the Name, the Stone Held Back Until After the Knife, a Survey-Clerk's Correction in Ledgerhand, a Grandmother's Charcoal, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A mother's lullaby in the hard clipped Rim speech, set in Grathic letters because Keldish is cut in bone and does not travel; the verses said to the arm and to the nail in the cradle board, never to the man who will one day sing them, the endings struck off, the refrain counted down the fingers of one hand; a mine-reeve's red checking at the second corner, a survey-clerk's correction above in narrow upright Ledgerhand, the child's grandmother in thick charcoal underneath, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim
codex.provenance: Sung first over a cradle in a room above the shaft mouth at Keld Keep, and again, after the cradle had stood empty three years, to the iron nail in its board; set down in Bone of Y.H. 812, the winter her youngest son turned twelve, by his mother, a woman of the count's row who has never gone below; written in charcoal on the back of a shift-tally spoiled by slate dust, with a notch cut in the edge where no Grathic word would come, carried down the Rim Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with a cart of warm-stone and copied at Greybank onto a voided weigh-slip, where a survey-clerk set his figure above hers. It survives with a shaving of bone at the head, coal smut in the second fold, a thumb of tallow, a curl of the child's first hair in the sewing, a dry barley crust, the dent where a warm-stone stood on the leaf and went cold, a red thread from the mine-reeve's checking, a frost-feather gone by noon, a small-ale ring at the foot, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the notch in the edge, the clerk's correction above, the grandmother's charcoal underneath, and the line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: A Letter from the Counting House at Greybank to the Ember Bowl in the Bowl of Sere, Concerning the Price of Northern Measures, the Forty That Are Not Found but Made, a Beautiful Return That Would Not Hold a Cup, and the Shape a House Must Buy; with the Answer in the Margin, a Correction in Ledgerhand, and a Rowing Song from the Pulled Benches
codex.kind: A merchant's letter in iron-gall on the back of a barley tally spoiled by damp, folded thrice and sealed with a thumb of red lead-glaze; carried south from Greybank by a grain factor's clerk as far as the Peat Line and from there by a carrier of eels to the Bowl of Sere; answered in the recipient's hand along the gutter, corrected on the outer fold at the Council room in Vhal, and kept since in the Ember house's box of southern contracts
codex.provenance: Written at the Sere counting house in Greybank, eighteen leagues downriver of Sill, in the last tend of Grain, Y.H. 813, by Corven Dells, a factor's under-clerk who buys northern measures for the Ten Bowls, to Ovia Gilded, keeper of the bowls in House Ember at the Bowl of Sere; answered in her hand in the gutter, borrowed at Vhal by a factor's clerk who could not let paper lie, and returned to the box of contracts in the Bowl. It survives with barley dust worked into the head and the gutter, a round wine ring the width of a cup, a thumb of red seal at the outer fold that comes away on the finger, a pale tideline of salt along the lower margin, one figure gone over in the damp and written again underneath, an answer in a sloping southern hand, one correction in the narrow upright hand of the College, a round nought set in the place of a missing oar, and a line at the foot that nobody has claimed

codex.title: The Mercy Telling at Mud End, Being Six Stories Spoken on the Long Night in the Peat Byre, the One Told to the Floor, and the Figure a Clerk Set Against the Dead
codex.kind: A byre-keeper's record of a winter telling, set down for the settling of which death was called merciful and not for the comfort of the reader; the rules in the hand the byre keeps, the stories in the words they were spoken, a score in peat-blocks on the trodden floor, the figures of a factor's clerk entered over them, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written on the Long Night of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in the peat byre at Mud End three leagues downriver of Sill, by the woman who keeps the byre where the moot sits when the peat is too wet to stand on; copied out in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a spoiled winter-peat tally, folded into oiled sacking and kept in a wall-niche behind the peat-stack under a flat stone. It survives with a peat thumb at the head, a press of wet wool across the first leaf, a small ale ring, a grey Ash print along the gutter, frost-crisp at one edge, one sheep's-wool fibre off the Tallow road, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor's clerk come up from Greybank to count the winter peat, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody's.

codex.title: The Milk Sea, Being an Account of Vhalen and the Sallow Coast, Set Down by an Eel-Man of the Fishstairs Who Went Up the Salt Road with Smoked Eels and Coarse Pots and Came Back with Salt, Glass, and a Rope That Would Not Rot
codex.kind: A river-man's travel account, set down first on the backs of dried eel-sacks and copied forward on the back of a spoiled Court salt warrant; part road-log, part inventory, part complaint, with the figure of a Council tally-clerk set in the margin, the verbs put back underneath in the writer's own charcoal hand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at the Quay in Vhal in the last tend of Ilmen, Y.H. 813, by a man of the Fishstairs in Sill who went up the Salt Road in Stone of Y.H. 812 with two baskets of smoked eels, a cart of coarse ware from Nine Pots and two bales of wool, and came back at the turn of the year with a sack of salt, a bottle of cliff-glass, a coil of tarred rope and a silver mark that had been counted so often it had gone thin at the edge. Set down on the backs of eel-sacks, copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court salt warrant spoiled by the damp, sewn with eel-sinew into a scrap of oiled sailcloth and carried upriver in a clay tube stoppered with wool. It survives with a white salt bloom in the gutter, a thumb of tar at the head, a green bead of cliff-glass pressed into the second fold, a fish-hook nick, a peck-hole where a brine-gull took the leaf for a crust, a ring of warm wine near the song, a rope-burn along the outer edge, a grey Ash print nobody will own, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Council clerk, the writer's charcoal words restored beneath it, and a line at the foot in a hand that answers to no name

codex.title: The Mine's Own Appetite, Being a Soldier's Field Notes on the Warm-Stone Grub of the Ninth Gallery Beneath Keld Keep; with the Gallery Verse as It Is Sung, a Tally of Grubs and Blocks, a Mine-Reeve's Ruling in Ledgerhand, a Cutter's Line in Broad Charcoal, and One Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A soldier's field book on one small beast, set down as the record of shifts stopped and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in the hard short Rim speech written in Grathic letters, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled seam-tallies, the gallery verse as it is sung, a ruling in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the mine-reeve's clerk, a warm-stone cutter's line in broad charcoal, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Bone and Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Senn of the Ninth, one of the Warden's men set over the warm-stone working beneath Keld Keep, who carried a short clamp and a lamp and stopped a shift for the first time in his ninth year down; set down at the end of shifts against the wall where the rock sweats, first on the backs of rim-seam tallies spoiled by slate-damp and then on three folds of oiled survey-cloth sewn with wire, carried up the shaft in a coat pocket against a flint and a shaving of warm-stone. Copied forward at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a voided requisition for lamp-oil. It survives with coal dust ground into the head off a block carried two shifts in the pocket, the sweetish smell of hot lead gone into the grain of the second leaf, a warm-stone shaving shut in the fold that kept its heat one night on a stone floor and is cold now, a scorch where a lamp guttered and caught the corner of the third leaf, the charcoal rubbed thin where the wrap was carried against the thigh, one ruling in Ledgerhand standing above the words it corrects, a cutter's line in broad charcoal at the foot of the tally, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: The Mixing Bench, Being the Standing Rules of the Glaze-Mixers of High Kiln for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices at the Glaze Room of House Clay, with the Years Set in a Table, the Tally of Hands, the Mixing-Song Pasted Inside the Lid, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A bench-copy of the room's standing rules in the hand of the woman who keeps the mixing bench and the tasting-spoons; the rules in the short sayings of the terrace, the years and the faults in tables, the mixing-song pasted to the inside of the jar-lid, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Court clerk, one line struck in charcoal by a mixer who would not sign it, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody has claimed
codex.provenance: First gathered at High Kiln in Y.H. 691, the year the house entered the sweet sickness in its own account and then wrote the word out of it again, and copied forward from the bench and the tasting-spoons and not from a book; this leaf written in Grain of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by the woman who has kept the mixing bench and the spoons for nineteen years, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813. It survives folded in a grey cloth under the jar that stands cold under its glaze, with the sweet green of lead glaze worked into the grain at the head and into the creases of the writer's thumb, a white crust of dried slip at the fold, the sweetish edge of the mix still in the paper after a year, a ring where a tasting-cup of barley-water stood from one question to the next, a green bead pressed into the second fold by a girl with sweetness still at her mouth, a thumb of tallow, a grey print along the outer fold that is not hers and that she has not swept, two corrections in the Court's upright hand, one charcoal line struck and written again beneath, and a line at the foot nobody will own

codex.title: The Moot Board at the Cross, Being the Prices Cried at Sill Market and the Dues of the Roads That Go Out of It, with the Counts That Go Round the Square Set Beside the Printed One
codex.kind: A pig-weigher's fair copy of the board at the moot-post, being the prices of the last market of Stone carried forward into Ilmen and the dues paid at this end of each road; corrected in a Court clerk's soft-cuffed hand and a carter's, with a third hand at the foot that nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written and kept at the Cross in Sill by the man who weighs the pigs on Account-day, who has held the moot board since the year before the Long Cold; the figures taken at the last market of Stone, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, and copied forward at the market mornings of Ilmen, Y.H. 813, as the levy was called for the thaw. Set on the back of a Court notice gone soft at one corner and kept under the moot-post's nail in the finger's width of shade, where a basket may be set beside it. It survives with pig-bristle in the head, a tallow thumb, barley grease from a crust laid down and not eaten, eel slime at the foot, a green bead of lead glaze from the Glaze Room rolled into the fold, marsh mud on the Reedholt corner, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first price to the last, a grey Ash print along the margin that nobody will own, two corrections in hands that are not the writer's, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim.

codex.title: The Reedholt Mud-Wife's Book, Being Remedies for the Mire-Fever, the Ankle-Cold, the Reed-Wolf's Bite, the Birth-Print, the Bought Breath and the Third Night, Set Down in Grathic Letters Though Fen Cant Is Not Written, with a Physician's Objections Pressed in the Margin, a Factor's Clerk's Corrections, and a Knot for the Word That Cannot Be Written
codex.kind: A reed-midwife's book of remedies in the Fen manner, written in Grathic letters learned off an eel-trader, the cures in a mud-wife's hand and said to the ground, words that cannot be written tied as knots in the margin, a physician's objections pressed in from Sill, the corrections of a factor's clerk in Ledgerhand, a song sung half through the nose with the last word falling into mud, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at Reedholt in the east marsh between Ember and Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year and the Long Cold, by Lull Mud, a mud-wife who caught children on the boardwalks and laid out the drowned of the drained cuts for twenty-one years; begun on a leaf of oiled reed and two strips of birch bark spoiled by a wetting, sewn with eel-sinew, tied with grey wool and carried in a dry tin slung under the hut boards; copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a spoiled peat-tally. It survives with a peat thumb worked into the head, a bog-water tideline that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a press of wet sedge across the third, a scratch from a reed-wolf's tooth at the corner of the tally, a dried smear of fever-mud, one knot of grey wool tied through a hole in the first strip which the writer will not untie, a small round pale place where a collector's cuff was laid and nobody will own the cuff, three objections in the hand of a physician come down the marsh road from Sill, corrections in the narrow upright hand of a factor's clerk, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: Of the Finding and the Naming of Vessels, Being Title the Second of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied for the Assessor's House at Sill with the Margin Kept by the Clerk Who Writes the Names
codex.kind: An extract from the Court's ordinances, written out for the assessor's house in Slate Row, Sill, with the marginal hand of the clerk who keeps that house's foundling slate, a hearth-maid's crossed mark in charcoal, one correction in the narrow upright hand of the College, and one line struck through and left legible
codex.provenance: Copied at Sill in Slate Row in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates on Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813; two leaves folded into a board cover and kept in the assessor's house built in Y.H. 776, taken down when a child with no house is brought to be named. It survives with slip dust in the gutter, a tallow thumb at the head, a brown grease spot where a crust was laid, a drop of sour milk, a grey Ash print worked into the outer fold of the board, and a narrow pale crease where the leaf was carried in a coat pocket against a wrist.

codex.title: The Nest in the Warm Crack, Being a Watchman's Field Notes on the Tallow-Wasp at the Rendering House Beyond Sill
codex.kind: A watchman's field book on one small beast, set down as the record of rounds kept over the rendering fires and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled fat-tallies, a verse of the vats as the lamp-women say it, one ruling in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the factor's clerk at Greybank, a line traced in rancid tallow by a lamp-woman who would not give her name, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Tallow and Ember of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by one of the Thane's men set to keep the rendering house two leagues north-east of Sill, who took the wasps' nests and burned them as he was bid; set down at the end of rounds in the shed with a tallow lamp under the draught of the flue, first on the backs of fat-tallies spoiled by a spill, then on three folds of birch bark sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a coat pocket against a flint. Copied forward at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813. It survives with a brown tallow thumb ground into the head, a grey bloom of sour fat along the fold, a press of wet wool across the first leaf, a singe where the flue drew a spark onto the third, a small round mark where a buyer set a mark-piece down and took it up again, the charcoal rubbed thin where the wrap was carried against the thigh, one ruling in the clerk's Ledgerhand, one line traced in rancid tallow by a lamp-woman, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: The Night-Roll of the Waiting Room, Being the Vessels Held at Sill Between the Drawing and the Banking through Bone and Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, with the Hour, the Embers, the Note, the Return Due, and What Was Said After the Slate Was Shut
codex.kind: A page from the Waiting Room book at Sill, ruled in Ledgerhand by the clerk of the room, the remarks terse and in the same hand; a column of night-sayings struck through by a College clerk and kept on the back of the leaf where his correction cannot reach, one figure set above by a factor's clerk, a pallet-song with the answer left out, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in the Waiting Room off Slate Row in Sill through the third tend of Bone and the whole of Ash, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Ilmen of Y.H. 813, when the book was ruled anew and the old leaves put under the pallets. The room is the one where the collected are kept overnight before the banking; the book lies on the shelf by the door with the tube's wool sleeve and a tin of tallow ends. It survives soft at the fold and damp along the foot, with straw from the pallets worked into the gutter, a tide-line from the washing of the floor, a cold dark spot where a warmed stone stood and went cold, grey Ash off a corner rubbed into the head, the pale ring of a cup set down and not lifted, a press of grey wool where a sleeve lay, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, one hair from a head shut in the fold, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, one column struck on the face and preserved on the back, one figure set above in a borrowed hand, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Nine Pots Book of Bones, Being Remedies for the Crushed Hand, the Bone Set Wrong, the Four-Kiln Cough, the Feud-Cut, the Sweet Line, the Birth-Flower and the Child That Comes Cold, Set Down in the Dust of the Shared Pit with the Errors Left Standing
codex.kind: A bone-setter's and midwife's book of remedies in the Nine Pots manner, set down on the back of a spoiled road-tally with the counts cut into the margin by a tally-point; the cures in a bone-setter's blunt hand, the objections of a physician come down from Greybank pressed blue-grey into the gutter, the corrections of a College clerk in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a moot-man's line in charcoal at the foot of the remedies, a setting-song with the name of the road left out, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at Nine Pots, eight leagues west of Sill on the feud road, between Stone of Y.H. 811 and Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the Long Cold and the Thin Year, by Talla of Nine Pots, a bone-setter who has dressed the kiln hands and caught children in the potters' houses for four-and-twenty years; begun on the back of a road-tally spoiled when a rain took the figures out of it, cut at the edge with a tally-point, folded into oiled sacking and carried in the breast of a potter's apron, and copied at Greybank in Smoke of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a discarded weigh-slip. It survives with chalk worked into the grain at the head, a blue-grey tideline off the Ferr ford that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a thumb of clay-pit slip in the gutter, a cupworm cocoon pressed into the fold, a ring of barley-water, a scorch where a spark off the fourth kiln caught the corner, a green bead of High Kiln glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl with the sweetness at her mouth, three objections in the cold margin hand of the physician, the clerk's upright hand above the cures, the moot-man's charcoal at the remedies, and the line at the foot

codex.title: The Sermon at the Counting Stone, Being What a Reader of the Return Said Over the Five Open Wells on a Morning in Stone of Y.H. 812, with the Nine Cups Cut in the Stone, the Warming-Song Left with the Four Stopped Cups as They Stand, the Ledger of the Wells, a Clerk's Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A sermon of the Temple of the Return preached at the shrine of the counting stone among the Nine Wells on the Keel, five leagues short of the Hearthseat; the sayings in the clean voice of the Hearthseat set down in Grathic, the song with the four stopped cups left as they stand, the nine cups in a well-ledger, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk of the College of Assessors come up from Slate Row, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Preached on Stone 22, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by a reader of the Return come up from the Hearthseat, at the counting stone between the five open wells, on a morning when steam stood a hand high over the water and the road was frozen hard enough to carry a cart; written that evening by the woman who keeps the counting stone and draws the water for the five, in charcoal and tallow on the back of a measure-slip spoiled at the Weighing, folded with a lead stop out of one of the four cups shut in the crease, and kept since in a tin under the stone's lip where the drawers leave their bits. It survives with lime bloom worked into the head and gutter, warm-stone grit in the grain, a wet ring where the dish of water stood from the first voice to the last, a copper bit shut in the fold, a grey Ash print along the gutter off a cuff nobody will own, a pale ring of spilt milk on the second leaf, the lead stop, one correction in a clerk's hand that takes the verbs out and numbers the four nil, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied once at Greybank in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the four cups left stopped.

codex.title: The Ninefold Coming Back, Called the Litany of the Long Night
codex.kind: A prayer of the Return, said in the dark on the Long Night, at the bedside of the dying, and over a birth-slate; with the household's answer
codex.provenance: Written in charcoal and tallow on a leaf of birch bark by a hearth-maid of Low Kiln in Sill in Y.H. 811, the Long Cold, and added to in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year; she set her mark in the corner in place of a name, being two fingers crossed. The leaf is kept folded in the fold of a grey wool birth-cloth that passes from hearth-maid to hearth-maid in the low houses, and is taken out only after dark. It bears a tallow thumb, a smear of bone-pale slip, a spot of green from a glaze-room mouth, a charcoal print shaped like a pot's foot, and two corrections in different hands. It survives because the cloth is washed oftener than the leaf.

codex.title: Of the Paper Called The Sealed Vessel, and of the Nine Who Read It: Being an Extract from the Annals of the First Seam, with the Seven Propositions as the Tin Keeps Them, the Year-Entries in the Number-First Hand, the Burning-Song Carried Up the Shaft, Two Corrections in the Upright Hand of the Court, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A survey-clerk's extract from the annals of the Tenth Clamp, copied out of the tin lined with warm-stone that stands in the survey room off the Duelling Floor; the year-entries in the number-first hand, the propositions taken down from the paper itself with the Court's corrections set above them, the nine readers entered by seat and not by name, a song taken down from a carrier who would not give his number, a curl of burnt paper pasted into the gutter, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written beneath Keld Keep in the First Seam in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the clerk who keeps the survey tally; he states his number before this and withholds both, which is the custom of the room. Copied from the paper in the tin on the Last Day, when the ash in the corners is not swept, and carried up the Rim Road with a lead cart, then entered forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives as five leaves of rough survey paper sewn with wire into a board cover gone soft at the seam: warm-stone dust ground into the inner margin off the tin, coal smut at the head, a curl of burnt paper from one of the eight copies pasted into the gutter, a smear of hot lead at the fold, a frost-feather pressed flat between the third and fourth leaves and gone by noon, a hard drop of tallow, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the clerk did not make and has not swept, and a correction in the narrow upright hand of a Court survey-clerk which takes the verbs out.

codex.title: The Ninth Gallery Book of Remedies, Being Remedies for the Sweet at the Gum, the Rope-Coloured Hand, the Descent Boy's Fortnight, the Warm-Stone Burn, the Member Gone Dark, the Cut from a Seam-Shard, the Second Chill and the Birth-Flower, Set Down Beneath Keld Keep with the Errors Left Standing
