codex.kind: A mine-leech's and midwife's book of remedies in the hard short Rim speech, written in Grathic letters learned off a Court survey-clerk with the Keldish endings left in where they will not fit; the cures in a leech's hand on the backs of survey sheets gone soft with slate-damp, the objections of a physician come down from Greybank pressed coal-grey into the margin, the corrections of a survey-clerk of the Court in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a clamp-master's line in charcoal at the foot of the remedies, a watch-song with the place where the tenth should stand left as it is sung, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in the Ninth Gallery beneath Keld Keep between Stone of Y.H. 812 and Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the Long Cold and the Thin Year, by Orva of the Ninth Gallery, a leech who dressed the hands of the Duelling Floor and caught the children of the survey families for seven-and-twenty years; begun on the backs of rim-seam survey sheets spoiled by slate-damp, folded into oiled survey-cloth and carried up the shaft against a shaving of warm-stone, then down the Rim Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with a survey party bound for Greybank, where it was copied onto the back of a voided seam-tally. It survives with coal dust ground into the grain at the head, a tideline of slate-water that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead shut into the sewing, a scorch where a spark off the hot-lead corner caught the third leaf, a shaving of warm-stone pressed flat in the fold which kept its heat one night on the stone floor and is cold now, a ring of barley-water gone grey at the edge, a thumb of tallow, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own, objections in the cold margin hand of the physician, corrections in the upright hand of the survey-clerk, the clamp-master's line in charcoal, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: The Book of the Open Bowl, Being the Seven Remedies of a House-Physician in the Bowl of Sere, with the Eighth Place Left Standing
codex.kind: A bowl-house physician's book of remedies in the southern courtesy hand, written in the thin gold so that no clerk could mistake physic for a contract; the cures in a house-leech's hand, the leaning entries of the tally-clerk above them, a northern bond-woman's charcoal underneath, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own; with one song for the third hour and an eighth place kept empty
codex.provenance: Written in Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in a house of the Ten Bowls in the Bowl of Sere, by Orylla Vanee, a house-physician who kept the sick-bowls and attended both the slave births and the exhibited returns; set down in thin gold on prepared paper, the back of the leaf carrying the thick gold of a contract that was never signed. Carried north with a consignment of oil and tallow-wasp resin and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold. It survives with the thin gold worn from half the remedies so that the uncleared contract shows through, the yellow dust of the burning winds worked into the sewing rather than lying on the face, a thumb of olive oil, a resin smear that caught dust and will not come out, a wine-ring at the foot, a scorched corner where the leaf lay near a court fire, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, a grain of southern wheat stuck fast in the resin, and a single pale hair in the fold that is not gold. The corrections stand above in the leaning hand of the house tally-clerk and underneath in the charcoal of a woman of the grain mills who would not give her name.

codex.title: The Pail Song, Being the Drawing-Song of the Yard Well in Low Kiln, Sung at the Bucket-Round in Frost, with the Pails Counted Going Up from the Stone Lip, the Fourth Left Standing for the Well, the Frost-Bloom Knocked Grey, a Kiln-Master's Ruling in Broad Charcoal, a Factor's Clerk's Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss from a Woman of the Bucket-Round, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A work song of the drawing, in the low hard speech of the yard, said to the rope and answered at the stone lip; the verses counted in pails going up from the well, with the fourth pail left standing where the frost wrote and not carried; the rubrics of the lip in the writer's charcoal thinned with well-water, a kiln-master's ruling in broad charcoal, a factor's clerk's figures standing above in Ledgerhand, a gloss pressed into the margin by a woman of the bucket-round, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim
codex.provenance: Sung at the yard well four doors down the Clay Yard from the Vail kiln-house in Low Kiln of Sill and set down in Frost of Y.H. 813 by a woman who has drawn at that well eleven winters and knows by the feel of the rope when the bucket has cleared the lip; written in charcoal thinned with well-water on the back of a bucket-tally spoiled by a wet thumb, folded twice and tied with grey wool to the hook of the well-rope under a broken pot turned mouth-down against the frost, carried up the Clay Road with a consignment of coarse tile and copied forward at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 814 onto the back of a factor's voided weigh-slip. It survives with a pale stone-lip thumb worked into the grain at the head, a frost-bloom raised white along the gutter and gone grey where the bucket touched it, a chip of the north lip in the fold, a rope-fray across the third verse, a pail-ring gone cold on the second leaf, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl with sweetness at one mouth-corner, a sour small-ale ring at the foot, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own, the kiln-master's broad ruling, the clerk's figures standing above, the bucket-round woman's gloss in the margin, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: The Dry Man of Mud End, Being a Peat-Byre Tale Told in Stone, with the Bog-Wager, the Riddle Put to the Byre and Not to the Room, the Nine Houses, the Hide That Was Won and Left Unnamed, a Factor's Clerk's Entry Set Over It, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A byre-woman's telling of a night in the deep cold, set down for the settling of an argument about a hide of peat and not for the improvement of the reader; the tale in the words it was told, the riddle in the words it was put, the standing-song as it goes round the fire, the wager in a column of peat-measures, the figures of a factor's clerk entered over them, a reeve's gloss in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year after the Long Cold, at the moot-byre of Mud End three leagues downriver of Sill, by the woman who keeps the byre-fire, the peat measure and the bench the moot sits on; told to her by a man come up the marsh road out of the Fenmarch with dry boots in deep weather. Set down in charcoal on the back of a hide-tally spoiled by a wet thumb, carried up the river road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the damp, where a factor's clerk borrowed the leaf and set his figures above hers. It survives folded in a strip of bog-fibre sewn with eel-sinew and kept in the tin behind the peat measure, where nothing else in this house is kept dry: wet peat worked into the grain at the head, a tallow thumb at the fold, the press of a frozen wool sleeve across the first leaf, a small-ale ring gone dark where a cup stood from the first asking to the last, a peat-shaving shut in the fold, a strip of bog-fibre in the gutter, frost raised out of the paper on the carry up from the ford, grey Ash along the outer fold which the writer did not put there, one correction in the narrow upright hand of the factor's clerk, a gloss in the sloping hand of a reeve who could not get back over the marsh, and a line at the foot which nobody has claimed

codex.title: The Line Book, Being a Page from an Assessor's Ledger Kept at the Peat Line in the Last Tend of Bone, Y.H. 813, with the Figure Cried and the Figure Entered, the Eels That Go South, the Thin Returns Bought Cheap, the Eleven Months Set Beside the Mark, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A page from a factor's ledger kept at a tally-post on the Peat Line, in the service of the house at Greybank; figures in Ledgerhand copied from the rail-board and the reed tally, the remarks terse and in the hand that touches the slate before it looks at the person standing, one column struck by a College clerk and drawn back underneath, one figure struck and set above in a second hand, a word scraped away with a knife-point, and a line at the foot nobody will claim
codex.provenance: Written at the Peat Line where the mud road comes down to the tally-post, in the last tend of Bone, Y.H. 813, the year after the Thin Year, by the assessor a factor out of Greybank keeps at the rail to count what goes south; copied forward at Greybank onto the back of a peat-docket voided by the Long Cold and kept in the factor's tin among the dockets that are paid and the dockets that are not. It survives folded to the pocket and soft at the hinge, with black peat worked into the gutter and the creases of the thumb, dried eel slime along the fore-edge, a white salt bloom at the head that comes and goes with the weather, a green bead of Cliffs glass in the lower corner, a fish-scale pressed flat in the second fold, a frost-feather gone by noon, a tallow thumb at the foot, a pale round ring where a cold iron tube was set down and taken up, a wet corner where two figures have run and stand as entered all the same, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with a knife-point, two corrections in borrowed hands, and one line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Peat-Wife's Book of Mud End, Being Remedies for the Byre-Cough, the Peat-Knife Cut, the Child Come Up Drowned, the Sweet Line, the Birth-Flower, the Chill That Follows the Warming and the Sleep That Is Called Merciful, Set Down Among the Nine Houses with the Errors Left Standing
codex.kind: A peat-wife's and midwife's book of remedies in the Mud End manner, written in Grathic letters learned off a man come up from Sill to measure the peat banks who could tally but could not spell what he wrote; the cures in a healer's hand on the back of a peat-tally spoiled by a wet thumb, the objections of a physician come down the mud road from Sill pressed hard into the margin, the corrections of a factor's clerk in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a charcoal line from a reeve up the marsh road, a byre-song with the tenth place left as it is sung, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at Mud End, three leagues downriver of Sill, between Bone of Y.H. 813 and Ilmen of Y.H. 814, the Thin Year, the Long Cold and the thaw that followed it, by Marda of Mud End, a peat-wife who has caught the children of the nine houses and set the arms of the turf-cutters for three-and-twenty years; begun on the back of a peat-tally a wet thumb spoiled at the moot byre, folded into oiled sacking and carried in the breast of a wool apron against a square of birth-cloth, and copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 814 onto the back of a discarded rent-roll at Greybank. It survives with peat worked into the grain at the head, a silt tideline off the Ilm that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a peat-fibre stiff in the fold, straw from the dry bed in the moot byre, a ring of barley-water gone sour over one word of the ninth row, grey Ash off a cuff worked into the gutter, a scorch where a spark off the peat fire caught the corner, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl with the sweetness at one mouth-corner, three objections in the small hard hand of the physician, corrections in the upright hand of the factor's clerk, a reeve's charcoal line beside the remedies, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: The Phial Left Sealed, Being a Letter from the Bowl of Sere to the Factor's House at Greybank, Concerning the Emptying of the Bowl, the Three Returns of a Mother, a Northerner Exhibited at the Feast, and a Sixty-Mark Phial That Was Not Opened; with the Household's Ledger of Returns, the Feast Song as It Is Sung, the Answer Written in the Margin, the Factor's Clerk's Correction in Ledgerhand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A private letter on the thin gold-ink paper of a house of the Ten Bowls, folded thrice and carried north with a grain factor; the cursive of a Sere house at a table set for Company, the ledger of returns in the house's careful hand, the feast song in the court's own singing, the sister's answer set small in the margin, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the factor's clerk at Greybank, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim
codex.provenance: Written in the open court of the Bowl of Sere in the last tend of Grain, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Ilyra Gilded of a house of the Ten Bowls, to her sister Maris Gilded, who keeps that house's northern account at Greybank; carried north with the grain factor, delivered in Stone of Y.H. 813, answered in the margin at the factor's house, borrowed there by a clerk who set his correction above the writer's words, and kept since in a tin of account leaves among which it is the only sheet with gold on it. It survives with the gold worn thin at the folds, a ring of red wine where the bowl was set down, a scorch at the second corner taken from the open court fire, a bead of cliff-glass pressed into the lower margin by a northerner who was exhibited at the feast, slate dust worked into the gutter, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, and the line at the foot

codex.title: The Prayer Before the Tube, Being What a Collector Says into the Wool on the Clay Road, with the Manner of It, the Four Sayings Turned End for End, the Answer Made with the Hands, a Clerk's Correction and a Hearth-Maid's Margin
codex.kind: A collector's own order of service, carried in the wool sleeve of the cold-iron tube and said low before the draw; written without a name, in charcoal on the back of a voided district tally, with the rubrics of the road, seven parts and the answer made after each, the four sayings in the order a collector comes to them rather than the order the notice prints, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor's clerk, the thick charcoal of a hearth-maid come up from Low Kiln, and two lines at the foot that will not lie down together
codex.provenance: Written between Greybank and Sill on the Clay Road in the last tend of Ash, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a collector of the lower road who signs with a crossed tube and not with a name, and carried back through the Five in the wool sleeve of the tube, which is why there is iron in every fold; borrowed at Greybank by a clerk of the factor, who set the four sayings right at the head and wrote against the grey fingers, and read over by a hearth-maid from Low Kiln on a market morning at the Cross, who put four lines in the margin with a stick of charcoal. It survives as one leaf folded small enough for a coat pocket: cold-iron filings ground into the head, a grey wool fibre from the tube's sleeve, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, frost-crisp along one edge where it lay against the outer fold of a coat on the Rim Road in Stone, a tallow thumb, a ring of small ale gone dark, silt in the gutter from the assessor's step at Sill, and a grey Ash print along the foot that nobody will own.

codex.title: The Price Board at Greybank, Being the Rates for Goods, Carriage and the Tolls of the Four Roads, Copied from the Beam Beside the Quay
codex.kind: A weigh-clerk's fair copy of the public board, with the dues of the Clay, Salt, Rim and Hearth roads set after it, corrected in two borrowed hands and left standing in a third
codex.provenance: Written and kept at Greybank, eighteen leagues downriver of Sill, by the clerk who tends the weighing beam on the quay; begun in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, after the Long Cold, and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates in Y.H. 813. The board itself hung on the quay wall beside the grain doors and was scraped and rewritten each tend; this leaf was pinned inside the Vhaleni counting house for the factor's use, and survives soft at the nail-hole, with a white salt bloom along the gutter, a tar thumb at the head, a dark streak of eel slime at the foot, a green bead of cliff-glass in the lower corner, a spot of barley grease, a grey Ash print along the margin, two corrections in hands that are not the writer's, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.

codex.title: The Price-Current at the Tide-Tally, Being the Rates of the Quay and the Dues of the Salt Road, the Shore Road and the Passages of the Sallow, Set Down for Captains and Carters
codex.kind: A tally-keeper's fair copy of the figures cried on the Quay, written on the one dry sheet in a house where every other paper is made to rot; the pans price set beside the pass price and both beside the beam price, the Council's finer name written above the tally-man's plain one, corrected in three borrowed hands and left with one line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at the tide-tally house on the Quay at Vhal in Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the year after the Thin Year, when the east wind had held through the Five and the first carts came over the coast pass with the winter's glass; written up again at the three Account-days of Tallow and copied at Greybank onto the back of a voided weigh-slip for the factor's use. It survives as one leaf of good paper deliberately kept dry, sewn with tarred net-twine into a fold of oiled sailcloth and kept in a tin on the shelf above the tally bench, with a white salt bloom worked into the head, a tar thumb at the fold, a press of wet rope across the lower leaf, a green bead of Cliff glass in the corner, a brine-gull's peck through one word of the song, a wet ring where a cup was set down and taken up before it was seen, a grey Ash print along the gutter which the writer did not make and has not swept, three corrections in hands that are not his, a child's sums done wrong on the back, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Quart Set Down at the Ninth Pot, Being a Winter Wager on the Nine Pots Road, the Road-Song as It Is Sung, and the Figure a Clerk Set Against the Frost
codex.kind: An alehouse keeper's telling of a night in the deep cold, set down for the settling of an argument about a quart and not for the improvement of the reader; the five quarts in a charcoal column, the sayings in the words they were spoken, the road-song as it is sung, the figure of a clerk entered over them, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year after the Long Cold, at the alehouse called the Ninth Pot in Nine Pots, eight leagues west of Sill, by Cilla who keeps the bench and the fire behind it; set down because a man came the next morning and asked whether a quart had been drunk at the end of the bench and she could not tell him. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a spoiled kiln tally, sewn with eel-sinew into a fold of oiled paper and kept in the jar beside the bench. It survives with a tallow thumb at the head, a small-ale ring, a press of wet wool across the first leaf, frost-crisp at the fore-edge, grey Ash in the gutter, a scorch where the leaf was held too near the fire, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the Sill table, one saying in charcoal in a wheel-man's hand, and one line at the foot in a hand that is nobody's.

codex.title: The Quay Tally at Vhal, Being the Rates of the Sallow Market at the Flood and at the Ebb, with the Dues of the Salt Road, the Coast Pass and the Waters of the Quay, Copied from the Board Beside the Tide-Tally House
codex.kind: A tally-man's fair copy of the shore-board, written on salt-paper he keeps dry against the practice of the country; the figures sloped as tallies are sloped, the verbs written back under the Council's correction, one rate gone void by rain, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at the tide-tally house on the Quay at Vhal by one of the men who read the draws under Kett of the Quay; begun in Ember of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, after the Long Cold, copied forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and written up again at the turn of Grain. It survives in a tarred tin lined with dry rushes, sewn with tarred net-twine, the leaves kept dry though the Council's own paper is made to rot; with a white salt bloom at the head, a tar thumb at the fold, a fibre of wet rope pressed into the second leaf, a brine-gull's peck through one figure, a fish-hook nick at the head, a wet corner where two rates have gone and are void by law, a green bead of Cliffs glass in the lower corner, a grey Ash print along the margin that nobody will own, two corrections in hands that are not the writer's, and one line at the foot nobody will claim.

codex.title: The Quench Song, Being the Drinking-Song of the Glass Furnaces at Vhal, Sung at the Trough After the Last Pot Is Drawn, with the Jar Going Round the Hands, the Revolt Year Kept Back, a Furnace-Master's Ruling in White Slip, a Clerk's Correction Going Soft on Salt-Paper, a Glazer's Charcoal Underneath, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A drinking-song of the third furnace, in the rough tide-speech of Vhal set down in Grathic letters; the verses said to the trough and to the jar as it goes round, one verse to a hand at the quench, the refrain let fall into the water and not given to the company; the kept verse held back until the yard is empty; the furnace-master's ruling in white slip on the brick margin, the tide-clerk's leaning hand going soft on salt-paper above, a glazer's charcoal underneath, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim
codex.provenance: Sung at the quench-trough of the third furnace at Vhal in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year after the Long Cold, and set down that night by the woman who carts sand and lead to the third furnace and has done it eleven winters; written in charcoal on the back of a sand-tally spoiled by a wet thumb, folded in a scrap of oiled sailcloth with a twist of wet rope, and kept in a clay pot stoppered with wool in the sand-shed, where the damp comes up off the shore. A clerk of the tide-tally house borrowed the leaf on a morning when the winter glass was counted and asked what the women sang at the quench, and wrote the answer down while it was still being said, with the doing taken out and a term set where a place should stand; his hand is on salt-paper and the damp has eaten most of it, so that of four corrections two are figures, one is the ghost of a verb, and one has gone clean away. It survives with a white salt bloom at the head, a pale streak of lead worked into the grain, a tar thumb at the fold, a strand of wet rope pressed into the second leaf, a blue-green chip of Cliffs glass in the lower corner, a scorch where the leaf lay too near the furnace mouth, a grain of sand that has cut a line through one word of the fourth verse, a ring of sour wine gone dark at the foot, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own, the furnace-master's ruling in white slip, the clerk's soft hand above, the glazer's charcoal underneath, and the line at the foot

codex.title: The Question Said to the Stone, Being the Tale of a Riddle Night at the Cold Lamp in Ash, with Three Answers Given to the Stone, a Fourth Kept, and the Survey-Clerk's Entry Set Over All of It
codex.kind: A lamp-woman's telling of a winter night, set down from the mouth of an old shift-man for the settling of an argument that was never entered; the questions in the hard Rim speech with the endings struck off, the answers said to the stone and not to the room, the wagers in warm-stone shavings laid on the lamp-sill, the tally cut in the edge of a weigh-slip, a survey-clerk's figures entered above in Ledgerhand, a clay-man's gloss in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, at the weigh-lamp beside the shaft mouth in Keld Keep, by the woman who tends the lamp and sells a stone's shaving by the half-mark to men going down; told to her by an old shift-man who had been forty years at the weigh and would not state his number. Carried down the Rim Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with a survey party's spoiled slips and copied at Greybank onto the back of a weigh-slip gone soft at the fold, where a survey-clerk of the Court borrowed it and set his hand above hers. It survives folded in a twist of oiled lamp-wick in the tin under the sill: coal smut ground into the head, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead shut in the fold, iron filings along the gutter, a frost-feather pressed flat that was gone by noon, a tallow thumb, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first question to the fourth, one correction in the narrow upright hand of the Court, a gloss in the sloping hand of a clay-man who could not get back over the pass, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody's

codex.title: The Year the Row Was Raised, Being an Extract from the Moot Book of Sill, in Which the Court Came to Stay, a House Was Built East of the Cross, and the Figure Came to Be Read Twice; with the Old Counts Set Beside the New, the Masons' Raising-Song, Three Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A keeper of the moot book's extract from the town's year-chest at Sill; the year-entries in a broad round hand gone soft with damp, the treaty written out before them in an older and harder hand, the Row set down as a list of rooms with what went into each, the two figures entered in a column no clerk of the College has ever signed, the raising-song taken down from a mason who would not give his day's wage, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a College clerk, one in the soft-cuffed hand of a factor's man come up from Greybank, one charcoal line left by a hearth-maid from Low Kiln, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at Sill in the moot room off the Cross in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the keeper of the moot book, who has no name on any roll and is entered in the factor's list at Greybank only as *the chest*; copied from the town's year-book begun in Y.H. 418 and kept since in the moot-chest beneath the moot-post, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. The leaf for Y.H. 776 was copied first in Smoke of that year, on the back of a spoiled slate-warrant, and has been copied forward four times since. It survives folded in a strip of oiled harness leather: lime dust worked into the head, a slate shaving shut in the second fold, silt from the sill dried pale in the gutter, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl come up from High Kiln with the sweetness still at her mouth, a mason's iron nail gone rusty in the sewing, a short square of bare paper where a word was scraped away and no other put in, a tallow thumb at the head, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first entry to the last, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the keeper did not make and has not swept, and the line at the foot which has never been claimed

codex.title: The Rat at the Lip, Being a Hunter's Field Notes on the Lead-Rat of High Kiln and the Lower Ferr; with the Catching-Song as It Is Said, a Tally of Tails and Cups, a Physician's Year, a Glaze-Mixer's Correction in Slip-White, and a Ruling in Ledgerhand
codex.kind: A hunter's field book on one beast, set down as the record of catches and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on the backs of glaze-tallies spoiled by a spill of slip, the catching-song as it is said over the bench, a physician's year copied out of a page come down the Ferr, a glaze-mixer's correction in slip-white, and a ruling in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk of the factor at Greybank
codex.provenance: Written in Grain and Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Skell of High Kiln, a rat-catcher who took the beasts for their tails and kept the cup-shelves of the Glaze Room, and who writes at the end of a round with a tallow end in a dish and the sweet still at the back of his throat; set down first on the backs of glaze-tallies gone soft with slip and then on three folds of birch bark sewn with eel-sinew, carried in a coat pocket against a flint and a twist of tallow. Copied forward at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold. It survives with the sweet green of lead glaze ground into the head off a gnawed rim carried three days in the pocket, a brown slip thumb at the fold, a grey tail-grease smear along the fore-edge where the leaf was wiped on a sleeve after a catch, a greenish ring where a tasting-cup stood from the first round to the last, a scorch where a spark off the glaze kiln took the corner of the third leaf, the charcoal rubbed thin where the wrap was carried against the thigh, a physician's year copied in the writer's own hand, one line in slip-white from the glaze-mixer, one ruling in Ledgerhand standing above the words it corrects, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own

codex.title: The Reading of the Slate, Being Certain Articles of the Ordinance of the Keeping for the Drawing, Banking and Returning of Measures
codex.kind: An extract from the Court's ordinances, copied out for the use of the open-air table at the Cross in Sill, with the marginal hand of the clerk who keeps that table
codex.provenance: Copied in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the unnamed clerk of the Court's table at the Cross in Sill, and carried into Y.H. 813 at the Opening of the Slates; a quire of four leaves sewn with wire into a board cover, kept in the drawer of the table and taken out at market mornings. The cover is warped from a winter against the outside wall of Slate Row. The lower corner of the second leaf carries a tallow thumb, the inner margin a grey streak, the top edge a candle-singe, and there are three corrections in the clerk's own hand and one in a hand he did not own.

codex.title: The Sermon at the Reeve's Stone, Being What Was Said at the Foot of the Standing Post Over the Peat-Blocks on the Morning a Reeve Was Chosen in Reed of Y.H. 813, with the Standing-Song Left as It Is Sung, the Blocks in a Tally, a Factor's Clerk's Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A sermon of the Fenmarch preached at the small shrine of the reeve's stone at the foot of the Standing Post, over the peat-blocks laid in the niche at the choosing of a reeve; the sayings in the bitten speech of the marsh set down in Grathic, the standing-song with the gap left the length of the sound a boot makes coming up, the blocks in a tally, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor's clerk come out from Greybank, and one line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Preached by an old woman of the Post who had laid a peat-block in the niche at one and twenty standings, on the morning of Reed 20, Y.H. 813, when the marsh stood for a new reeve and the water was up in the prints of every boot; written that evening by the woman who keeps the boardwalk and the bog-tally at the Standing Post, in charcoal and with the point of a worn count-stick, on the back of a bog-tally spoiled by a wet figure, folded into oiled sacking and tied with a strip of bog-cow hide. It survives with peat worked into the grain at the head in a brown thumb, a press of wet sedge across the first leaf, a dark tideline along the gutter where marsh-water stood on it through a night, a sedge-awn shut in the fold, a small horn-shaving from the count-stick caught in the second crease, a grey Ash print nobody will own, a tallow thumb, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first voice to the last, the wing-case of a beetle pressed flat in the lower corner, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor's clerk come out from Greybank to count the winter thin returns, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied once at Greybank in Ember of Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the gap left the length it is sung.

codex.title: Of Consent, the Clip at the Wrist, and the Refusal That Is Not Entered, Being Title the Fourth of the Ordinances of the Keeping: with the Table of Consents, the Form of Consent Left Blank, the Consent-Song Said Under the Clip, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: An extract from the Court's ordinances, written out for the slate at the watch beside the Cross in Sill, with the marginal hand of the clerk who enters consents before the collector's tube is set; the articles in Ledgerhand and the verbs restored beneath them, the consents and the hours in a table, the form of consent left blank, the consent-song said low under the clip, one word scored away with the edge of a cold-iron clip, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed
codex.provenance: Copied at Sill in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, from Title the Fourth of the Ordinances of the Keeping as set down in the first years after the Rising of Y.H. 668 and confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of Y.H. 418, added to in Y.H. 782; survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, kept under the consent-slate at the watch: a grey Ash thumb at the head, a scorch where the watch-fire was too near, a dark score gone green at the edge where the clip was laid, pale slip from a swaddling cloth along the gutter, a brown crust-mark at the second fold, a thread of grey wool through the tie-hole, a tide-line along the foot from the market boards after rain, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own

codex.title: The Return Book at Greybank, Being the Pourings of the Last Tend of Ash in the Thin Year, with the Figure Entered, the Figure Paid, and the Note the Cradle Gave
codex.kind: A page from the bank assessor's own return-ledger, kept under the return-slate in the lower room; figures in Ledgerhand copied from the collector's slate and the factor's tally, terse remarks in the hand that set the warm into the cradle, a column of likenesses struck out and drawn back, one correction in the College's narrow upright hand and one in the factor's, and a line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at Greybank, eighteen leagues downriver of Sill, in the last tend of Ash, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, carried through Stone and the Five and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813; kept in a board cover beneath the return-slate and taken down when a whole return is disputed. It survives with an iron-gall thumb at the head, a smear of pale slip from a swaddling cloth, a tallow print where the lamp was held low, a cold-iron shaving worked into the gutter, a thread of grey wool from a cradle blanket, a damp tide-line out of the lower room, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, two corrections in borrowed hands, and one line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Riddle Bench at the Cross, Being Five Cold-Night Questions, the One That Was Not Answered, and the Tally Left in Charcoal on the Bench Top
codex.kind: A tapster's record of a winter contest, set down for the settling of arguments and not for the improvement of the reader; the rules in the hand the house keeps, the riddles in the words they were spoken, a charcoal tally of one night, the figures of a Court clerk entered over them, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year after the Long Cold, at the alehouse called the Banked Coal at the Cross in Sill, by the woman who keeps the bench and the fire behind it; copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a spoiled tally leaf from the Court's table, sewn with eel-sinew into a fold of oiled paper and kept in the jar by the hearth. It survives soft at the fold and stained at the head, with a tallow thumb, a ring where a quart stood all night, a press of wet wool across the first leaf, a spot of barley grease, a grey Ash print along the gutter, the charcoal rubbed thin where a sleeve has gone over it, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Court clerk, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody's.

codex.title: The Rim Road Book, Being the Account of Hedd, an Under-Clerk of the Factor's House at Greybank, Who Went Up to Keld Keep with Fine Ware and a Sealed Letter and Came Back with a Warm-Stone Gone Cold, a Shaving of Lead in the Fold, and a Figure He Was Told Was Current; with the Charges of the Road, the Courtesy of the Number Before the Name, the Table of What Was Sent and What Came Back, the Road-Song Never Sung Downward, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: An under-clerk's road account, set down first in the upright hand he keeps for the factor and then in charcoal on the backs of spoiled requisitions when the upright hand would not hold what he had seen; the figures in the factor's hand, the mountain sayings kept in the hearing with the endings struck off, the verbs put back underneath every borrowed correction, one notch cut in the edge where a Keldish word would not go into the south's letters, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward
codex.provenance: Written at Keld Keep and at the survey post in the Cold Pass in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by Hedd, an under-clerk of the factor's house at Greybank, who went up the Rim Road in Frost with a crate of High Kiln fine ware, a letter the factor sealed, and nine marks of the Court's money, and came down in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with the letter delivered, the money mostly spent, a warm-stone that held nine days and not the tenth, and a leaf of the survey turned face down which he has not read; set down on the backs of requisitions for warm-stone voided by the Long Cold, copied at Greybank onto the reverse of a spoil ledger and sewn with wire into a scrap of oiled survey-cloth. It survives with coal smut ground into the head off the sleeve used to hold the sheet down on the weigh, a shaving of warm-stone shut in the second fold which kept a little heat one night on a stone floor and is cold now, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead rolled into the gutter, frost raised out of the grain on the climb over the pass and gone by noon, a hard drop of tallow at the fold, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, one correction in the red checking-hand of the mine-reeve's clerk, one in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Court survey-clerk at Greybank, a notch cut clean through a word in the edge, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own

codex.title: The River Collector's Book, Being the Measures Drawn Aboard the Boat on the Lower Ilm Between Sill and Greybank in the Last Tend of Reed and the First of Tallow, Y.H. 813, with the Embers, the Note, the Return Due, and What the Water Took
codex.kind: A page from the river collector's own ledger, kept in an oiled fold under the stern seat; figures in Ledgerhand copied from the slate, the remarks terse and in the hand that held the cold iron tube, the note-column struck by the College and drawn back underneath, a numbering in a borrowed hand where the writer left a place, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written aboard the collector's boat on the lower Ilm from the last market of Reed through the first tend of Tallow, Y.H. 813, carried down to Greybank and back, and kept in an oiled-paper fold beneath the stern seat beside the tube in its wool sleeve. It survives soft at the fold, with river silt worked into the gutter, a white salt bloom at the head where the Sallow wind came up the water, dried eel slime along the fore-edge, a pale round ring pressed into the paper where the cold tube was set down, a tallow thumb at the foot, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a grey Ash print along the margin nobody will own, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, two corrections in borrowed hands, and one line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: Of the Roll of the Dead, the Remembering, and the Account Not Closed, Being Title the Ninth of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied into the Bank at the Hearthseat with the Roll-Clerk's Margin, the Tallow Gone White, a Fish-Scale Pressed Flat, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: An extract from the Court's ordinances, written out for the roll-clerk's counter at the bank in the Hearthseat, with the marginal hand of the clerk who carries names forward and reads them on the Remembering; the articles in Ledgerhand and the verbs restored beneath them, the roll set in a table, the form of a carry-forward left blank, the roll-song as it is said at the reading, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed
codex.provenance: Copied at the bank in the Hearthseat in the last tend of Ash of the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, from Title the Ninth of the Ordinances of the Keeping as set down in the first years after the Rising of Y.H. 668 and sent down to the factor at Greybank in Y.H. 418, added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year; survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, kept under the roll-sheet in the bank: a grey Ash thumb at the head, tallow gone white and hard in the gutter, a fish-scale pressed flat at the second fold, iron filings in the crease where a tube-wrap lay, a crumb of barley bread at the foot, a damp line along the lower margin where a pail stood, a bone-stylus score where a word was taken out, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own.

codex.title: Of the Shutting of the Pass and the Seven Years, Being an Extract from the Roll of the Cold Pass Kept at Keld Keep, with the Warden's Claim Entered in the Number-First Hand, the Reeves' Answer Out of Grath, the Four Terms Cut on the Slate in Slate Row, the Road-Song Carried Down the Rim Road, the Corrections of a Court Clerk in Ledgerhand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A survey-roll keeper's extract from the Warden's roll at the pass, copied into Grathic letters with the Keldish endings struck off; the seven years in the number-first hand, the claim set down as an entry with a nought beneath it, the reeves' answer in a sloping margin hand, the four terms cut from the slate in Sill's Slate Row, a carter's song taken down at the post, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor's clerk, one nought cut in chalk, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at the survey post in the Cold Pass, ten leagues beyond Keld Keep, in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the keeper of the roll, who states his measure before this and has set no name to it: nine and twenty when he was put to the roll, and not the number he went down with. Copied from the Warden's roll of Y.H. 741 to 747, carried down the Rim Road in Stone of the same year with a lead cart, copied at Greybank in the Five, and entered at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives as six leaves of rough survey paper sewn with wire into a board cover gone soft at the seam: coal smut ground into the head, an iron-red thumb at the second corner, a nought cut in chalk at the foot of the figures column, a frost-feather pressed flat between the fourth and fifth leaves and gone by noon, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead shut in the fold, a hard drop of tallow, and a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the keeper did not make and has not swept. A factor's clerk borrowed the leaf at Greybank on a market morning and set his upright hand above two of the entries; the carter's song was taken down from a man who would not give his number either.

codex.title: The Root-Wife's Book of Remedies, Being Remedies for the Sleep That Does Not Wake, the Mould on the Wound, the Sweet Line, the Fever That Cooks, the Second Chill, the Birth-Flower, the Kiln's Breath, a Cut from a Pot-Shard and the Cold That Stays, Set Down on the Bank Below Sill with the Errors Left Standing
codex.kind: A root-wife's and hedge-leech's book of remedies in the Grathic bank-speech, written on the back of a herb-price tally spoiled by rain; the cures in a root-digger's blunt hand, the objections of a physician come down from Greybank pressed into the margin, the corrections of a College clerk in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a collector's ruling in cuff-grey at the foot of the remedies, a drying-song with the place where the eleventh should stand left as it is sung, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written on the bank of the Ilm between the Fishstairs and Mud End, two leagues below Sill, between Bone of Y.H. 812 and Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the Long Cold and the Thin Year, by Besse of the Banks, a root-wife who dug the silt banks and the ditch along the marsh road and sold steeped draughts and dried roots at the Cross on Account-days for one-and-twenty years; begun on the back of a herb-price tally that a rain took the figures out of, folded into oiled reed and carried in a string bag against a twist of tallow and a lump of bank-clay, and copied at Greybank in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, onto the back of a voided grain-warrant. It survives with root-fibre worked into the grain at the head, a green mould bloom that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a brown tideline of root-tea down the gutter, a seedpod shut in the fold, a thumb of tallow, a grey Ash print nobody will own, a ring of barley-water, a scorch where the drying-fire caught the corner, bank-clay pressed into the outer fold, objections in the cold margin hand of the physician, corrections in the upright hand of the College clerk, the collector's grey ruling, and the one line at the foot.

codex.title: The Sack-Book of Fenna Tallow, Being the Prices She Asked and Gave on the Circuit from Sill to the Salt Pans and Back, with the Dues of Every Road Written on the Same Leaf as the Goods, a Page the Rain Took, Three Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Verse Carried in the Mouth
codex.kind: A pedlar's pocket ledger, kept in a waxed oilcloth sack under the small goods; figures set down on such paper as came to hand, each road's due written against the goods that paid it, with an entire salt-paper leaf lost to weather and its debt entered from the other end; corrected in three borrowed hands and never copied fair
codex.provenance: Kept by Fenna Tallow, a pedlar of Sill who walks the Clay, river, marsh and Salt roads with tallow, needles, coarse pots and small news; begun in Grain of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, written up behind carts, at the Cross, at the Greybank beam and at the tide-tally house, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813; the last figures set down at the Cross on Ash 10 of that year. It survives in the oilcloth sack in four kinds of paper --- the back of a Court notice gone soft at the fold, a weigh-slip the beam clerk had done with, a strip of birch bark out of the Fen, and a leaf of salt-paper kept dry against the practice of the country --- with a tallow thumb at the head, barley grease in the first gutter, a pig bristle pressed into the Sill leaf, eel slime along the river page, a fish-hook nick, marsh mud on the Nine Pots corner, a drop of Sere wine gone brown, a grey Ash print nobody will own, a pressed reed, a scorch where the book lay too near a brazier, one leaf dissolved by rain so that two figures are gone, and corrections in the hands of a Slate Row clerk, a factor's clerk and a Council clerk, none of them mine

codex.title: The Litany of the Sallow Draw, Being the Order of the Return as the Dippers of Vhal Say It at the Salt Pans Before the Nets Go Out
codex.kind: A litany of the Return said at the pans in the half-light, the pan-master reading and the dippers answering, with the draw read between the stations and the answer made twice: once to the water and once into the knot-count; written on salt-paper, which will not outlast the wet, and copied forward every spring; with the rubrics of the pans, seven stations and their answer, the draw-song, the correction of a Council tally-clerk which the salt has eaten clean through, a salt-wife's knot, and a line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in charcoal rubbed with salt on salt-paper at the Salt Pans outside Vhal in the last tend of Stone, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the pan-master's daughter who counts the draw, and copied forward each spring because the paper goes soft in the damp; the surviving leaf is the third copy, made at the pans in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, the fourth station supplied from memory and not agreeing with the second copy held at the tide-tally house, which has itself gone nearly to pulp. It survives with salt bloom in the gutter that has eaten the clerk's ink and left the charcoal standing, tar worked into the head from the net-coil, a splash that took out the fifth answer, a knot of tarred twine tied through the lower corner, the white print of a bare foot at the foot, a crust of coarse salt in the fold that crunches when the leaf is opened, and a line nobody will own.

codex.title: The Salt Country, Being the Road-Account of Dessa Reed, a Potter's Daughter out of Low Kiln in Sill, Who Took a Cart of Flat Tile and Fish-Dishes up the Salt Road to Vhal and Came Back with Sallow Salt, a Coil of Tarred Rope and a Contract the Rain Had Eaten; with the Prices of the Quay, the Four Questions and the One Answer, the Net-Song Said at First Light, Three Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A pot-woman's road-book, set down first in charcoal on strips of birch bark on the road and copied at Greybank onto the back of a spoiled salt-docket; the road and the prices in the writer's short clay-hand, the coast sayings kept in the hearing and not made into proverbs, the verbs left in under every borrowed correction, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward
codex.provenance: Written in Ember and Grain of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year after the Long Cold, at Vhal and on the Salt Road, by Dessa Reed, a thrower's daughter of the Clay Yard in Low Kiln, Sill, who took tile and fish-dishes up the Salt Road and came down in Grain with a sack of salt, a coil of rope, a green bead of cliff-glass given for a bit and a promise, and a tide contract gone soft with rain; copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a salt-docket voided by the damp and carried down the Clay Road to Sill. It survives folded into oiled sailcloth under the wheel-shed bench, stiff with salt and soft by turns: a white bloom at the head that has eaten the last letters off two words, a thumb of tar at the fold off the coil she carried home, a brine-gull feather pressed into the second leaf, a green bead of cliff-glass flattened into the lower corner, tarred rope fibre worked into the third crease, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, a ring of small ale near the song, a tide-name written in salt in the margin which the sun took by noon and left a white place, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with a knife-point, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, three corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own

codex.title: The Salt Litany of the Return, Being the Dippers' Prayer at the Pans Outside Vhal, with the Rubrics of the Dawn, the Five Drawings of the Net, a Council Clerk's Correction Gone Soft in the Rain, a Boat-Woman's Margin, and the Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A dipper's order of service for the Return said at the salt pans at dawn, before the net goes in and after it comes up; written on the back of a Council tide-tally spoiled by rain, in Grathic letters learned off a factor's man, the tide-words that will not go into Grathic tied as knots in the margin, with the five drawings and their answer, a Council clerk's correction eaten away by the damp, a boat-woman's charcoal in the margin, a green bead of cliff-glass, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at the Salt Pans outside Vhal in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a dipper of the second net who signs with a wet knot and not with a name; carried up the Salt Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold. It survives in a dry tin among a boat's things, soft at the fold and sweet at the edges, with a white bloom of salt worked into the head, a tar thumb, a brine ring, a fish-hook nick, a green bead of cliff-glass pressed into the lower corner, one word taken clean off the third leaf by rain, the Council hand gone down to a figure with no verb, a boat-woman's margin in charcoal, knots tied through three holes, and the line at the foot which has never been claimed

codex.title: The Sermon at the Blessing Stone, Being the Old Words Said Over the Traps on Ilmen 15 of Y.H. 813, with the Manner of the Standing, the Low Half-Song as It Is Sung, the Count of What Was Set Down and What Was Entered, a Greybank Clerk's Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A sermon of the Fish Blessing preached at the shrine of the blessing stone at the Weir, one league upriver of Sill; the sayings in the short wet speech of the weir set down in Grathic letters, the half-song with the held line left the length it is sung, the count of the stone in a table, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor's clerk come up from Greybank, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Preached by an old hearth-maid of Sill who has stood on the flat stone at the blessing for nine and twenty springs, on Ilmen 15, Y.H. 813, the forty-fourth day, while another hearth-maid sprinkled salt along the weir head with a flat hand and the traps stood with their mouths upriver; written that evening by the younger of the two in charcoal on the back of a birch-bark tally gone soft at one edge, in the Eel House out of the rain, and folded into a length of grey wool tied with an eel-sinew. It survives with salt dried white worked into the grain at the head off the flat hand, a silt tideline along the foot from the leaf carried downriver in an apron, a wet ring where a cup stood from the first voice to the last, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, a small eel scale pressed into the fold, a thumb of silt on the line about the extra knot which the writer did not make and has not wiped, the clerk's correction standing above the charcoal, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied once at Greybank in Ash of Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the held line left the length it is sung.

codex.title: The Salt That Follows, Being a Coast-Soldier's Field Notes on the Salt-Thing of the Sallow Tides and the Pans Outside Vhal
codex.kind: A soldier's field book on one shape, set down as the record of shore-watches kept over boats lying off the pans and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in the Vhaleni tide-words written in Grathic letters, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled tide-tallies, a verse as it is said going out on the first watch, a ruling in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk of the Council room, a second line of his gone soft with the damp, a dipper's words in pale ink on salt-paper, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by one of the Council's men set over the shore-watch and the cure-shed at the salt pans outside Vhal, who kept the rain-barrels and counted what the boats lost between dusk and morning; written at the end of watches in the shed with a tallow end in a pot and the Sallow coming up over the stones; set down first on the backs of tide-tallies spoiled by sea-water and then on three folds of salt-paper stiffened with tar, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a tarred wrap in a coat pocket. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813. It survives with a white bloom of salt come up out of the paper at the head, tar at the fold, a Sallow tideline along the gutter that has taken two words off the third watch, a wet ring where a barrel-stave stood on the leaf, a grey smear at the fore-edge where a sailor with cold fingers touched it, a fish-hook nick, a pinch of cure-salt shut in the second fold, a scorch where the watch-lamp caught the lower corner of the last leaf, the charcoal rubbed thin where the wrap was carried against the thigh, one ruling in Ledgerhand standing above the words it corrects, one line of the same hand eaten down to a figure with no verb, a dipper's line in pale ink on salt-paper soft at one corner, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: The Salt Walk, Being the Standing Rules of the Dippers of Vhalen for the Taking, Walking, Trying and Naming of Apprentices at the Pans Outside Vhal, with the Table of Walkings, the Net-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in a Council Clerk's Hand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A dipper's leaf of rules from the west pan, written in the leaning low hand with the ends of words let fall; the rules set in short sayings, the walkings and the faults in tables, the net-song pasted inside the cover, a tide-name written in salt in the margin and gone before noon, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Council clerk, one line struck in charcoal by a pan-master who would not sign it, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Gathered at the Salt Pans outside Vhal in Frost of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813 by Halla Salt, a dipper of the west pan who has taken the young out barefoot at the Salt Walk for one and thirty years and keeps the pan's leading rope and its tide-name in her mouth; written on salt-paper leaves she keeps dry in a tin that once held salt and has never been washed, sewn with tarred net-twine and carried up the Salt Road with a glass consignment, where a clerk of the Council corrected it at Greybank. It survives with a white salt bloom at the head that has taken the last letters off a word and left the rest readable, a thumb of tar at the fold off the leading rope, the press of a wet net across the song, a peck-hole where a brine-gull took the leaf for a crust, a fish-hook nick, a ring of small ale at the foot left by a ship's master who would not drink with dippers, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that is not hers and that she has not swept, a tide-name written in salt in the margin which the sun took by noon and left a white place, two corrections in the Council's upright hand, one charcoal line struck and written again beneath, and a line at the foot nobody will own

codex.title: The Salt Wife's Book, Being Remedies for the Glass-Sickness, the Chill, the Bite and the Third Night, Set Down at the Quay in Vhal
codex.kind: A boat-midwife's and healer's book of remedies in the Vhaleni tide-words, written in Grathic letters so a girl of the Quay could read it; the cures in a salt-wife's hand, a lowland physician's objections in the margin, and the corrections of a Council clerk set down on salt-paper that has since gone soft, with one song for the third night and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at the Quay in Vhal in Ember and Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Eda of the Quay, a midwife who went aboard with the eel-boats and kept the households of the glass-workers; begun on the back of a Council tide-table spoiled by rain and sewn with eel-sinew into an oiled sailcloth wrapper, carried up the Salt Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a discarded weigh-slip. It survives in a dry tin among a boat's things, soft at the fold and sweet at the edges, with a green bead of cliff-glass pressed into the head, a thumb of tar, a white bloom of salt along the gutter, a ring of brine, a fish-hook nick, one correction the damp has eaten down to a figure with no verb, and a line struck through and written again underneath in the writer's own hand.

codex.title: The Second Chill, Being a Letter from Wenna, an Old Hearth-Maid at Cold Acre, to Milla, Newly Set to the Birth-Slates in Low Kiln, on the Warming of Stones, the Three Days, the Collector's Tube, and the Name Written Before the Face Is Looked At; with the Answer in the Margin, a Clerk's Entry in Ledgerhand, and a Washing Verse in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A private letter in a hearth-maid's small careful hand, written on the back of a birth-slate rubbing taken before the ink had set; folded thrice and tied with a twist of grey wool, carried down from the ridge in a potter's wife's apron, answered along the margin in a younger hand, corrected on the back at the Court's table in Slate Row, and kept since in the birth-flower shrine's slate-box among the slates that have been answered
codex.provenance: Written at Cold Acre, two leagues north of Sill on the ridge where the one well does not freeze, in the last tend of Tallow, Y.H. 813, by Wenna, who has kept the birth-slates of that ridge for thirty-one years, to Milla, a maid newly set to the slates in Low Kiln after the kilns were brought up. Carried down the ridge road in a potter's wife's apron, answered in the margin, and borrowed at the Court's table in Slate Row, where a clerk set a correction on the back in the neat upright Ledgerhand. It survives folded in the shrine's slate-box: beeswax from the shrine candle worked into the grain at the head, a thumb of slip from the hand that held the rubbing, one drop of birth-water gone brown in the fold, grey Ash along the gutter where a cuff was laid, a curl of grey wool through the tie-hole which the writer will not untie, a tallow thumb at the outer fold, a tideline where well-water came up over the lower leaf, the clerk's correction standing above the words, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Second File, Being the Names Removed from the Rolls at the College of Assessors in the Hearthseat, with the Figures Struck, the Figures Set Above, and the Reasons Not Entered
codex.kind: A leaf copied forward from the College's second file at the Opening of the Slates; figures in Ledgerhand, terse remarks in the hand of the junior set to the tin, the names withheld into another hand, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the College, a column struck and drawn back, and a line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: Copied at the Hearthseat in Slate Row, in the College of Assessors, on Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, the Opening of the Slates, from the tin that lies beside the sealed-file room; carried in the inner pocket of a junior's coat until the copying was checked. It survives with slate dust worked into the gutter, an iron-gall thumb at the head, a damp tide-line along the foot out of the sealed-file room, a grey Ash print nobody will claim, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a small square of bare paper where a name was scraped away with a knife, one column struck and drawn back underneath, two corrections in the narrow upright hand, and one line at the foot that has never been owned

codex.title: The Second Plank at the Weir, Being the Market Rates of the Ilm and the Tolls of the Roads That Come Down to It, Set Down by the Woman Who Keeps the Landing
codex.kind: A landing-keeper's board copied into a quire, the price of the river set before the price of the road, the fifth road written first and the other four come down to it; corrections in borrowed hands, a grandchild's crooked sums in the corner, and a line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at the Weir, one league upriver of Sill, by Hanne, keeper of the landing and the second plank, in Stone of Y.H. 813, the winter after the Thin Year, when the Ilm lay under ice and the eels were under the ice; set down first in charcoal on the back of a spoiled eel-docket and written up again at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 814. It survives under the second board of the landing, folded in oiled reed and lashed with eel-sinew: eel slime dried to a varnish at the head, river silt worked into the gutter, a white salt bloom off the Sallow wind along the fore-edge, a green bead of lead glaze brought down on the High Kiln wind pressed into the lower corner, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, a reed pressed flat across the verse, a tallow thumb where the lamp was held, a wet ring where a cup was set down and taken up before it was seen, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which is not hers and which she has not swept, a child's crooked sums in the bottom corner, corrections in hands that are not hers, and one line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Sermon at the Broken Pot, Being What Was Said at the Bone Orchard on the Remembering of Y.H. 812
codex.kind: A pot-break sermon preached at the shrine of broken pots outside Sill's north gate, over the year's pots and the one pot nobody brought; the manner of the breaking in the niche-keeper's hand, the sayings in Grathic, the breaking-song in verse, the row of pots in a tally, a factor's clerk's correction in Ledgerhand set above the keeper's verbs, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Preached by an old woman of Sill who had broken pots at the Bone Orchard for one and thirty years, on the Remembering of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, over the pots set in the niche a league north of the Cross; written that evening by the woman who keeps the niche, in charcoal and with the point of a broken nail on the inner face of a grave-tile that came away whole when it should have broken, and kept under the flat stone among the sherds. It survives with grey Ash ground into the slip along the gutter, a salt bloom in a hairline at the head, a tallow thumb where the tile was held down on a man's knee, a green bead of lead glaze caught in a chip of the rim, a morsel of dry clay in the fold, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor's clerk come out from Greybank that takes the verbs out and numbers the nameless pot as nil, and one line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand nobody will own. Copied forward in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the empty place left the length it is.

codex.title: The Sermon at the Counting Stone, Being What Iyn of the Listening Stone Said to a Boy at His First Sitting in Bone of Y.H. 812, with the Sayings Said Twice, the Sitting-Song Left with a Season in It, the Sittings in a Register, a Survey-Clerk's Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A sermon of the Vorr preached at the shrine of the counting stones five leagues above Keld Keep in the high Rim; the sayings in the slow long-vowelled Rim speech set down in Grathic letters, the sitting-song with every line said twice and the season left the length it is kept, the sittings in a high-path register, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Court survey-clerk come up from Greybank, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Preached on Bone 12, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, at the third stone from the high path, by Iyn of the Listening Stone at the setting-out of a boy's first Long Sitting; written that evening by the woman who keeps the sitting-register at Keld Keep, in charcoal on the back of a rim-seam rubbing spoiled by a wet slate, folded with a pinch of blighted-seam dust in the crease and sewn with wire into oiled survey-cloth, and kept in the register-box beside the high-path door. It survives with pale lichen worked into the head off the north stone, the print of a doubled last joint pressed in tallow at the second corner, rime from the high path ground into the fold, a warm-stone shaving that held its heat one night on the stone floor and is cold now, a thread of copper wire off the spoiled rubbing, a wet ring where a dish of meltwater stood from the first saying to the last, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the dust shut in the crease, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Court survey-clerk come up from Greybank to count the winter lead, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied once at Greybank in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the season left the length it is kept.

codex.title: The Sermon at the Glaze Cliffs, Being What an Old Dipper Said Over the Beads on a Morning in Ash of Y.H. 812, with the Draw-Song Left as It Is Sung, the Bead-Row in a Tally, a Court Clerk's Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A sermon of the Sallow pans preached in the bead-niche under the blue-green cliff where the glass-sand is dug; the sayings in Vhaleni set down in Grathic as I heard them, the draw-song with the ebb-line left as it is sung, the beads in a tally, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk come down from Greybank, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Preached in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, on a morning when the draw ran seaward against the wind, by an old dipper of the pans who had trailed a net at dawn for more years than he would give; written that evening by the keeper of the glass tally in the shed below the cliffs, on the back of a salt-paper contract gone damp and therefore void, folded with a green bead in the crease and tied with a tarry end of net-cord. It survives with salt bloom worked into the head and the gutter, glass dust in the grain, a green stain along the fold that smells sweet in heat and is not sweet to the tongue, one brine-gull feather, a wet ring where a dish of sea-water stood from the first voice to the last, a tarry fibre at the tie, the damp of the voided contract eating the lower corner, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Court clerk come down from Greybank to count the winter salt, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied once at Greybank in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the ebb-line left the length it is sung.

codex.title: The Sermon at the Lying-Place, Being What Bogga of the Reed Said Face Down at the Far Dry in Reed of Y.H. 813, with the Answer Held the Length of a Breath Under Water, the Pressings in a Notched Stick, a Factor's Clerk Gone Brown in the Bog-Water, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A sermon of the Marsh Mother preached at the shrine of the lying-place in the peat-dries of the bog-hunter, four leagues east of Reedholt in the black peat; the sayings in Fen Cant set down in Grathic letters by the bog-hunter's daughter, who heard them with her ear in the mud, the words that will not go into Grathic tied as knots in the margin, the lying-song with the answer held the length of a breath under water, the pressings in a notched count-stick kept under a loose board in oiled sacking, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor's clerk come out from Greybank to weigh the winter turf, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Preached by Bogga of the Reed on the fourth morning of Reed, Y.H. 813, when the black peat had given under a fortnight of rain and the pot at the end of the stand had gone cold twice, to the peat-cutters and two mud-wives come up from Reedholt and one child who had cut her first bundle in the dark and brought it back wet; written that evening by the daughter of the bog-hunter, who keeps the far dry for her father, in charcoal rubbed with peat on the back of a peat-warrant spoiled when the tally board was lifted in the rain, folded into oiled sacking with the notched stick and kept under the loose board at the dry. It survives with peat worked into the grain at the head off the writer's own thumb, a brown bog-water tideline along the gutter that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a wet reed pressed across the third leaf from a morning the dry stood under water, grey off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying, a hair of the bog-cow caught in the fold which the bog-hunter will not name, a chip of black peat shut into the lower corner that is warm when the leaf is opened of a morning and cold by noon, a knot of grey wool through a hole in the first leaf which the writer will not untie, the clerk's correction standing above in ink the damp has gone brown, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied once at Greybank in Bone of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a voided turf-warrant, with the verbs put back and the held answer left held.

codex.title: The Sermon at the Smith's Niche, Being What Was Said Over the Mended Tubes at the Forge in Low Kiln on a Morning in Bone of Y.H. 813, with the Hammer-Song Left with the Stroke Not Struck, the Pegs in a Mending-Tally, an Assessor's Clerk's Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A sermon of the common Grathic telling preached at the small shrine of the smith's niche behind the forge in Low Kiln of Sill, over the clipped ends of collectors' tubes set in the wall; the sayings in the flat working speech of the yard set down in Grathic, the hammer-song with the unstruck stroke left as it is not struck, the pegs in a mending-tally kept in charcoal on the back of a weigh-slip spoiled at the Cross, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of an assessor's clerk come up from Greybank to weigh the winter iron, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Preached by Harn the smith, who has kept the forge eleven years and mends the collectors' cold-iron tubes there, on Bone 15, Y.H. 813, the month of hunting and repair, while the kiln behind his bench kept four and did not give the fifth; written that evening by a woman of the Clay Yard who brings the forge its broken barrow-irons and keeps its tally in charcoal, on the back of a weigh-slip gone soft where a wet thumb passed over the figure, folded into grey wool and tied with annealed wire, and kept behind the loose peg in the niche wall with the clipped ends of tubes. It survives with blue bloom off Keldish iron ground into the head, cold-iron filings in the gutter, brick dust off the kiln behind the bench, a scorch where a spark off the hearth took the corner off one line, a tallow thumb off the forge lamp, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first voice to the last, a grey Ash print nobody will own, a green bead of lead glaze pressed in by a girl from the Glaze Room, a clipped end of a tube shut in the second fold which answers neither full nor flat when tapped, and one correction in the narrow upright hand of a clerk come up from Greybank. Copied once at Greybank in Ash of Y.H. 813 into the factor's file of yard sayings, with the verbs put back and the stroke left unstruck.

codex.title: Half for the Man Come Aboard, Being the Share-Rope of the Quay Children at Vhal, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Turning, the Empty Bollard, and What the Clerk Made of It
codex.kind: A rope-woman's gathering of a children's skipping game, set down in Grathic letters for a man from the factor's house though the play is in Vhaleni; the counting-out and the skipping verse in the salt-flat speech of the Quay, the manner of the play in the writer's own hand, a table of shares corrected in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Court clerk come down the Salt Road, a gloss in the leaning hand of a Council tally-man, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Salt of Y.H. 813 on the Quay at Vhal by Eda Quay, a woman who twists warp and mends nets, on the back of a voided salt-paper tide contract from the tide-tally house; set down with a tarred stick and salt, because ink will not sit on a rope-woman's table. The contract was spoiled by damp, which is accounted a virtue in Vhal, and the writing on the back outlasted the writing on the face. Kept coiled inside an old warp in a nail-keg under the net-rack. It survives soft and stiff by turns, with a white salt bloom at the head, tar fibre worked into the fold, a brine-gull feather pressed between the second and third leaves, a green bead of Glaze-Cliff glass in the lower corner, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, one correction in Ledgerhand, one gloss in the leaning Council hand, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Rules of the Ways, Being the Standing Rules of the Shipwrights of Vhal for the Taking, Keeping, Trying and Paying Out of Apprentices in the Yards of the Quay, with the Table of Years, the Faults in a Second Table, the Launching-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in the Narrow Upright Hand of a Council Clerk, One Line Struck in Charcoal by a Shipwright Who Would Not Sign It, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A yard-leaf of rules in the hand of the under-shipwright who keeps the moulds and the roll of hands at the third yard, written on salt-paper kept dry against the practice of the country and sewn with tarred net-twine to a board cover; the rules in the short sayings of the Quay, the years and the faults in tables, the launching-song pasted inside the cover, a shaving of keel shut in the second fold, two corrections in the Council's upright counting-hand, one line struck hard in charcoal by a shipwright who would not put his name to it, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: First gathered at Vhal in Y.H. 605, the year the Council of Tides put the building of its galleys out to contract and a yard that had kept its rules in the mouth was made to set them down so that a price could be argued with; copied forward from the mould-loft and not from a book. This leaf written in Ember of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by Rena of the Ways, an under-shipwright who has kept the moulds and said the curse at the laying of every keel for three and twenty years, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813.
