It survives hung on a nail in the mould-loft, soft at the fold and stiff with tar at the head, with a white salt bloom that has eaten the last letters off one word, a tar thumb off the ways-rope, a dry shaving of keel shut in the second fold, a fibre of wet rope pressed across the song, a brine-gull's peck through a rule, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, a ring of red wine with salt at the rim from a launching nobody paid for, a pitch-scorch that took the corner of a line without taking the sense, a green bead of Cliffs glass pressed in by a girl who would not ask after the curse, a grey print along the outer fold that is not hers and that she has not swept, two corrections in the Council's narrow upright hand, one charcoal line struck and written again underneath, and a line at the foot nobody will own

codex.title: The Shirt Left Rough, Being a Letter from the Wash-Hearth in Low Kiln to the Washing Bench at Stonemouth, Concerning a Child's Shirt That Would Not Rinse Clean, the Grey That Stays Where It Was Put, and the Question of What a Cloth Holds After It Has Held a Body; with the Answer in the Margin, a Weigh-Clerk's Correction in Ledgerhand, a Washing-Song, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A private letter on the back of a washing tally spoiled by lye, written in charcoal ground with soap-ash and gone over in iron-gall where the fat would not take it, folded thrice and sewn with a flax thread drawn from the hem of the cloth it speaks of; carried five leagues upriver on the frozen river road in a carter's coat in Stone of the Thin Year, answered along the margin at the lime yard in Stonemouth, borrowed at the weigh-clerk's bench by the landing where a clerk of the factor at Greybank laid his cuff on the leaf before he looked at it and set a correction on the back in narrow upright Ledgerhand, and kept since in a dry tin under the bench among the soap-ends and the spoiled tallies. It survives with lye gone white in the grain at the head, a thumb of tallow at the second fold, a blue-green speck of lead glaze off somebody's cuff, a wet ring where a dish of water stood from the first line to the last, frost-crisp along the gutter from a night in the carter's coat, one word struck through with a lye-sour thumbnail and written again underneath in the recipient's hand, and a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, on the ninety-fourth morning of the ice, at the wash-hearth off the Clay Yard in Low Kiln of Sill, by Milla, who keeps that hearth and the linen of eleven houses, to Sanna, who keeps the washing bench at the lime yard in Stonemouth, her sister by a mother who washed for the quarry and died of the white cough. Carried up the north river road when the ice would not bear a barge, answered in the margin at Stonemouth in broad lime-pale charcoal with the ends of words let fall, corrected on the back at the weigh-clerk's bench, and kept since in Milla's tin. The shirt itself went back to the house unrinsed and is not in this letter, which is the only thing in it I am sure of.

codex.title: The Shut Furnaces, Being an Extract from the Glass-Book of the Furnaces below the Glaze Cliffs, Concerning the Rising of Y.H. 626, the Year the Contracts Were Allowed to Lapse, the Men Set to the Pulled Benches, and the Pots Entered at Vhal That No Fire Had Made; with the Furnace-Song, the Table of Pots, Two Corrections in the Narrow Hand of the Council Room, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A furnace-tally keeper's extract from the glass-book, copied out of the tin lined with sand in the tally shed below the Cliffs; the year-entries in a leaning counting-hand on salt-paper kept dry against the practice of the country, the figures of pots set against the figure made up in the Council room, the song taken down from a furnace-man who would not sing it where a clerk could hear, one correction in the narrow upright hand of the Council, one in a Court hand borrowed from Greybank, a word scraped away and not written back, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in the tally shed below the Glaze Cliffs outside Vhal in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by the keeper of the furnace tally, who signs with a tally-cut and not a name and keeps the verbs in; copied from the furnace register begun in Y.H. 626 and kept since in a tin lined with sand, carried up the Salt Road at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and copied at Greybank onto the back of a weigh-slip voided by the Long Cold. It survives as five leaves of salt-paper stiffened with tar and sewn with eel-sinew: glass dust ground into the grain at the head, a green bead of cliff-glass pressed into the second fold with a sweet smear that has never dried, a white bloom come up out of the paper and not out of the sea, a scorch where the shed lamp caught the third leaf, a thumb of lead at the foot, a fibre of wet rope in the stitch, a peck from a brine-gull that took the corner and not the word, a square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, one correction standing above the words it corrects, and a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the keeper did not make and has not swept

codex.title: The Silt Song, Being the Shovelling-Song of the Fishstairs at Sill, Sung Clearing the Steps After the Breaking, with the Loads Counted Going Up, the Fourth Step Kept for the Water, a Landing-Clerk's Ruling in Broad Charcoal, a Factor's Clerk's Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss from a Woman of the Eel-Stalls, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A step-woman's work song in the low speech of the landing, said down into the silt and not up over the bridge; the verses counted in barrow-loads going up, with the fourth step kept and not entered; the manner of the clearing in the writer's own charcoal, the landing-clerk's ruling in broad charcoal, a factor's clerk's figures standing above in Ledgerhand, a gloss pressed into the margin by a woman of the eel-stalls, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim
codex.provenance: Sung at the Fishstairs below the north bridge in Sill and set down in the last tend of Silt, Y.H. 813, the year the sill-note came a week early, by a woman who clears the steps after the Breaking and has counted the loads going up for nine springs; written in charcoal thinned with silt-water on the back of a landing-tally spoiled by a wet thumb at the out-of-line step, folded into four and tied with grey wool to a nail under the eel-stall board; copied forward at Greybank in Grain of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a factor's voided weigh-slip. It survives with grey silt worked into the grain at the head, a silt tideline along the gutter, a chip of sandstone from the third step in the fold, a fish-scale pressed flat in the lower corner, a brine-gull's peck through one word of the sixth verse, a green bead of lead-glaze pressed into the lower margin, a small-ale ring gone sour at the foot, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own, the landing-clerk's broad ruling, the factor's clerk's figures standing above, the eel-stall woman's gloss in the margin, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: The Sixth Bite, Being a Winter-Hunter's Field Notes on the Ice-Mouse of the Frozen Ilm
codex.kind: A trapper's field book on one small beast, set down as a record of snares and not a book of reasons; the set-lines in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled fish-bills, the counting verse as it is said on the bank, a midwife's note in a small hand, a collector's ruling in Ledgerhand, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Tebb of the north bank, a hunter of the frozen fields above Sill who set snares in the eaves and under the river ice and sold the skins for a bit apiece; set down on the backs of fish-bills gone stiff with frost and on one spoiled toll-tally, sewn with eel-sinew into a scrap of oiled sacking and carried in a coat pocket against a tallow end. Copied forward at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold. It survives with frost-white ground into the head, a thumb of dried silt at the fold, a mouse-drop the size of a barley grain on the second leaf, a singe where the tallow end caught the lower corner, a coin-rub where a bit was carried loose in the pocket, a collector's ruling in narrow Ledgerhand across the fur column, a midwife's note in a small hand beside the sixth bite, a grey Ash print nobody will own, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own

codex.title: The Sixth Repair, Being a Letter from the First Seam to Nine Pots, Answered in the Margin and Entered Over by the Court
codex.kind: A letter between brothers, the one hand Keldish and number-first, the other Grathic and given to proverbs; a tally of repairs set down in a small table, the sentence of the Vorr kept as it was spoken, the answers of the man addressed written in the margins, the corrections of a Court survey-clerk laid in Ledgerhand over both hands, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, in the survey room off the Duelling Floor beneath Keld Keep, by Varek of the First Seam, a clerk of the rim-seam tally, to Ollen of Nine Pots, a thrower, his brother by a mother who came down from the clay country and never learned to say a number before a noun. Set first on the back of a survey sheet spoiled by wet slate and carried down the Rim Road and the Clay Road in Seed of Y.H. 813 with a survey party bound for Greybank; answered in the margins at Nine Pots and corrected at Greybank by a clerk of the factor's office who borrowed the leaf on a market morning and would not give it back until the verbs were out of it. Kept since in a clay tube stoppered with wool on the shelf of the thrower's shed in Nine Pots. It survives with coal dust at the head, a smear of hot lead at the fold where the leaf lay against a surveyor's cuff, bone-coloured slip dust worked into the gutter, a thumb of tallow, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first question to the last, the figure for the sixth repair struck through and written again underneath in the writer's own hand, and a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own.

codex.title: The Slack Tide, Being a Winter Riddle Night on the Quay at Vhal, Five Questions Scored in Chalk on the Tarred Post, the One Put from the Door, and the Tide That Was Named and Has Not Come
codex.kind: A tavern-keeper's record of a cold-month contest, set down for the settling of arguments and not for the improvement of the reader; the rules in the hand the house keeps, the riddles in the words they were spoken, a score in chalk on the tarred door-post, the figures of a Council clerk entered over them, a boat-master's note in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year after the Long Cold, at the alehouse called the Slack Tide on the Quay at Vhal, by the woman who keeps the house and the lamp over the door; set first on the back of a spoiled tide-tally from the house beside the Council room and on two strips of salt-paper that would not hold ink, sewn with eel-sinew into a fold of oiled sailcloth and kept in a dry tin under the till, where nothing else in this house is kept dry. It survives with a thumb of tar at the head, a white salt bloom along the gutter, a press of frozen rope across the first leaf, a green bead of cliff-glass in the lower corner, a fish-hook nick, a coal-smudge near the fifth question, the chalk rubbed thin where a sleeve has gone over the post, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the Council of Tides, one note in the blunt hand of a boat-master, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody's.

codex.title: The Smoke-Side Dog, Being a Soldier's Field Notes on the Kiln-Hound at the Old Kiln
codex.kind: A soldier's field book on one beast, set down as the record of a watch and not natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on a spoiled levy-roll, a watch-song as it is sung, a kiln-master's correction in slip-white, a clerk's ruling in Ledgerhand
codex.provenance: Written in Bone and Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Hobb of Sill, one of the Thane's men watching the Old Kiln road, in the watch-shed with a tallow end; set down on three levy-rolls spoiled by rain, then on the back of a granary docket, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a coat pocket. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813. It survives with soot ground into the head, a brown spot on the second leaf, a wet boot-print from the Slip Brook, a singe from the fire-pot, the charcoal rubbed thin, two corrections from the factor's clerk, one line in slip-white from the kiln-master, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own

codex.title: The Song of the Borrowed Ground, Being a Drinking-Song of the Peat-Dries on the Peat Line, Sung Sitting with the Cup Passed Hand to Hand and Nobody Pouring for Himself; the Verses Said to the Fire and the Last Word Let Fall into the Floor, with a Knot in the Margin for the Word That Cannot Be Written, a Reeve's Score in Peat, a Factor's Clerk's Figure Set Above, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A peat-dry woman's drinking-song, set down in Grathic letters though Fen Cant is not written; the words in the thick half-sung speech of the dry, the refrain kept by the table, a knot tied through a hole for the word that goes out at the back of the throat, a reeve's score in peat along the head, a factor's clerk's correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand above the lines, a mud-wife's small gloss pressed into the margin, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at a peat-dry on the Peat Line three leagues in from the Standing Post in Reed and Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by Oda Sedge, a woman who keeps the cup and the coals at the dry and has cut peat there since the Glaze Wars were ended; set down because a factor's clerk come up from Greybank to count the winter peat asked what was sung when the cutting was done and the cup went round, and wrote the answer down with the verbs taken out. Written first on a leaf of oiled reed and the back of a spoiled peat-tally, sewn with eel-sinew and tied with grey wool, carried under the boards to Greybank at the Opening of the Slates in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied onto the back of a factor's voided grain-warrant. It survives with a peat thumb worked into the head, a bog-water tideline that has eaten two words clean off the third verse, the press of wet sedge across the second leaf, a small-ale ring gone sour at the foot, a smear of eel slime at the fore-edge where a man set the cup down with his hands still wet, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which a collector's cuff left and nobody will own, a knot of grey wool through a hole in the first leaf which the writer will not untie, the reeve's peat score standing above the clerk's figure standing above the words, and one line at the foot that has never come forward

codex.title: The Song of the Fold, Being the Lullaby a Woman of Low Kiln Sang to a Child Come Back from the Bank
codex.kind: A mother's lullaby for the third watch, taken down from her own mouth by a woman who keeps the drying racks; the song in the low half-sung speech of the yard, the rubrics of the room in the writer's charcoal hand, a Court clerk's correction in Ledgerhand, a gloss pressed into the margin by a hearth-maid who used the words at bedsides, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim
codex.provenance: Sung in a kiln-house two doors up the Clay Yard in Low Kiln of Sill and set down in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a woman of the drying racks who had had a child come back to her from the bank in the Reed before; written in charcoal and tallow on the back of a birth-slate spoiled by a late entry, sewn with wire into a fold of grey birth-cloth and kept in a meal crock behind the lowest rack. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto a strip of sauce-paper from the factor's house at Greybank. It survives soft at the fold with a tallow thumb at the head, a crust-grease print on the second leaf, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, a ring where a cup of barley water stood from the first verse to the last, a green bead of glaze pressed into the lower corner, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Court clerk who borrowed the leaf on an Account-day, a gloss in the thick charcoal hand of a hearth-maid who carried the words to bedsides, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own

codex.title: The South Beam at the Peat Line, Being the Price-list of the Border Market and the Dues of the Grain Road, the Wine Road, the Mill Road and the Crossing, Set Down by a Clerk Who Keeps Both Ends of a Figure
codex.kind: A market clerk's fair copy of the board that hangs over the southern beam, with the figure asked set above the figure taken, the goods of the empire priced against the goods that come north out of the mud, the tolls of four posted roads and a fifth that is the drain, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at the Peat Line in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in the first market after the Long Cold, by the clerk who keeps the south beam for a factor of the Ten Bowls; carried north with a tally of eels at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and written up again at the third Account-day of Grain. It survives on the back of a grain-warrant discharged at the Line, sewn with a thread of grey wool into a fold of oiled silk and kept in the breast pocket against a wooden counting peg, with the yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the fold, a ring of warm wine the width of a cup at the head, a smear of myrrh across the second leaf, a white salt bloom along the lower margin, a dark streak of eel slime at the foot, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a thumb of oil from the wine jars, a small square scraped bare where a word would not stand, two corrections in hands that are not the writer's, and one line at the foot that nobody will claim.

codex.title: The Stand in the Peat, Being a Bog-Hunter's Field Notes on the Fen-Leech or Bog-Cow of the East Marsh
codex.kind: A hunter's field book on one beast, set down as the record of stands and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled peat-tallies, a peat-cutter's song in the words it is sung, two rulings in the narrow upright hand of the reeve's counting-man, a line in the pale salt-paper ink of a Vhaleni hide-buyer, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Reed and Tallow of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a hunter of the Standing Post who kept the east-marsh peat-dries for the reeve and took the beast for its hide and its horn; set down at the end of stands in the peat-hut with a peat-fire under a pot, first on spoiled peat-tallies and then on three folded strips of birch bark, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a coat pocket against a flint and a twist of tallow. Copied forward in Reed of Y.H. 813. It survives with peat worked into the head in a brown thumb, a press of wet sedge across the first leaf, a spot the size of a fingernail on the second leaf where a boy's blood fell, a horn-shaving caught in the gutter of the tally, a scorch where a coal from the peat-fire took the corner of the third leaf, the charcoal rubbed thin where the book was carried against the thigh, two rulings in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the reeve's counting-man, a line in the pale ink of a Vhaleni hide-buyer written on salt-paper gone soft at one corner, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: The Standing List of the Road House on the Clay Road, Being the Prices of the Market and the Tolls of the Roads, Copied Out Each Tend for Carters and Neighbours
codex.kind: A housekeeper's bill-book, the fresh leaf hung by the door and the old leaves kept behind the meal tub; market prices set beside the prices of this house, the road dues under them, two corrections in borrowed hands, a child's crooked sums in the corner, and a line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written and kept at the road house on the Clay Road, a day's walk downriver of Sill where the river road comes up from the south bridge, by the woman who has kept the house two and twenty years; begun in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, after the Long Cold, copied forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and last written up in Smoke of that year. It survives as a sewn book of rough leaves soft at the stitch, kept behind the meal tub against the wall: ale rings on the first leaf, a candle scorch at the second corner, grey silt worked into the gutter by wet boots, a grey Ash thumb at the head, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower margin, tar at the fold, a pressed reed between two leaves, a bit gone verdigris that has never been spent, two corrections in hands that are not the writer's, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.

codex.title: The Dry Stick at the Standing Post, Being the Rates of the Fen Market in Bits, Barter and Notched Sticks, with the Dues of the Boards, the Cuts, the Ditches and the Line, Cut by the Woman Who Keeps the Dry Tally and Copied onto Oiled Reed for a Man from the South
codex.kind: A post-tally copied from a notched stick into Grathic letters on a strip of oiled reed; the rates of the Post set before the dues of the ways, with one figure cut through and cut over again by a reeve's point, a factor's clerk's noughts set in the places, a knot tied in the margin for a word that cannot be written, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Cut at the Standing Post in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, when the bog bore a skin that would not take a cart, and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, as the first eels went up to the Line. The copy was made on the Post's own oiled reed and carried down to Greybank by an eel-trader who would not give his name, where a clerk of the factor borrowed it and set his hand above two entries. It survives lashed with eel-sinew under the Post's loose board: a peat thumb ground into the head, a reed-fibre shut in the second fold, a bog-water tide-line along the gutter that has taken one word off a row, a small eel-bone laid across the figure for bought breath, a wet boot's print over the dues of the boards, a grey Ash print along the margin nobody will own, one notch cut through a figure and cut over again, four noughts in a narrow upright hand, a knot of grey wool tied through the first leaf, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Stock Book of the Lower Yard, Being the Goods, Vessels and Days of a Kiln-House in Low Kiln Valued for the Clay Levy, with the Household's Charcoal Count Set Beside and One Column Left Unfilled
codex.kind: A page from a Court assessor's stock book; figures in Ledgerhand, terse remarks in the hand that set them, the house's own tally in charcoal on the back of a spoiled slip-tally laid against it, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the College, a figure scraped away, and a line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in a kiln-house of the lower yard in Low Kiln, Sill, in the Thin Year Y.H. 812 at the clay levy, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813; kept folded in the assessor's board cover and taken down whenever a levy is disputed. It survives with iron-gall at the head, bone-pale slip worked into the gutter, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a tallow thumb against the foot, grey Ash in the outer fold, charcoal dust along the back, a pale ring where a wet pot stood, a small square of bare paper where a figure was scraped away, two corrections in the College's narrow hand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.

codex.title: The Stone and the Slate, Being the Standing Rules of the Hearth-Maids of Grath for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Girls, with the Three-Day Reckoning, the Washing-Song Pasted in the Fold, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A folded leaf carried in the birth-cloth of a hearth-maid of Low Kiln; the rules set down in short sayings and half-sentences, the term and the faults in tables, the washing-song pasted into the fold, a narrow clerk's corrections struck through but left standing, one line in charcoal that a woman would not sign, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Gathered among the hearth-maids of Sill before the Rising and copied forward in the fold of a grey wool birth-cloth that goes where the maids go, rather than from any book; this leaf written at Low Kiln in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives soft at the fold and sour with lye, with a thumb of tallow at the stone clause, a print of grey Ash off a cuff at the head, a white bloom of dried soap in the gutter, a green bead of lead glaze at the lower corner off a girl come down from the glaze room, the press of a wet reed across the song, the small hollow where a warmed stone lay, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a clerk of Slate Row, one in the hand of a man come up from Greybank, a charcoal line struck and written again underneath, and a line at the foot nobody will own

codex.title: The Sweetness in the Glaze, Being a Rat-Catcher's Field Notes on the Lead-Rat of High Kiln and the Lead Run
codex.kind: A hunter's field book on one beast, set down as the record of rounds and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled glaze-tallies, a catcher's song as it is sung, a line in slip-white from a mixer of the Glaze Room, two rulings in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk come up from Greybank, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Ember and Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a rat-catcher of High Kiln who set wire in the glaze-stores and along the Lead Run and was paid by the tail; set down at the end of rounds in the store with a tallow end in a dish and the sweet edge of the glaze coming over the terrace on the wrong wind, first on spoiled glaze-tallies and then on three folds of birch bark, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a coat pocket. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813. It survives with a lead-blue smear ground into the head, a green stain at the corner of the second leaf where a tasting cup was set down, a press of wet slip across the first leaf, a singe at the lower corner from the tail-fire at the store door, the charcoal rubbed thin where the wrap was carried against the thigh, two rulings in the upright hand of the Greybank clerk, one line in slip-white from a mixer who would not give her name, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: The Tallow-Wife's Book, Being Remedies for the Vat-Scald, the Sweet Smoke, the Wool-Cough, the Nest-Sting, a Cut from a Vat-Shard, Milk That Will Not Come, the Birth-Flower and the Third-Night Chill, Set Down in the Fat-House with the Errors Left Standing
codex.kind: A tallow-wife's and midwife's book of remedies in the short fat-house speech, written in Grathic letters so a girl of Low Kiln might read it, with the smell of the rendering left in the words; the cures in a renderer's hand on the back of a spoiled fat-tally, the objections of a physician come down from Greybank pressed brown into the margin, the corrections of a factor's clerk in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a watchman's line in charcoal at the foot of the remedies, a pouring-song with the fourth cup left standing under the bench, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at the Tallow Works, two leagues north-east of Sill, between Tallow of Y.H. 812 and Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the Thin Year and the Long Cold, by Mella of the Works, a renderer of sheep fat who caught the children of the lamp-women and dressed the hands of the shed for nine-and-twenty years; begun on the back of a fat-tally spoiled when a spill of hot fat took the figures, folded into oiled sacking, tied with a hemp wick and carried in the breast of a wool apron against a square of birth-cloth washed thin, and copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a voided weigh-slip. It survives with a thumb of raw tallow worked into the grain at the head, a grey bloom of sour fat along the fold which has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a singe where the flue drew a spark out of the fire onto the third, a wick trimmed to a fingernail caught in the seam, a brown crust spot at the second fold, a flat square of grey wasp-paper pressed into the lower corner, a small round mark where a buyer set a mark-piece down and took it up again, a grey Ash print along the outer fold nobody will own, objections in the cold margin hand of the physician, corrections in the upright hand of the factor's clerk, the watchman's charcoal at the remedies, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: The Articles of the Tenth Clamp, Being the Standing Rules of the Order of the Tenth Clamp Beneath Keld Keep for the Taking, Cutting and Trying of Apprentices at the First Way, with the Table of Hands, the Iron-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, and the Master's Corrections
codex.kind: A board-copy of the Order's standing rules in the hand of the under-master who keeps the irons and the roll of hands at the mouth of the Duelling Floor; the articles cut in short Keldish clauses, the tables in number-first order, the iron-song in the hard Rim speech pasted inside the cover, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of a Court survey-clerk, one line struck in coal by the master of the floor, one objection in the leaning hand of a leech come up from the Ninth Gallery, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: First gathered beneath Keld Keep in Y.H. 747, the year the Cold Pass was shut and the border fixed by men who had never walked it, and copied forward each generation from the iron board beside the clamps rather than from paper, which is why the rule about the rope-coloured hand is worn through at the corner and the rule about the nail is as sharp as the day it was cut; this leaf written in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by Vek of the Tenth Clamp, the under-master who keeps the irons, and carried down the Rim Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with a survey party bound for Greybank, where it was copied onto the back of a spoiled tally-roll. It survives with coal dust ground into the head off the master's sleeve, a smear of hot lead at the fold where a passing was measured two hours early, iron filings caught in the gutter from the clamps on the floor, a scorch where a lamp-spark took the corner of the second leaf, a thumb of tallow, a ring of frost raised out of the paper on the climb over the Cold Pass, a splinter of warm-stone sewn into the board cover which keeps the whole leaf a little warm, one correction in the narrow upright hand of the Court, one line struck hard in coal by the master, one objection written twice and struck twice by a leech from the Ninth Gallery, and a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own

codex.title: The Third Brazier, Being a Measure-Night at the Shaft Head in Keld Keep, with Five Questions Put Down the Hole, the Sixth Written by the Mine-Reeve and Not Scored, the Coals Laid Down and Not Taken Up, a Survey-Clerk's Figures Over Them, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A brazier-keeper's record of a cold-month contest, set down for the settling of an argument about a coal nobody claimed and not for the improvement of the reader; the manner of the room in the hand that keeps it, the questions in the words they were put down the shaft, the answers as they were said into the mouth of it, four coals counted by the flat of a thumb, the mine-reeve's red cross and the survey-clerk's narrow figures set above, a boy's charcoal in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the year the lowlands call the Thin Year, in the warm-room at the head of the shaft in Keld Keep, by the woman who tends the third brazier and counts the coals that go into it; set down first in charcoal on the back of a spoiled rim-seam rubbing and copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813, when the Rim Road opened, onto the reverse of a Court survey-sheet voided by wet slate and carried up from Greybank, where a survey-clerk of the factor borrowed the leaves and set his figures above hers. It survives folded in oiled survey-cloth and sewn with wire, kept under the third brazier where nothing else in this room is kept: coal smut ground into the head off the hand that counts, slate dust in the gutter, a warm-stone shaving shut in the fold that has gone colder than the ledge, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead nobody claimed, a frost-feather along the lower edge gone by noon, a red thumb at the fold which the mine-reeve left when he set his slate down, a line of charcoal in a boy's hand, grey Ash along the outer fold which the writer did not put there and has not swept, one correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, and a line at the foot which has never been claimed

codex.title: The Third Saying, Being a Mother's Lullaby of Reedholt in the East Marsh, Sung to a Child Three Nights Old on the Boards the Night Before the Hearth Drawing; with the Reed-Name Said Three Times into the Ground, the Knot of Grey Wool, the Board That Is Lent, the Fifth Place Left Unscored, a Factor's Clerk's Correction in Ledgerhand, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A mother's lullaby in Fen Cant, the thick half-sung English of the east marsh, set down in Grathic letters learned off an eel-trader out of Sill; said through the nose and low, with the last word let fall into the mud under the boards and not finished, the name said three times and never written, the word that will not come into Grathic tied as a knot of grey wool in the margin, the fifth place left unscored; a factor's clerk's correction standing above in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a woman of the peat-dry in charcoal underneath, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim
codex.provenance: Sung at Reedholt in the east marsh on the night before the Hearth Drawing, Stone 12 of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year after the Long Cold, by a woman of the peat-dry to her child three nights old; set down in charcoal and peat-water on the back of a peat-tally spoiled by a wetting, sewn with eel-sinew into a fold of oiled reed, tied with grey wool and kept in a dry tin slung under the hut boards; carried up the marsh road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a factor's voided weigh-slip, where a clerk set his hand above hers. It survives with a brown peat thumb worked into the head, a bog-water tideline that has taken two words off the second leaf, a press of wet sedge across the third, a thread of grey wool laid in the fold where the fifth verse should stand, a small round pale place where a collector's cuff was laid at the drawing and nobody will own the cuff, a scratch from a reed-wolf's tooth at the corner, a small-ale ring gone dark at the foot, the clerk's correction above, the peat-dry woman's charcoal underneath, and one line at the foot that has never come forward

codex.title: The Three That Stand, Being a Letter from a Peat-Dry at the Edge of the Quiet Acre to a Reeve of the Standing Post, Concerning a Year of a Child's Breath Bought at Greybank, the Twelve Knots, the Peat That Did Not Take This Winter, and the Name Said into the Ground; with the Answer in the Margin, a Factor's Clerk's Correction in Ledgerhand, and a Song Said to the Ground
codex.kind: A private letter on the back of a peat-dry rent-tally spoiled by a factor's man writing a figure on it, written in charcoal thinned with peat-water, folded four times and tied with grey wool to a knot-stick; carried up the marsh road in an eel-trader's creel in the last tend of Stone, answered along the margin at the Standing Post in Ilmen, borrowed at Greybank where a factor's clerk set a correction in Ledgerhand, and kept since under the Post's loose board among the reeves' sticks
codex.provenance: Written at a peat-dry two boardwalks short of the Quiet Acre in the Fenmarch on Stone 22, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Tess of the Dry, who keeps the cuttings and learned her Grathic letters off a man come to take a receipt, to Dill Peat, a reeve of the Standing Post chosen by standing in the last feud, who is her sister; carried up the marsh road after the ice went off the cuts, answered in the margin in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 after the child came back, borrowed at Greybank where a factor's clerk corrected the leaf on the back, and kept since under the loose board at the Post. It survives tied to its stick of twelve notches, with a thumb of wet peat worked into the grain at the head, a bog-water tideline along the gutter that has taken two words clean away, a pressed bog-myrtle leaf in the second fold, a smear of eel slime at the outer crease, a grey Ash print nobody will own, a scorched corner where the leaf lay near the peat fire, salt bloom at the foot from a cuff that had been in the pans, the twelve knots still on the stick, and a curl of grey wool through the tie-hole which the writer will not untie. The clerk's correction stands above the words and the verbs stand underneath it, and one line at the foot is in a hand nobody has claimed

codex.title: The Tide Keeps the Count, Being the Salt-Pan Children's Skipping Game at Vhal, with the Counting-Out, the Twelve Bits, the Turn of the Rope, the Half That Is Not a Share, and What the Council Clerk Made of It
codex.kind: A salt-pan children's rope-skipping game in the Vhaleni speech, set down in Grathic letters on salt-paper the writer keeps dry against the practice of the country; the counting-out and the verse in the children's own half-sung voices, the manner of the play in a pan-woman's small hand, a correction in the leaning hand of a Council clerk, a note in a dipper's charcoal, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Set down at the Salt Pans outside Vhal on the Sallow coast in the last tend of Ember, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Venna of the Pans, a woman who keeps the drying frames and learned her letters off a tally-man come down to weigh a rack of salt; written on the back of a tide-sheet spoiled by a figure put on it in the rain, and kept dry in a tarred tin lined with rushes, because a wet document is no document by the Council's own law. It survives with a white salt crust along the gutter, a tar thumb at the head, a fibre of wet net-cord pressed into the second fold that goes soft when the weather goes soft, a green bead of Cliffs glass, a brine-gull's peck through one word of the verse, a fish-hook nick, a ring eaten through by red wine, a wet corner where two lines have gone void and the space left standing, a grey Ash print nobody will own, one correction in the leaning hand of a Council clerk, a note in a dipper's charcoal, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody has claimed

codex.title: The Toll-Bag at the Meal Mill, Being the Price of Barley and Meal, the Charge of the Stone, and the Dues of the Roads That Bring a Sack to the Hopper, Set Down in the Meal-Book by the Miller's Daughter
codex.kind: A meal-book leaf written in charcoal thinned with meal-dust and gone over in iron-gall; the figure cried at the Cross set against the figure taken at the mill door, the stone's handful set beside the road's bit, the dues of the ways that carry grain set under both; corrected in the narrow upright hand of a factor's clerk, a carter's charcoal added at the bridge, a child's crooked sums in the corner, and one line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at the meal mill at Sill on the Ilm, in Stone of Y.H. 813, the year after the Thin Year, when the river lay under ice and the barley came down the ridge road frozen in the sacks; set down by the miller's daughter, who keeps the meal-book, on the back of a barley tally spoiled by a wet figure out of the Glaze Room, and written up again at the three Account-days of Stone as the bell went four, four and a gap over the water. Kept folded in the toll-bag on its nail behind the door with a barleycorn shut in the crease. It survives with white mill-dust worked into the head and the gutter, a brown silt tideline along the foot from a morning the leaf went down to the Fishstairs in an apron, a barley awn stiff in the second fold, a wet ring where a cup was set down and taken up before it was seen, a nick from a millstone dressing-pick at the fore-edge, a grey Ash print along the outer margin which the writer did not make and has not swept, two corrections in hands that are not hers, a child's sums done wrong in the bottom corner, and one line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Turning of the Fire, Being the Watch-Song of the Kiln-Mouth in Low Kiln, Sung at the Firing and Again at the Second Firing
codex.kind: A firing song of the clay yard, called to the damper and answered into the mouth, the words in the low half-sung speech of the yard; written in charcoal thinned with brick-dust, the rubrics of the mouth in the same hand, a kiln-master's correction in broad charcoal, a factor's clerk's figures in a narrow upright Ledgerhand, a gloss in the thick charcoal of a woman who rakes the lower fire, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Set down in Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by an old woman who turns the fire at a kiln two doors above the Vail in Low Kiln of Sill, who learned her letters off a tile-counter and has no slate in the yard; written on the back of a firing-tally spoiled by a wet thumb while the second firing was being counted, tied with grey wool to the handle of the damper under a broken pot turned mouth-down against the rain. Copied forward in Tallow of Y.H. 813 onto a strip of oiled paper from the wheel-shed after the first leaf scorched. It survives with a brick-dust thumb at the head, a long scorch along the lower edge where the leaf lay too near the mouth, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the corner, a small-ale ring through the third verse, a grey Ash smear in the gutter that nobody will own, a sherd pressed between the fourth and fifth leaves, one line eaten away by the heat and not written in again, one correction in broad charcoal, four in the narrow upright hand of the factor's clerk at Greybank, a gloss from a woman at the tubs, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never been claimed

codex.title: Of the Overnight Keeping, the Two Benches and the Cup Left Standing, Being Title the Twelfth of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied for the Room-Slate in Slate Row at Sill, with the Room-Clerk's Margin, the Cup-Ring, a Cold-Iron Score, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: An extract from the Court's ordinances, written out for the room-slate in the Waiting Room off Slate Row at Sill, with the marginal hand of the clerk who sets the verbs back after a day's drawing; the articles in Ledgerhand and the verbs restored beneath them, the nights and the things not entered in tables, the form of an overnight left blank, the bench-song pasted inside the cover, a ring where a cup stood, a bare square where a name was scraped away with a clip's edge, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed
codex.provenance: Copied at Sill in Slate Row in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, from Title the Twelfth of the Ordinances of the Keeping as set down in the first years after the Rising of Y.H. 668, confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of Y.H. 418, and added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year; it survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, kept under the room-slate on the shelf beside the door and taken down when the evening figure has been read: a grey Ash thumb at the head, cold-iron filings worked into the gutter off a tube-wrap set down while a clerk went for water, a pale round ring where a cup stood from the first watch to the morning, a brown crust-print at the second fold, a curl of grey wool through the tie-hole that nobody will untie, a tallow thumb, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl with the sweetness still at her mouth, a damp tide-line along the foot out of the boards, a bare square where a name was scraped away with a clip's edge and no other put in its place, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot that has never been owned

codex.title: The Twelve Turns, Being the Wheel-Song of Low Kiln, Said Kneeling to the Lump while the Wheel Runs, with the Turns Counted and the Wetting Kept Outside the Count, a Wheel-Shed Rubric in Slip-Thinned Charcoal, a Kiln-Master's Correction, a Factor's Clerk's Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Rack-Woman's Gloss in the Margin, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A thrower's work song in the low Grathic of the wheel-shed, said down into the lump and not up into the shed; the turns counted in threes of twelve with a hand kept for the wetting, the rubrics of the seat and the slip bowl in the writer's charcoal hand, a kiln-master's correction in broad charcoal, a factor's clerk's figures standing above in Ledgerhand, a rack-woman's thick-charcoal gloss pressed into the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim
codex.provenance: Set down in Ember of Y.H. 813, the kiln month, by Venna of the Wheel, a thrower at a wheel two doors down the Clay Yard from the Vail kiln-house, who has kneeled at it six-and-twenty years and can find a centre by the feel of it before the first turn; written because a factor's clerk come up from Greybank on an Account-day stood in the shed door and asked a girl at the bench what the wheels said while they turned, and wrote her answer down with the turns taken out and a figure put in the place of the wetting. Written first in charcoal thinned with slip on the back of a wheel-shed tally spoiled by a fall of slip, folded into four, tied with grey wool and carried under the board of the shed; copied forward at Greybank in Bone of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a voided weigh-slip. It survives with wet slip worked into the grain at the head, a dry line of slip across the second leaf where a sleeve passed at the third turn, a barley-water ring through the fifth verse, a small sherd pressed flat between the third and fourth leaf with the well almost rubbed away, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner, a long hair the colour of wet wool caught in the seam, a grey Ash smear along the gutter that nobody will own, the kiln-master's broad correction, the rack-woman's gloss, the clerk's figures standing above, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: The Two Figures, Being an Extract from the Chronicle of the Standing Post Concerning the Thirty-One Years, the Figure Read at the Ferry and the Figure Paid at the Reed, with the Years as the Reeves Kept Them, the Court's Annals Set Beside Them, the Fen Song, and the Corrections of a Factor's Clerk
codex.kind: A reeve's-clerk's extract from the chronicle of the Standing Post in the Fenmarch, copied out of the tarred box under the third board of the walk; the years in a broad standing hand gone stiff with peat water, the Court annals in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor's clerk come up from Greybank, the two figures entered in a column that no clerk of the Keeping has ever signed, one song taken down in Reed from a singer who would not give her name, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at the Standing Post in the Fenmarch by the clerk who keeps the reeves' chronicle, a man with no slate-name who signs with a thumb pressed into peat, in Reed and Ember of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813; copied from the post's original begun in Y.H. 420 and kept since in a tarred box under the third board of the walk, where the peat water reaches the nails in the wet season. It survives as six leaves of stout foolscap sewn with wire and folded in oiled sailcloth, with black peat worked into the gutter and the creases of the thumb, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the clerk did not make and will not sweep, a twist of wet reed fibre pressed flat in the second leaf, a strip of Vhaleni salt-paper gone soft at the edge and pasted over the sixth clause, a dark streak of eel slime at the foot, a tallow thumb at the head, a bead of green cliff-glass in the lower corner, the broad reeve's correction standing above the narrow Court correction standing above the text, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward

codex.title: The Articles of the Two Knives, Being the Standing Rules of the Number-Cutters of Keld Keep for the Taking, Holding and Trying of Apprentices at the Descent and at the Mouth, with the Table of Counts, the Knife-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A pattern-copy kept by the woman who holds the second tin at the shaft mouth; the articles cut in short Rim clauses into Grathic letters with the endings struck off, the years and the faults set in tables of number-first order, the knife-song pasted inside the cover, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Court survey-clerk, one in the coal-pressed hand of the master of the floor, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed
codex.provenance: First cut on the pattern-board at the mouth in Y.H. 747, the year the Cold Pass was shut and the border fixed by men who had not walked it, and copied forward from the patterns and not from a book, which is why the rule about the stone is worn through where a hundred thumbs have wiped it and the rule about the second setting is as sharp as the day it was cut; this leaf set down in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 by the keeper of the second tin, who keeps the figures that were cut out of arms, and carried down the Rim Road in the dust of a lead cart toward Greybank, where it was copied onto the back of a spoiled shift-tally. It survives with coal smut ground into the head off the sleeve she wipes the tin with, an iron-red cross from the mine-reeve's point against the rule about a figure the roll did not give, a warm-stone shaving shut in the fold that is still warm on the coldest morning, a bead of lead out of the Ninth Gallery, a frost-feather pressed flat between the second and third leaves and gone by noon, a clamp-scratch across the song made by a man showing his brother how the iron bites, a notch cut at the edge with a tally-knife where a word would not come, grey Ash along the outer fold off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying, a thumb in coal dust nobody will claim, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot that is nobody's

codex.title: The Child Who Remembered the South, Being an Extract from the Dispensation-Book of the Factor's House at Greybank Concerning the Year 766, the Thin Child Who Spoke in a Southern Voice, the Phial Bought Without a Payer, and the Page Corrected by a Physician; with the Child's Sayings, the Corking Verse, Two Hands of Correction, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A clerk's chronicle-extract from the dispensation-book of the factor's house at Greybank, copied out of the tin behind the counter; the year-entries in a sloping tally hand, the physician's page copied as it stands with the struck word still legible, the licence tallies set in a table, the child's sayings taken down in the hearing and not translated, the corking verse sung at the counter, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written at Greybank in the factor's counting house in the last tend of Ash, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the keeper of the dispensations, whose office stands on the factor's roll and whose hand does not; copied from the book of phials kept in a tin behind the counter since Y.H. 683, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives as four leaves of foolscap sewn with wire into a board cover soft at the hinge: barley dust worked into the head off a measure that went over in the granary yard, a bloom of Sallow salt along the gutter which comes and goes with the weather, a shaving of phial-cork shut in the second fold, a husk of southern grain stuck fast in the gutter, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the keeper did not make and has not swept, a ring where a dish of barley-water stood from the first entry to the last, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away and no other put in, two corrections in borrowed hands, and the line at the foot

codex.title: The Unstruck Stroke, Being a Letter from the Bell-Founder at Keld Keep to the Man Who Rings the Market Bell at Sill, Concerning the Fifth That Is Not Struck, the Counting of the Strokes, the Song of the Bell, the Answer Written in the Margin in Charcoal, and What the Court Entered Over Both
codex.kind: A private letter on the back of a bell-founder's charge-sheet gone stiff with tallow, written in iron-gall and the point of a chisel, folded thrice and sewn with a fibre of bell-rope; carried down the Rim Road and the Clay Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with a consignment of clamps, answered at Sill in Reed of Y.H. 813 on the back of a spoiled Weighing notice, borrowed at the factor's house at Greybank, and kept since in a dry tin among the founder's small tools
codex.provenance: Written in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, in the foundry under the west wall of Keld Keep, by Vesk, a founder who casts and recasts the bells of the Rim and the Clay Road, to Bram, who rings the market bell at the Cross in Sill; set first on the back of a charge-sheet spoiled by a spill of tallow, carried down the Rim Road and the Clay Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with a survey party's clamps, answered at Sill in Reed of Y.H. 813, and borrowed at the factor's house at Greybank, where a clerk of the College set a correction in Ledgerhand. It survives sewn with a fibre of bell-rope: bell-metal filings worked into the head, a thumb of tallow at the outer fold, a greenish shaving of the same metal pressed flat into the second fold, a frayed strand of rope caught in the stitch, a grey Ash print along the gutter where a cuff passed, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first counting to the verse, a bloom of frost from the Cold Pass gone soft on the last leaf, one word struck through with a chisel-point and written beneath in the recipient's charcoal hand, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody has claimed.

codex.title: The Untaken Turn, Being the Well-Game of Cold Acre, with the Passing, the Bringing Back, and What a Clerk of the Factor Made of the Warm That Is Not Counted
codex.kind: A well-woman's setting-down of a children's passing-game in the Cold Acre speech, written with a charred stick on the back of a meal-mill tally gone soft at one corner; the verses in the children's own half-sung words, the manner of the play in the writer's hand, a correction in the margin by the woman who winds the well-rope, the factor's clerk's ruling in Ledgerhand above the eighth line, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Set down in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, at Cold Acre on the ridge two leagues north of Sill, by the woman who keeps the well-rope there, on the back of a barley tally from the meal mill that had given up its figures at one corner; carried down the ridge road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank, where a clerk of the factor's house borrowed the leaf for a morning and gave it back with the verbs taken out. Kept since under the loose stone of the well-curb, in the nick where the rope is coiled, which the children do not lift. It survives with a thumb of well-clay at the head, a grey Ash print nobody will own along the gutter, a white frost-ring that has eaten two words off the fourth line, a barley awn stiff in the fold, a nick from a turnip knife at the fore-edge, a thread of sacking caught in the second leaf, the rope-woman's correction standing in the margin, the clerk's ruling standing above the eighth line, and the line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Up-Haul, Being the Bank-Rope Song of the Ilm, Sung Going Up from Greybank with Salt and Iron, Set Down from a Towman's Mouth with the Rest Beats Kept and a Factor's Clerk's Figures in the Margin
codex.kind: A work song of the towpath, counted in the feet and not in the hands; the verses in the low hard Grathic of the bank, said into the rope; the rubrics and the unsung fourth verse in the charcoal hand of a girl at the eel-stalls who wrote what was dictated to her; a factor's clerk's figures in a narrow upright hand down the margin; a grey Ash print nobody will own
codex.provenance: Sung on the up-haul between Greybank and Sill since before the Glaze Wars and set down in Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the thaw year, by a bank-walker out of the Fishstairs who had begun to lose the fourth verse and the use of her left hand, dictated to a girl at the eel-stalls who wrote it on the back of a weigh-slip from the factor's house at Greybank gone soft with salt. The girl put the verses in the order of the pulls and left the rubrics out, having never hauled. The slip survives folded twice against a storm, tied with tarred twine nobody will own, with a tar thumb at the head, a silt tideline along the gutter, a crust of salt on the second leaf, a rope-burn across the third verse, a fish-scale pressed flat in the lower corner, a splinter of corduroy from the Clay Road in the fold, the clerk's figures standing in the margin, and the fourth verse in a hand that is neither the walker's nor the girl's

codex.title: The Ordinance of the Waiting Room, Being an Extract from the Court's Ordinances for the Keeping Overnight of Vessels Before the Banking in Slate Row at Sill, with the Table of Nights, the Form of a Waiting-Entry, the Pallet-Song Pasted Inside the Tin, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: An extract from the Court's ordinances, written out for the under-clerk who keeps the waiting-book beside the collector's table in Slate Row at Sill; the articles in Ledgerhand with the people restored beneath them, the nights and the faults in tables, the form of a waiting-entry left blank, the pallet-song pasted inside the tin, a scorch off the lamp, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed
codex.provenance: Copied at Sill in Slate Row in Bone of Y.H. 813, the year after the Thin Year and the Long Cold, by the under-clerk who keeps the waiting-book and carries the night's figures up the Clay Road to the bank at Greybank; the ordinance first gathered at the Hearthseat in Y.H. 669, the year after the Ash Rising that Pell Varr put down, and copied forward at each Opening of the Slates from the College book and not from the tin; carried through the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 814. It survives as four leaves of foolscap sewn with wire and kept in the tin beside the waiting-book, soft at the fold, with a damp tideline along the foot from the wall of the room, grey Ash off a cuff worked into the gutter, a pale round ring where a tube was set down and which is not a wound, a tallow thumb at the head, iron filings ground in from the wool sleeve, a curl of grey wool from a cradle blanket caught in the sewing, the sweet green of lead glaze pressed in by a girl come up from High Kiln with the sweetness still at her mouth, a scorch in the second leaf where the lamp was held too near while a woman was speaking, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Want in the Count, Being the Hopping Game of the Drying Racks in Low Kiln
codex.kind: A children's counting game, set out with its words, the scored ground, the forfeits, and the two hands that disagree over the empty place
codex.provenance: Set down by an old woman of the drying racks in the Clay Yard, Low Kiln, Sill, in Ilmen of Y.H. 813, having no slate-name and signing with a thumb pressed into slip; written in charcoal on the back of a spoiled drying tally and kept folded in the band of a cast-off apron. It survives with the score of a knuckle in slate dust, a tallow thumb, a drop of barley grease, a green bead of lead glaze from a girl who leaned over to see the writing, a grey print of Ash, and one correction in the narrow hand of a clerk borrowed from Slate Row. The game is held to be older than the bell at the Cross.

codex.title: The Warm Streets, Being an Account of the Keel and the Court City of the Hearthseat, Set Down by a Carter Who Went Up the Hearth Road with Sallow Salt and Came Back with a Figure He Could Not Change; with the Prices of the City, the Hall Seen from the Yard, the Four Sealed Wells, the Road-Song, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A carter's road account, set in charcoal and in a small careful hand on the backs of three salt-dockets and a Court grain-warrant spoiled at one corner; the road and prices in the carter's hand, the city's sayings copied as he heard them, the song taken down in the carters' yard at Greybank, one correction in the narrow upright hand of the College, one in the hand of a factor's clerk, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward
codex.provenance: Written at Greybank in the factor's counting house in the last tend of Bone, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a carter of the Hearth Road who signed nothing and scored the mark of a cart-wheel in the corner with a nail; he went up in Grain with Sallow salt out of the Court granaries and came down in Ash with the same team, three silver marks the poorer, a copy of the notice printed beside the Hall, and a green bead of cliff-glass given him for a bit and a promise in the lower court. Copied forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, onto the back of a grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold. It survives folded into the nail-box under the factor's counter, soft at the fore-edge and sour with salt: a white bloom along the gutter, a thumb of tallow at the head, slate dust worked into the fold from a surveyor who borrowed the leaves and would not sit down, iron filings caught in the second crease, a green bead of cliff-glass pressed flat into the lower corner, a ring of small ale near the song, a damp tide-line where the leaf lay a night against the quay wall, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with a knife-point, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own

codex.title: The Warm Within, Being a Book of Remedies Gathered in Low Kiln
codex.kind: A hearth-maid's book of household physic for births, chills, burns, coughs, bites and the second chill; the remedies in Grathic, with a Court clerk's corrections in Ledgerhand and one song for the third night
codex.provenance: Set down in Low Kiln in Sill between Y.H. 809 and Y.H. 812, the Long Cold and the Thin Year, by a hearth-maid of the district who attended births and put no name to a book an officer might read; written in charcoal and tallow on the backs of spoiled birth-slates and on a quire of sauce-stained paper from the factor's house at Greybank, sewn with wire into a board cover. It survives behind the meal bin of a house east of the Clay Yard, soft at the fold: a bone-pale slip thumb at the head, a tallow print where a mother held it down in a draught, a green bead of glaze from a girl with sweetness at her mouth, a grey Ash print along the gutter, a streak of barley grease, one correction in the narrow hand of a Court clerk who borrowed the leaf on an Account-day, and one line struck out and written again in the writer's own hand. Copied forward in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs left where she put them.

codex.title: The Stone Against the Belly, Being the Sayings of the Hearth-Maids of Grath, Gathered at the Birth-Slate Bench in Sill and Glossed for a Girl Who Has Not Yet Held a Newborn
codex.kind: A hearth-maid's gathering of the proverbs, bench-instructions, slate-warnings and small refusals of the women who deliver and enter the children of Grath, set in the common tongue on the backs of birth-slates spoiled by a figure put in the wrong column; the sayings said low to the stone, the slate and the fire, the glosses in the writer's own charcoal, with a collector's clerk's correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, an old woman's addition in broad charcoal, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Gathered at the birth-slate bench in her own house in Sill through Ash and Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, and written up in the Five at the turn into Y.H. 813 by Dessa Marsh, a hearth-maid who has delivered children in Low Kiln and at the Cross for two and twenty years and keeps the birth-slate book because the Court pays her to; written in charcoal on the backs of spoiled birth-slates washed with barley-water, sewn with wire into a fold of old wool and kept under the loose board beside the bench; carried once to Slate Row in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 where a collector's clerk borrowed it and set his hand above hers. It survives with charcoal ground into the head, a tallow thumb at the fold, a barley-water ring gone dark, a browned crust pressed flat between the second and third leaves, a hair from a newborn's head shut in the gutter, a small-ale ring, a scratch of cold-iron filings, grey Ash along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, and the line at the foot which nobody has claimed

codex.title: The Little Litany of the Return, Being the Questions Put to the Little Ones at the Wash-Hearth Below the Sill, with Their Answers as They Give Them, the Dame's Rubrics, a Clerk's Correction, a Mother's Margin, and the Line at the Foot Which Was Never Taught
codex.kind: A catechism of the Return said at the wash-hearth in Low Kiln, the dame asking and the children answering, the answer held through a silence the dame will not fill; set down by the dame who keeps the hearth with the manner of it, eight stations and their answer, a College clerk's correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a mother's note in the margin, a child's crooked mark, and a line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Low Kiln of Sill in the last tend of Ash, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Wenna, who keeps the wash-hearth below the sill and teaches the little ones their first words of the Keeping, in charcoal on the back of a broken slip-tray tally spoiled by a wet thumb, folded with a copper bit shut in the crease and kept among the hearth things under the third flagstone; corrected in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 by a clerk of the College come up from the assessor's house in Slate Row; copied forward once into a quire of birch bark. It survives with tallow worked into the grain at the head, pale slip along the gutter, a grey Ash print off a child's cuff, a ring of sour milk on the second leaf, a charred edge where the leaf lay too near the banked coals, one word scraped away with a knife and not replaced, a crooked mark in a child's hand, the clerk's correction standing above the words it corrects, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward.

codex.title: Of the Weighing and the Reading of the Year's Measures, Being the Ordinance Copied Out of the College Book in Slate Row for the Clerk Who Keeps the Notice Beside the Weighing Hall, with the Figures as They Were Read, the Fire Behind the Grating, the Vorr's One Sentence Set at the Edge, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: An extract from the Court's ordinances, written out for the notice-board beside the Weighing Hall in the Hearthseat, with the marginal hand of the under-clerk who carries the day's figures up to the Steward's room; the articles in Ledgerhand and the verbs restored beneath them, the order of the day and the figures in tables, the form of a reading left blank, the stair-song pasted inside the board, a scorch off the grating, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed
codex.provenance: Copied at the Hearthseat on the Keel on Weighing of Y.H. 812, the second of the Five, the day the year's measures are read aloud in Slate Row; written by the under-clerk who keeps the printed notice and carries the figures to the Steward's room, from the ordinance book held by the College of Assessors; carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813. It survives as four leaves of foolscap sewn with wire and kept in the notice-board's tin: an iron-gall thumb at the head, slate dust in the gutter off a district slate laid there while a runner gave her figure, a scorch in the second leaf where a spark came off the grating, grey Ash off a Kept room's skirting worked into the fold, a curl of grey wool from a cradle blanket, a tallow thumb at the foot, a pale ring where a collector set his tube down, a green bead of lead glaze pressed in by a glaze-mixer come up from High Kiln, a tide-line from the cold of the sealed-file room along the foot, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed

codex.title: The Weighing Physician's Book, Being Remedies for the Beautiful Return, the Quiet Dream, the Greyed Hand, the Weighing Chill, the Kept Room and the Fever That Cooks, Set Down in the Hearthseat with the Errors Left Standing and a Clay-Yard Woman's Thumb in the Margin
codex.kind: A physician's book of remedies in the soft, ledger-leaning manner of the Keeping, written in Grathic with the verbs thinned almost to Ledgerhand; the cures in a neat physician's hand on the back of a spoiled Weighing notice, the objections of a clay-yard hearth-maid pressed in tallow and slip into the margin, the corrections of a College of Assessors clerk in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a song for the Weighing with a place left where the fifth stroke should stand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in the Hearthseat on the Keel between Ash of Y.H. 812 and Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the Long Cold and the Thin Year, by Senn, a physician of the Weighing Hall who examined the Kept in their rooms at each Weighing and held the hands of the returned on the third day; begun on the back of a Weighing notice spoiled when the ink ran in the damp, on which *one in twelve* is still legible through every remedy, folded into four and carried in the inner pocket of a clean coat. It was never copied at Greybank: the fair copy was taken by the College and lost, and the rough leaf survives in the physician's own room off the Weighing Hall, with the printed figure showing through, a press of tallow and a thumb of clay slip in the margin where a woman from Low Kiln laid her hand, grey Ash off a Kept room's skirting board worked into the gutter, a scorch where a spark off the grating of the Hearth-fire caught the second leaf, a pale clip-ring pressed into the third, objections in the rough hand of the clay-yard woman, six corrections in the upright hand of the College clerk, and the one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own

codex.title: The Sermon at the Well That Never Freezes, Being What Was Said at Cold Acre in the Ninety-Four Days, with the Drawing-Song, the Twelve Links, and the Column Nobody Filled
codex.kind: A well-shrine sermon of the common Grathic telling, preached at Cold Acre two leagues north of Sill over the stone lip and the clay dish; the manner of the drawing in the tally-woman's hand, the sayings in Grathic, the drawing-song with the gap left as it is sung, the column of the slate set down as a table, one correction in the narrow upright hand of an assessor's clerk come up from Greybank, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Preached by Nils of Cold Acre, who has kept the well-rope and the shrine at the stone lip for two and thirty winters, on a morning in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, while the Ilm lay under ice for the ninety-fourth day and the well gave as it gives; written that evening by Kess of Cold Acre, who keeps the barley measure and the seed account for the six houses, in charcoal on a strip of birch bark gone soft at one edge, folded and tied with a spent length of the well-rope and kept in the thatch of her own roof above the beam and out of reach of the frost. It survives with lime worked into the grain at the head, a frost-crisp along the gutter where the bark lay a night under the eaves, a wet ring on the second leaf where a dish of water stood from the first voice to the last, a barley awn shut in the fold, a grey Ash print nobody will own, a tarry fibre of well-rope caught in the tie, one correction in the narrow upright hand of an assessor's clerk come up from Greybank to measure the winter wells, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied once at Greybank in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the empty column left empty.

codex.title: The Wet Carrying, Being the Rack-Song of Low Kiln, Sung Going Up from the Wheel to the Drying Racks
codex.kind: A work song of the carrying in the low speech of the yard; the call set to the pace of the feet and the answer to the set-down, with one verse kept back until the factor's man has gone back over the bridge; written in charcoal thinned with slip, the rubrics of the rack in the same hand, a factor's clerk's correction in Ledgerhand, a gloss from a woman at the tubs, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Set down in Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a woman of House Silt who keeps the drying racks three doors up the Clay Yard from the Vail kiln-house; written on the back of a rack-tally spoiled by a wet thumb while the second firing was being counted, and tied with grey wool to the bracket of the lowest rack under a broken pot turned mouth-down against the rain. Copied forward in Reed of Y.H. 813 onto a strip of oiled paper from the wheel-shed after the flood took the first leaf. It survives with a raw-slip thumb at the head, a green bead of lead-glaze pressed into the lower corner, a barley-water ring through the second verse, a long grey Ash smear along the gutter that nobody will own, a scratch where a rack-hook caught the fold, one line of the song eaten away by rain and not written in again, one correction in the narrow upright hand of the factor's clerk at Greybank, a gloss in the thick charcoal hand of a woman at the tubs, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own

codex.title: The Wheel Song, Being the Throwing-Song of the Women of the Clay Yard at Low Kiln, Sung at the Wheel in the Shed Beside the Slip Brook, with the Draws Counted Going Up, the Round Kept on the Board, a Kiln-Master's Ruling in Broad Charcoal, a Factor's Clerk's Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss from a Woman at the Drying Racks, and One Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A thrower's work song in the low speech of the yard, said to the wheel and not across the shed; the verses counted in draws going up, with the fourth kept as the thumb coming away and the round the pot leaves on the board kept and not entered; the manner of the throwing in the writer's own charcoal, the kiln-master's ruling in broad charcoal, the factor's clerk's figures standing above in Ledgerhand, a gloss pressed into the margin by a woman of the drying racks, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim
codex.provenance: Sung at the wheel in the wheel-shed beside the Slip Brook in Low Kiln of Sill and set down in the last tend of Ember, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, the thirty days when every kiln in Grath fired at once and the whole country smelled of woodsmoke, by a woman who has thrown at that wheel for eleven seasons and centers every lump on the round the last pot left; written in charcoal thinned with slip-water on the back of a potter's tally spoiled by a wet thumb, folded into four and tied with a curl of eel-sinew against the dust, carried north with a consignment of coarse tile and copied at Greybank in Silt of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a factor's voided weigh-slip. It survives with a slip thumb worked into the grain at the head, a pale tideline from the Brook along the gutter that has taken the edge off one word of the fifth verse, a curl of eel-sinew caught across the second leaf, a dry grey flake from the board pressed in the fold, a damp round from a wet pot's foot dried to the colour of the board on the third leaf, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner, a small-ale ring gone sour at the foot, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own, the kiln-master's broad ruling, the clerk's figures standing above, the rack-woman's gloss in the margin, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: The White Hands, Being the Drinking Song of the Stonemouth Quarry, Set Down in the Ale-Room Beside the Lime Kiln
codex.kind: A quarrymen's drinking song in Grathic, called over small ale after the lime draw and never at the quarry face; the words in a housekeeper's small hand, the count as the men keep it, the lift said by the whole room, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk come up from Greybank, a face-man's note in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Set down in Bone of Y.H. 811, the Long Cold, at Stonemouth where the Ferr comes into the Ilm, by the woman who keeps the ale-room beside the lime kiln and takes the men's names for their ale; written in charcoal and lime-dust on the back of a weigh-slip spoiled by wet slate, and copied forward in Bone of Y.H. 812 into a quire of three leaves sewn with eel-sinew. It survives in a cracked pot on the shelf behind the room door: white lime ground into the grain at the head and worked into the creases of the first leaf, a blue-grey streak where a sleeve wet from the Ferr touched the fold, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first question to the last, a thumb of tallow, a lap of sandstone grit in the gutter, a square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, the clerk's correction standing above the words, and a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own.

codex.title: The White Seam, Being the Hopping Rhyme of the Children of Stonemouth Behind the Lime Kiln, with the Counting-Out, the Nine Hops, and What the Weigh-Clerk Set Against It
