codex.kind: A wash-woman's gathering of a children's counting game, set down in charcoal and lime-dust on the back of a spoiled lime-warrant; the counting-out and the hops in the children's own half-sung Stonemouth speech, the manner of the play in the writer's small hand, a correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the weigh-clerk at the landing, a gloss pressed into the margin in charcoal by a dresser of stone who has caught children in this yard for three-and-twenty years, and one line at the foot in the print of a child's white thumb
codex.provenance: Written behind the lime kiln at Stonemouth where the Ferr comes into the Ilm five leagues upriver of Sill, in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a woman who takes in the quarrymen's washing and cannot get the lime out of her own hands; set down on the back of a lime-warrant spoiled by a wetting, carried downriver at the Opening of the Slates in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a voided weigh-slip. Kept folded in the bundle of coat-cuffs she takes home on the cart. It survives with lime worked into the grain at the head, a blue-grey streak in the gutter off a sleeve wet from the Ferr, a small round mark where a two-mark piece was set down to hold the leaf and taken up again, a ring of small ale at the fold, the flat white print of a thumb where the leaf was held in a draught, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which nobody will own, the weigh-clerk's correction standing above the children's words, the stone-dresser's charcoal pressed in beside the second line, and one line at the foot that nobody will claim

codex.title: The Wind in the Clay, Being the Beating-Out Song of the Clay Yard at Low Kiln, Sung Over the Lump Before It Goes to the Wheel, with the Strokes as They Are Counted, the Listening Where No Stroke Falls, a Kiln-Master's Correction in Broad Charcoal, a Factor's Clerk's Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, and One Verse at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A beater's work song in the low Grathic of the yard, said down into the lump and not up into the shed; the verses counted in the cut, the turn and the fall, with the fourth place kept for the flat of the hand; the rubrics of the bench in the same charcoal and tallow hand; a kiln-master's correction in broad charcoal, a factor's clerk's figures standing above in Ledgerhand, a rack-woman's gloss pressed into the margin in thick charcoal, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim
codex.provenance: Set down in Smoke of Y.H. 813, the month of the second firing, by Gella, a woman of Low Kiln who beats the clay at a bench three doors up the Clay Yard from the Vail kiln-house and has done it two-and-twenty years, having begun to feel a hollow in a lump before she cuts it; written in charcoal thinned with slip and tallow on the back of a glaze-house mixing tally spoiled by a fall of slip, folded into four, tied with grey wool and carried in the breast of her apron against a square of sacking gone soft at the seam; copied forward at Greybank onto the back of a weigh-slip gone stiff with salt. It survives with wet slip worked into the grain at the head, brick dust ground into the fold, a wire-nick through the second leaf, a barley-water ring through the third verse, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner, a long hair the colour of wet wool caught in the seam, a small dry flake of a hollow lump pressed flat between the third and fourth leaf, a grey Ash smear along the gutter that nobody will own, the kiln-master's broad correction, the rack-woman's gloss, the clerk's figures standing above, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: The Words That Hold, Being an Extract from the Survey-Roll of the First Seam Concerning the Year 717, the Surveyor Who Set Two Words Against the Oldest Repair, and the Order That Took Him Up the Shaft; with the Layers as the Roll Keeps Them, the Two Translations Set Side by Side, the Song Said at the Mouth, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A surveyor's annal, being an extract from the roll kept in the survey room off the Duelling Floor beneath Keld Keep; the year-entries in the number-first hand, the oldest repairs set down as the seam showed them, the Court's word and the Keldish word standing side by side and neither chosen, the removal order in the upright Ledgerhand of a clerk who was not in the shaft, the mine-reeve's red check entered where it fell, a saying of the shaft mouth, two corrections in borrowed hands, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward
codex.provenance: Written in the survey room off the Duelling Floor in the First Seam beneath Keld Keep in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the keeper of the survey-roll, who signs with the office and not with a name and keeps the verbs in; copied from a roll carried forward in the surveyor's tin and from a rubbing of the crossed entry of Y.H. 588, and carried up at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813. It survives as five leaves of slate-rubbing paper sewn with iron wire and folded into a strip of harness leather gone soft at the stitch: coal smut worked into the grain at the head, slate dust in the gutter, a red point from the mine-reeve's checking-stone at the second corner, a shaving of warm-stone gone cold in the fourth leaf, a frost-feather pressed flat that was gone by noon, a tallow thumb at the foot, a square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with a knife-point and not written back, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a clerk come up from the Hearthseat, one in the round hand of the Warden's hall, and a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the keeper did not make and has not swept

codex.title: The Year Without Contracts, Being an Extract from the Tide-Roll of the Council of Vhal Concerning the Rising at the Glass Furnaces in Y.H. 626, the Suspension of Salt-Paper for a Year, the Hands Sent to the Pulled Benches, and the Articles That Followed; with the Sheets as the Roll Kept Them, the Anneal-Song, the Table of Hands, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A clerk's chronicle-extract from the Council's tide-roll, copied out of the tarred tin under the Council table; the year-entries in the flat scrivener's hand, the figures set above what the furnaces sent down, the hands entered as a round sum with the names beneath in the gutter, the anneal-song taken down at the third furnace, one word struck and written above in the narrow upright hand of the Council, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward
codex.provenance: Written at Vhal in the Council room off the Quay in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the second clerk of the tide-roll, who has kept it through five Councils and signed none of them; copied from the roll begun in Y.H. 599 and kept since in a tarred tin beneath the Council table, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives on Council salt-paper kept dry against the practice of the country, sewn with tarred net-twine into a fold of oiled sailcloth; salt bloom worked into the head that comes and goes with the weather, glass dust from the furnaces in the grain of the second leaf, a thumb of tar at the fold off the council table's rope, a green bead of cliff-glass pressed into the lower corner by a girl who would not give her name, a ring of small ale at the head, a scorched place where the leaf lay near the brazier in the Long Cold, the figure for the sheets struck and written again underneath in the writer's own hand, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward

codex.title: The Years Between, Being an Extract from the Book of the Two Hundred Quiet Years Kept in the Lower Room at Greybank: Of the Making of the Return Compulsory, the Coming of Lead-Glaze Downriver, the Pale Line at the Gum, and the First Survey of the Rim-Seam in Y.H. 260; with the Clean Roll Set Above the Survey Sheet, the Glaze-Women's Song, Two Corrections in Ledgerhand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A copy-roll keeper's extract from the book of the years between, copied out of the Hearthseat annals and set beside a Keld survey sheet gone soft with wet slate, a glaze-women's song taken down at High Kiln, a sentence in a second hand on the back of a slate out of the Old Kiln, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the factor's office, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in the lower room of the bank at Greybank in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the keeper of the copy-roll, who signs with the office and not with a name and keeps the verbs in; copied forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, from a book kept behind the winter tallies since Y.H. 300. It survives as six leaves of thin ruled roll-paper sewn with iron wire into a board cover soft at the fold: iron-gall worked into the creases of a thumb, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower margin by a glaze-woman come up from High Kiln, slate dust in the gutter, a tallow end burnt short against the head, a ring of small ale where the song was taken down, a square of bare paper where a word was scraped away and not written back, a strip of the survey sheet folded over the entry of Y.H. 260 and gone soft at the edge, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the keeper did not make and has not swept, and the line at the foot

codex.title: Twelve and Out, Being the Rope-Game of the Stone Step at Low Kiln, with the Counting-Out for the Two That Hold, the Twelve Passes, the Verse of the Twelfth, a Rope-Mender's Note in the Margin, the Figures a Clerk Set Above, and One Line at the Foot in a Child's Hand
codex.kind: A children's skipping game of the stone step, set down in Grathic on the back of a bucket-tally spoiled where a pail was set down; the counting-out and the twelve passes in the children's own half-sung speech, the manner of the play in the writer's small charcoal hand, a rope-mender's note pressed into the margin, a factor's clerk's figures standing above in the narrow upright Ledgerhand, and a line at the foot in a child's hand that has not come forward
codex.provenance: Written in Reed of Y.H. 813, the reed-cutting month, at the stone step of the Vail kiln-house in Low Kiln of Sill, by a woman who sweeps that step and mends the well-rope when it frays and has learned her letters off a broken tally; written in charcoal thinned with step-dust on the back of a bucket-tally gone soft at the fourth knot, folded once and kept with the coil of cord under the step-stone. Copied forward at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 814 onto the back of a voided weigh-slip. It survives with grey step-dust worked into the grain at the head, a wet ring from the pail that has taken the point off one word of the seventh pass, a frayed knot of grey wool through a hole at the twelfth line which the writer tied and will not untie, a small milk tooth wrapped in a scrap of reed pressed in the fold, a tallow thumb at the second corner, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, the clerk's figures standing above the children's words, the rope-mender's note in the margin, and the line at the foot in a child's hand

codex.title: Twelve and the Dish, Being the Counting Rhyme of the Low Kiln Children, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Turns, and What a Clerk Made of It
codex.kind: A hearth-maid's gathering of a children's hopping game, set down in Grathic on the back of a spoiled Weighing notice; the verses in the children's own half-sung speech, the rules in the hearth-maid's small careful hand, a correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor's clerk borrowed at Greybank, a gloss pressed into the margin by a woman who has kept the birth-slates for nineteen years, and one line at the foot in a child's grey chalk
codex.provenance: Set down at the birth-flower shrine in Low Kiln of Sill in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, of an evening when the yard stood frozen and the children hopped the trodden-ash floor of a kiln-house two doors down the Clay Yard; carried to Greybank in the satchel of a hearth-maid come to have a widow's mark confirmed and copied onto the back of a Weighing notice gone soft at one corner. Kept folded in the shrine's slate-box among the birth-slates that have been answered. It survives with slip worked into the grain at the head, a green bead of lead-glaze in the fold, a tallow thumb at the second corner, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, a tideline where the notice went damp, a twist of grey wool through a hole in the first leaf which the writer will not untie, the clerk's correction standing above the children's words, the birth-slate woman's gloss in the margin, and a line of grey chalk at the foot in a hand that has learned its letters off a slate and will not be claimed

codex.title: What the Cord Keeps, Being the Sayings of the Eel-Folk of the Weir, Gathered in the Trap-House a League Above Sill and Glossed for a Girl Come Up from Low Kiln
codex.kind: A trap-woman's gathering of the proverbs, plank-maxims, eel-counts and river-curses of the Weir, set in Grathic letters on the backs of spoiled trap-tallies because the counts here are tied in cord and a cord will not lie flat on a clerk's table; the sayings in the short wet speech of the weir with the ends let drop into the water, the glosses in the writer's own charcoal, a knot tied in the margin where no Grathic word will come, a factor's clerk's correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a slate-runner's line in the slant of a carried hand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Gathered at the Weir in Ilmen and Silt of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, and written up in the trap-house through the high water by a woman who lifts the baskets at the turn and keeps the leading cord and the count of them in her sleeve; set down first in charcoal on the backs of trap-tallies spoiled by wet hands, carried downriver to Greybank in Grain of Y.H. 813 with a consignment of eels and copied there onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold, where a factor's clerk borrowed the leaves and set his hand above hers. It survives folded into a strip of oiled eel-skin and tied with a loop of grey wool, with river silt dried pale in the grain at the head, eel slime worked into the fold off the leading cord, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, a brine-gull's peck through one word of the song, a glass-eel thread fine as a hair in the lower gutter, a pressed reed across the third leaf, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, the knot standing in the margin, the clerk's narrow correction above the charcoal, the runner's sloping line below it, and the line at the foot which nobody has claimed

codex.title: What the Bowl Washes, Being the Sayings of the Sere Folk Kept in the Factor's House at Greybank and Glossed for a Girl Bought Down from the North
codex.kind: A kitchen-woman's gathering of the proverbs, courtesy-maxims, bowl-counts and small refusals of the southern folk, written in thin gold on the backs of grain-warrants voided by the Long Cold; the sayings in the long open speech with the ends thrown into the fire, the glosses in the writer's own hand in oil and charcoal, the courtesies set in a table, the washing-song left with a line unsung, a Court clerk's correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a northern girl's addition in charcoal at the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Gathered in the southern factor's house at Greybank in Ash and Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by Halia of the Kitchen, a woman of the Bowl of Sere who keeps the scullery and the room where the girls sit before they are sent south; written on the backs of grain-warrants voided by the Long Cold, in gold thinned with oil so that a saying does not last as long as a contract; copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a spoiled weigh-slip, where a clerk of the Court's factor borrowed the leaves and set his narrow hand above hers. It survives with the yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the head, a thumb of olive oil at the fold off the scullery cloth, a wine-ring gone dark at the third hour, a husk of southern grain stuck fast in the gutter, a fish-scale from the Peat Line tribute dried into the second leaf, a green-glazed shard from a northern bowl pressed into the fold, the place where an old name stood rubbed thin with oil and not written over, a grey Ash print nobody will own, and a loop of red wool through the first leaf which the writer will not undo

codex.title: What the Cold Is Full Of, Being the Sayings of the Wastelings, Gathered at the Survey Post Beyond the Cold Pass and Glossed for a Man Who Still Carried a Name
codex.kind: A post-keeper's gathering of the grunts, borrowed Grathic, gift-words, answers and refusals of the Waste, set in Grathic letters on the back of a spoiled rim-seam sheet because Waste Cant is not written and has no hand; the sayings in the few words the country uses, with a blank left where a sound has no word, the glosses in the keeper's own charcoal, a survey-clerk's correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a Keldish tally-man's line cut into the edge with a knife, and one line at the back in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Gathered over nine winters at the survey post in the Cold Pass, ten leagues beyond Keld Keep, in Ash and Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Vek of the Post, a Keldishman who came up with a lime cart in Y.H. 800 and was left to count the men who go through and the men who come back; first set in charcoal on the backs of spoiled survey sheets, then copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a requisition for warm-stone voided by the Long Cold, sewn with wire into a fold of oiled survey-cloth and carried down the Rim Road. It survives with frost raised out of the grain on the first leaf and gone by noon, coal smut at the fold, a flake of warm-stone that kept its heat one night on a stone floor and is cold now, a small grey stone stitched into the lower gutter, a white hair pressed between the third and fourth leaf, the Ash of an uncollected man along the outer fold which leaves no stain, the clerk's narrow correction standing above the keeper's words, the tally-man's line cut into the edge, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward

codex.title: What the Cold Keeps, Being an Account of the Country Beyond the Cold Pass
codex.kind: A quarryman's itinerary and travel account, set down on the back of a spoiled Keldish survey sheet and a strip of birch bark; part road-log, part inventory of what came back, part complaint, with the corrections of a Court survey-clerk in Ledgerhand, a Keldish surveyor's note in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Bone and Ash of Y.H. 811 at Keld Keep, on the Rim Road and beyond the Cold Pass, by Orrel of Stonemouth, a quarryman who went west as a hired guide to a survey party and came back down the Rim Road in Seed of Y.H. 812 with a stone in his pocket, one year gone by the slate and three by his face, and no memory of the debt he went to recover. Copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a discarded tally-roll, sewn with wire into a fold of oiled sailcloth and carried in a tin. It survives with coal dust ground into the head, a smear of hot lead at the fold that has burnt through one word, a crust of white frost along the gutter, a single white hair pressed between the second and third leaves, a small grey stone folded into the gutter, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Court survey-clerk, one note in the broad slow hand of the Keldish surveyor who borrowed the leaves, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.

codex.title: What the Dog Ate, Being a Grave-Guard's Field Notes on the Bone-Hound at the Greybank Burial Grounds
codex.kind: A soldier's field book on one beast, set down as the record of a watch and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on the back of a spoiled granary docket, a digger's song in the words it is sung, the factor's clerk's corrections in Ledgerhand in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written in Bone and Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Watt of Greybank, one of the factor's men paid by the tend to keep the south-bank burial ground; set down at the end of watches in the watch-hut with a tallow end in a pot, first on three dry grain-dockets from the Court's granaries and then on the back of a weigh-slip gone soft at one corner, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a coat pocket. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813. It survives with a grey Ash thumb ground into the head, a brown spot the size of a fingernail where a man's blood fell on the second leaf, a wet boot-print across the foot from a morning crossing the ford, a nick from a billhook at the fore-edge, the charcoal rubbed thin where the leaf was carried, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the factor's clerk, and the one line at the foot

codex.title: The Account Stands, Being the Sayings of the Keeping, Gathered in Slate Row at Sill and Glossed for a Girl Who Has Not Yet Had a Figure Read Over Her
codex.kind: A junior copyist's gathering of the proverbs, table-maxims, deduction-counts and small despairs of the officers of the Warm Court, set down in Ledgerhand on the back of a voided Weighing notice; the sayings in the clean passive with the doer left out, the glosses in the copyist's hand with the doer put back, a Provost's correction above, a Waiting-Room woman's charcoal objection in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
codex.provenance: Gathered in Slate Row at Sill through Ash and Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a junior of the College set to copying the Weighing notices, who writes in the narrow upright hand but has not yet been given a slate-name; written on the back of a notice voided by a figure entered in the wrong column and washed with barley-water, carried down the Clay Road to Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with a bundle of spoiled assessments, where a Provost borrowed the leaves and set his hand above the copyist's. It survives folded once under the loose board beside the notice-post, with a neat black thumb at the head, a barley-water ring gone dark, the round scratch of a tube-case, a corner cut away where a figure stood, grey Ash along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, and the line at the foot which nobody has claimed

codex.title: What the Road Took and the Market Gave, Being a Chapman's Book of Rates for the Ilm Circuit and the Roads Upon It, Copied into No Counting House
codex.kind: A pedlar's pocket-book of prices and road-dues, the board's figure set above the figure actually paid; figures in a rough travelling hand, one column left as a place and not a nought, the verbs put back where a borrowed hand took them out, two corrections in other hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own
codex.provenance: Written on the circuit between Sill, the Weir, Stonemouth, Nine Pots, Mud End and the Standing Post in the Thin Year Y.H. 812, after the Long Cold; carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and written up again in Reed of that year. It is a chapman's book, kept in the inner coat pocket where the pack-strap has worn a place through the leather, and it survives soft at the fore-edge with dried eel slime, grey silt worked into the gutter, a white salt bloom at the head, tar at the fold, a docken leaf pressed flat between two leaves, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a bit gone verdigris in the bottom margin, an Ash thumb at the head, iron-gall in two fingers, a small bare square where a word was scraped away, two corrections in borrowed hands, and one line at the foot nobody will own.

codex.title: What the Weir Keeps, Being a Letter from the Lower Boards below the Sill to a Boat-Sharer's Daughter on the Quay at Vhal, Concerning the Lean Draw, the Buyer Who Counted Twice, a Tally Kept in Bone Where No Clerk Will Read It, and the Tide That Ran Against the Wind; with the Answer in the Margin, a Factor's Clerk's Correction in Ledgerhand, a Sorting Song in a Hand Nobody Will Own, and What the River Left in the Gutter
codex.kind: A private letter cut on the back of a birch-bark sorting tally, written in charcoal and iron-gall, folded thrice and tied with a length of tarred cord; carried down the Ilm to Greybank and over the Salt Road to Vhal in a glass-carrier's coat, answered along the margin in a second hand, corrected on the outer fold at the factor's house, and kept since in a dry tin among the Quay's boat tallies
codex.provenance: Written at the Weir's lower boards, one league upriver of Sill where the Ilm drops four feet over a ledge of hard stone, in the last tend of Silt, Y.H. 813, by Halla, an eel-sorter who has worked those boards for nineteen autumns, to Nivva of the Quay at Vhal, who holds a twelfth of a salt boat through her mother and will not say it before a factor's man. Carried downriver on the ebb and over the Salt Road in a glass-carrier's coat, rained on at the coast pass, answered in the margin, and borrowed at the Court's factor's house at Greybank, where a clerk set a correction on the outer fold in the neat upright Ledgerhand. It survives folded and tarred in a dry tin: grey eel-slime rubbed thin at the folds, river silt worked into the grain at the head, a white bloom of salt along the gutter, a green bead of cliff-glass lodged in the lower corner, a nick from a fish-hook through the second fold, a thumb of tar at the tie, the clerk's correction standing above the words, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody has claimed.

codex.title: Where the Debt Goes Damp, Being the Account of Serric, a Buyer of Glass out of the Bowl of Sere, Who Went Up the Salt Road in the Thin Year with Crowns and Myrrh and Came Back with Green Glass, a Rope That Would Not Rot, and an Offer He Was Glad to Refuse; with the Table of What Was Carried and What Was Left, the Law That Perished in the Damp, the Song of the Salted Boat, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own
codex.kind: A buyer's travel account, set down first in the leaning counting-hand on the backs of spoiled salt-warrants at the Quay in Vhal and copied at Greybank onto the reverse of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold; the road and the figures in the buyer's hand, the coast sayings kept in the hearing and not translated, the verbs put back underneath every borrowed correction, one leaf gone soft where a contract's writing has come up in pale islands, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward
codex.provenance: Written at the Quay in Vhal and again on the Salt Road in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by Serric, a buyer of green glass for a house of the Ten Bowls in the Bowl of Sere, who went up in Ash with three gold crowns, a jar of myrrh and a commission from his house and came down in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with one sheet of Cliff glass, a coil of tarred rope that has lasted two winters, and an offer he did not take. Set down on salt-warrants spoiled in the damp, carried over the coast pass to Greybank and copied onto the back of a voided grain-warrant, then sealed in a tin of Sere wax and brought south. It survives soft at the fore-edge and sour with salt: a white bloom along the gutter, a flake of gold leaf shut in the second fold off a crown rubbed thin at the edge, green glass ground into the head, tar at the thumb, myrrh worked into the grain of the fourth leaf, a square where the paper has gone soft and the writing has risen in pale islands, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with a knife-point, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own
